items.title: Home
items.text:
An Open Python Ecosystem for GNSS-Transmissometry Canopy VOD Retrievals

canVODpy aims to be the central community-driven software suite for deriving canopy Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD) from the signal-to-noise ratio of the same GNSS signal, received at the same time by one receiver below the canopy and one with an unobstructed view of the sky.

Retrieve VOD from your GNSS data Contribute to canVODpy See canVODpy at work in molab

items.title: What makes canVODpy different
items.text:
• One output for every file format

    Reads RINEX v2.11, RINEX v3.04, stripped RINEX v3.05, NMEA v4.00 and Septentrio SBF. Every reader returns the same validated xarray Dataset, so the rest of canVODpy never depends on the file format.

    Reading GNSS files

  • Versioned storage

    Observations and VOD go into Icechunk stores. Every write is a commit that you can list, branch from and tag, like in git.

    Storage

  • No duplicates, no overlaps

    Before it writes, canVODpy skips each file that's already in the store, by its SHA-256 hash. A file whose time span overlaps data of another file already stored stops the run, naming both files.

    Storage

  • Hemispheric grids

    Seven grids divide the sky seen from the receiver into cells, among them equal-area, equal-angle, HEALPix, and geodesic grids. Each observation goes to the cell that contains it.

    Hemispheric grids

  • Parallel by default

    canVODpy reads and processes files in parallel worker processes, and sizes the workers to the machine, or to the limits you set.

    Parallel processing

  • Traceable

    Each release has a DOI. Each store records where its data came from, in metadata that follows DataCite and ACDD, and a STAC catalog describes all stores.

    Store metadata

items.title: Processing pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
    FILES["RINEX, SBF or NMEA files"] --> READ["Read"]
    SETTINGS["Settings<br/>local folder or GitHub link"] --> READ
    OVERLAY["Overlay file<br/>optional"] -.-> SETTINGS
    RECIPE["Naming recipe<br/>optional, local file or GitHub link"] -.-> READ
    READ --> ANGLES["Satellite angles"]
    ORBITS["SP3 orbits"] --> ANGLES
    ANGLES --> GSTORE["GNSS store"]
    GSTORE --> VOD["VOD retrieval"]
    VOD --> VSTORE["VOD store"]
    VSTORE --> PLOT["Hemispheric grids and plots"]

Dashed arrows are optional inputs: an overlay file changes settings for one run (Configuration), and a naming recipe recognizes files with other names (Naming).

For SBF files, the satellite angles can also come from the files themselves (processing.params.ephemeris_source: broadcast). For every step of a run, see What a run does.

items.title: Packages
items.text:
• canvod-readers

    Readers for the GNSS file formats, one output structure.

  • canvod-auxiliary

    Downloads SP3 orbits and CLK clocks and interpolates them to the epochs of the observations.

  • canvod-grids

    Hemispheric grids and the assignment of observations to their cells.

  • canvod-vod

    VOD from the zeroth-order tau-omega model, and the base class for other VOD calculators.

  • canvod-store

    The Icechunk stores for observations and VOD.

  • canvod-viz

    2D polar plots and interactive 3D Plotly plots of the hemisphere.

  • canvod-config

    Reads and validates canvod-settings.yaml.

  • canvod-utils

    Date utilities, diagnostics, and tools the other packages share.

  • canvod-preflight

    The canVOD file name convention: parses and builds canonical names, finds files whose time spans overlap.

  • canvod-ops

    Preprocessing steps applied before VOD, such as temporal aggregation.

  • canvod-store-metadata

    Writes, validates and exports the provenance metadata of a store.

  • canvodpy

    The command line interface, Site.pipeline(), and the factories for readers, grids, and VOD calculators.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: Contributions of all kinds are welcome: bug reports, bug fixes, features, documentation, and feedback. This guide covers the development setup and the contribution workflow. A step-by-step setup for a new machine is in the contributor setup guide.

items.title: Ways to contribute
items.text:
• Report bugs at https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/issues. Include your operating system, Python version, and the steps to reproduce.
  • Fix bugs: issues labeled "bug" and "help wanted" are open for pull requests. Comment on the issue first so nobody duplicates work.
  • Implement features: issues labeled "enhancement" and "help wanted" are open. Keep the scope narrow: one feature per pull request.
  • Improve documentation: docs, docstrings, or external articles. See the development guide.
  • Submit feedback: file feature proposals at https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/issues. Keep the scope narrow and explain the intended behavior.

items.title: Required tools
items.text:
Two tools must be installed before uv sync, which doesn't manage them: the uv package manager and the just command runner.

# macOS
brew install uv just

# Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://just.systems/install.sh \
    | bash -s -- --to ~/.local/bin

# Windows
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
winget install Casey.Just

The repository needs uv 0.13 (required-version in pyproject.toml), so every machine writes uv.lock the same way. Install a 0.13 release if uv refuses to start.

items.title: Contribution workflow
items.text:
# 1. Fork on GitHub, then clone your fork
git clone git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/canvodpy.git
cd canvodpy

# 2. Check the tools, install dependencies and hooks
just check-dev-tools
git submodule update --init --recursive
uv sync
just hooks
just agent-skills   # if you develop with Claude Code: the shared agent workflow

# 3. Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feature/my-feature

# 4. Make changes
# packages/<pkg>/src/canvod/<pkg>/   implementation
# packages/<pkg>/tests/              tests

# 5. Verify
just test && just check

# 6. Commit with Conventional Commits
git add packages/<pkg>/src/... packages/<pkg>/tests/...
git commit -m "feat(readers): add RINEX 4.0 support"

# 7. Push and open a pull request
git push origin feature/my-feature

items.title: Commit message format
items.text:
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

Types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci

Scopes, for example: readers, aux, config, grids, vod, store, viz, utils, naming, orchestrator, diagnostics, ops, ci, docs, deps (the list in [tool.commitizen.customize] of pyproject.toml)

git commit -m "feat(vod): add tau-omega calculator"
git commit -m "fix(readers): handle empty RINEX files"
git commit -m "docs: update installation instructions"
git commit -m "feat(viz)!: redesign 3D plotting API"   # ! = breaking change

See Conventional Commits for the full specification.

items.title: Git hooks
items.text:
just hooks installs Git hooks that run on their own. If a hook before the commit fails, the commit is rejected: your files stay staged, but no commit is created.

Hook When What it does ruff check --fix Before commit Lints Python; fixes what it can (unused imports, style) ruff format Before commit Formats Python code uv-lock Before commit Checks that uv.lock matches all pyproject.toml files trailing-whitespace Before commit Strips trailing whitespace check-added-large-files Before commit Blocks files larger than the size limit detect-private-key Before commit Blocks committed SSH/PGP keys end-of-file-fixer Before commit Ends files with exactly one newline check-agent-docs Before commit Checks that paths and just recipes named in AGENTS.md files and skills exist commitizen After writing the message Checks the type(scope): subject format ty-check Before push Type-checks the code with ty code-graph After commit, merge, checkout Updates the code graph in the background

When a commit is rejected:

  • ruff fixed your code: it changed the files in place. Stage the fixes and commit again: git add -u, then the same git commit.
  • commitizen rejected the message: write it as type(scope): subject, for example fix(readers): handle empty observation epochs.
  • uv-lock is out of date: run uv sync, git add uv.lock, and commit again.

More cases are in the hook troubleshooting.

items.title: Common commands
items.text:
just --list                    # Show all commands
just test                      # Run all tests
just test-coverage             # With coverage report
just test-package canvod-grids # Specific package
just check                     # Lint + format + type-check
just docs                      # Preview documentation
just docs-lint                 # Language check of the docs (Vale)
just docs-lint-changed         # Vale on the pages changed since origin/main
just docs-links                # Link check of the built docs (lychee)

items.title: Continuous integration
items.text:
Every push and pull request runs these checks on GitHub Actions:

  • Python Code Quality: checks that uv.lock is up to date and runs ruff (lint and format) and ty (types). It also builds and imports every package with only its declared dependencies and checks the paths named in AGENTS.md files and skills.
  • Test with coverage: pytest with coverage, uploaded to Coveralls and posted as a comment on the pull request.
  • Platform Tests: the test suite on Linux, Windows, and macOS.
  • Docs Quality: a language check (Vale) of the changed pages and root files, and a link check (lychee) of the built site.

items.title: Pull request guidelines
items.text:
1. just test && just check pass with no errors.
  2. The change follows CODING_STANDARDS.md (rules and per-change checklist); the reasons are in docs/adr/.
  3. Include tests for every new feature: every new public function and method has at least one test, edge cases and error paths (empty inputs, invalid parameters) are covered, and coverage doesn't decrease. Run just test-coverage to see which lines are covered.
  4. Update the Zensical documentation in docs/ with every change of behavior (new logic, new code, changed code), public API, or configuration. A pull request without docs to match is declined. The changed pages must pass Vale (just docs-lint-changed) and the built site the link check (just docs-links); CI runs both.
  5. Target Python 3.14.
  6. Add yourself to CONTRIBUTORS.md if this is your first contribution.

items.title: Licensing
items.text: canVODpy is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. By submitting a pull request, you agree that your contribution is licensed under the same terms. The LICENSE and NOTICE files at the repository root apply to all source files. Per-file license headers aren't required.

items.title: Releasing (maintainers)
items.text:
just release-status                              # commits per package since its last tag
just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0   # tests, versions, release commit on release/v1.1.0

Each package has its own version; the maintainer chooses them, and canvodpy is part of every release. Then open a pull request for the release branch; after it's merged, a maintainer runs just tag-release on main, pushes the tags, and starts the PyPI publish. The full steps are in the release process.

items.title: Free and open source software (FOSS) principles
Overview
items.text: canvodpy is developed as Free and Open Source Software (FOSS) following the principles established by the Free Software Foundation1 and endorsed by the Open Source Initiative.2 This commitment ensures the software remains freely accessible, modifiable, and redistributable, enabling transparent scientific research and fostering collaborative development within the GNSS and atmospheric science communities.

items.title: Free software
items.text:
Free software, as defined by the Free Software Foundation, guarantees users four essential freedoms:1

  1. Freedom to run the program for any purpose
  2. Freedom to study how the program works and change it
  3. Freedom to redistribute copies
  4. Freedom to distribute modified versions

The term "free" refers to liberty (libre), not price (gratis), emphasizing user autonomy over software control.

items.title: Open source software
items.text:
Open source software, as characterized by the Open Source Initiative, emphasizes development methodology and source code availability.2 The Open Source Definition requires:

  • Free redistribution without restrictions
  • Source code availability and modification rights
  • Derived works and modifications permitted
  • No discrimination against persons, groups, or fields of endeavor
  • License distribution without requiring additional agreements
  • Technology neutrality

items.title: Relationship and convergence
items.text: While historically distinguished by philosophical emphasis (free software prioritizing user freedom, open source emphasizing practical benefits), the vast majority of licenses satisfy both definitions.3 Modern practice increasingly treats these as complementary perspectives on the same software licensing paradigm, hence the unified term "FOSS" (Free and Open Source Software) or "FLOSS" (Free/Libre and Open Source Software).

items.title: License: Apache License 2.0
items.text: canvodpy is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0,4 a permissive FOSS license approved by both the Free Software Foundation5 and Open Source Initiative.6

items.title: Key provisions
items.text:
The Apache 2.0 license provides:

  • Permissive use rights: Commercial and non-commercial use without restrictions
  • Modification freedom: Unlimited source code modification and distribution
  • Patent grant: Explicit patent license from contributors to users
  • Trademark protection: Project name and marks remain protected
  • Attribution requirements: Copyright and license notices must be retained
  • No copyleft: Modified versions may use different licenses

items.title: Rationale for selection
items.text:
Apache 2.0 was selected for several reasons relevant to scientific software:

  1. Patent protection: Each contributor grants users a license to the contributor's patents that the contribution uses (section 3)4
  2. Clear terms: Well-documented license reduces legal ambiguity4
  3. Permissive integration: Compatible with most other FOSS licenses, enabling ecosystem integration

items.title: FAIR software principles
items.text:
The FAIR principles, originally developed for research data8, have been adapted for research software9 to enhance:

  • Findability: Persistent identifiers and metadata enable software discovery
  • Accessibility: Open access and clear licenses facilitate software reuse
  • Interoperability: Standards-based design supports integration
  • Reusability: Documentation and licensing enable legitimate reuse

canvodpy implements FAIR software through:

  • GitHub repository with persistent URL
  • Apache 2.0 open source license
  • Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18496233
  • Citation metadata (CITATION.cff, codemeta.json)
  • OpenSSF Best Practices certification
  • Automated FAIR compliance checking

Status: 5/5 FAIR recommendations met

Reference: FAIR Software Compliance Summary

items.title: OpenSSF best practices
items.text:
The Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) Best Practices badge program10 establishes security and quality criteria for FOSS projects. The program promotes:

  • Security awareness: Vulnerability reporting and response procedures
  • Code quality: Static analysis, testing, and code review practices
  • Development transparency: Public version control and issue tracking
  • Release integrity: Signed releases and supply chain security

canvodpy earned the OpenSSF Best Practices badge (passing level) by demonstrating:

  • Security policy with coordinated disclosure (SECURITY.md)
  • Static analysis (ruff, ty) and dynamic testing (pytest)
  • Public development on GitHub with issue tracking
  • Automated security scanning (OpenSSF Scorecard)
  • Reproducible builds with locked dependencies

Badge: OpenSSF Best Practices Project 12329

items.title: OpenSSF best practices badge application guide
Overview
items.text:
The OpenSSF Best Practices Badge (formerly CII Best Practices) is a certification that demonstrates your project follows open source security and quality best practices.

Application URL: https://bestpractices.coreinfrastructure.org/

items.title: Badge levels
items.text:
1. Passing (60%+ criteria) - Basic best practices
  2. Silver (100% passing + additional criteria) - Advanced practices
  3. Gold (100% silver + highest standards) - Exemplary practices

items.title: Step 1: Create account
items.text:
1. Go to https://bestpractices.coreinfrastructure.org/
  2. Sign in with GitHub
  3. Click "Add Project"
  4. Enter: https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy

items.title: Step 2: Complete questionnaire
items.text: The badge requires filling out criteria in these categories:

items.title: Basics (13 criteria)
items.text:
• Project website (https://canvodpy.eu/)
  • Basic documentation (README.md with clear description)
  • FLOSS license (Apache 2.0)
  • Change control (public version control - GitHub)
  • Bug reporting process (GitHub Issues)
  • Security reporting process (SECURITY.md)

items.title: Change control (11 criteria)
items.text:
• Public version control (GitHub)
  • Unique version numbering (semantic versioning)
  • Release notes (CHANGELOG.md)
  • Contributors file (CONTRIBUTORS.md)

items.title: Quality (17 criteria)
items.text:
• Coding standards (ruff, PEP 8)
  • Automated test suite (pytest on Linux, macOS and Windows)
  • Code coverage (test_coverage.yml workflow)
  • Build reproducibility (uv.lock, pinned dependencies)
  • Continuous integration (GitHub Actions, .github/workflows/)

items.title: Security (21 criteria)
items.text:
• Security policy (SECURITY.md) ✨ newly added
  • Vulnerability disclosure process (SECURITY.md)
  • Secure development knowledge (document that developers know secure coding)
  • Static analysis (ruff in code_quality.yml, CodeQL in codeql.yml)
  • Dynamic analysis (pytest, integration tests)
  • Dependency management (uv, Dependabot, pip-audit in dependency_audit.yml)

items.title: Analysis (6 criteria)
items.text:

  • Memory safety language (Python)
  • Address sanitizers (not applicable for Python)

items.title: Release process
items.text:
Maintainers only

This guide is for repository maintainers with push access to the main branch.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Before starting a release:

  • All CI checks passing on main
  • main branch is stable
  • All changes committed and pushed
  • You are a maintainer: main requires a PR (step 4), and only maintainers can create release tags (step 5)
  • The release files (pyproject.toml files, uv.lock, the CHANGELOG.md files, CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json, codemeta.json) have no uncommitted changes; just release refuses otherwise. Other changes in the working tree stay out of the release commit.

items.title: Release types
items.text:
Each package has its own version (Versioning); choose the increment of each package you release:

Type Version Bump Example When to use Patch 1.1.X 1.1.0 \(\rightarrow\) 1.1.1 Bug fixes only, fully backwards compatible Minor 1.X.0 1.1.0 \(\rightarrow\) 1.2.0 New features, backwards compatible Major X.0.0 1.4.0 \(\rightarrow\) 2.0.0 Breaking changes; requires an upgrade guide (Upgrading to v1.0.0 is the one for v1.0.0), linked from the README, the docs landing page, the changelog, and the release notes

canvodpy is part of every release, and its increment is at least the largest of the packages released with it.

To test a release first, publish it as a pre-release (1.0.0a1, 1.0.0b1, 1.0.0rc1); Versioning explains the stages and when to choose which. The steps below are the same.

The Development Status classifier in every pyproject.toml follows the release: 4 - Beta for a pre-release, 5 - Production/Stable for a stable release. The first stable release (1.0.0) changes it from 4 - Beta to 5 - Production/Stable in all packages, in a pull request before step 1; PyPI shows the classifier of each release.

items.title: 1. Prepare
items.text:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
just test && just check

items.title: 2. Choose the packages and versions
items.text:
just release-status

For each package: its version, its last release tag, and the commits since that tag that touched the package's folder. Release a package when its commits matter to its users, at the increment they call for.

items.title: 3. Create the release
items.text:
just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvod-grids=1.0.1 canvodpy=1.1.0

This command:

  1. Runs all tests (just test)
  2. Refuses the release, and says why, when canvodpy is missing, a version does not go up or is tagged already, canvodpy's increment is smaller than a package's, a package's range on another excludes the new version (or the current version of a package left out of the release), a citation file lacks its version or date field, a release file has uncommitted changes, or the branch release/v1.1.0 exists already (locally, or on the remote as of your last git fetch)
  3. Writes the new versions, canvodpy's == pins, a section in each released package's CHANGELOG.md (from the commits that touched its folder; canvodpy's lists the pinned versions), canvodpy's version and today's date in CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json and codemeta.json (Zenodo takes the version of the archived record from them), and uv.lock
  4. Creates the branch release/v1.1.0 (canvodpy's version) and commits exactly the release files: bump: canvodpy 1.1.0 (canvod-store 1.1.0, canvod-grids 1.0.1)

It creates no tag: the tags belong on the merged commit on main (step 6).

items.title: 4. Review
items.text:
git show --stat     # the version files, uv.lock and CHANGELOG.md files, nothing else

The changelog sections are generated from commit subjects; edit them in the release branch if a line needs it.

items.title: 5. Open a PR for the release commit
items.text:
main requires a PR. Push the branch and open one:

git push -u origin release/v1.1.0
gh pr create --title "bump: canvodpy 1.1.0 (canvod-store 1.1.0, canvod-grids 1.0.1)" --body "..."

Merge the PR once CI passes.

items.title: 6. Tag the merged commit
items.text:
A merge can give the release a different commit than the one on the branch, so the tags are created only now, on main:

git switch main
git pull origin main
just tag-release
git push origin v1.1.0
git push origin canvod-store-v1.1.0 canvod-grids-v1.0.1

just tag-release creates an annotated tag for every package version that has no tag yet, and prints the push commands; it does not push.

Push the canvodpy tag on its own, before the package tags. GitHub starts no workflow for tags when more than three tags are pushed at once, so a canvodpy tag pushed together with the package tags gets no draft release. The package tags start no workflow, so they can go in one push, however many there are.

items.title: 7. Publish the draft release
items.text:
The .github/workflows/release.yml workflow detects the canvodpy tag (v1.1.0) and creates a draft release whose notes are canvodpy's CHANGELOG.md section, including the package versions. Package tags get no GitHub release of their own. Review and publish at github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/releases.

Pushing the tags does not publish to PyPI: tagging and PyPI publishing are deliberately decoupled (see step 8).

items.title: 8. Publish to PyPI (separate, manual, whenever you decide)
items.text:
Not automatic. Trigger publish_pypi.yml on the canvodpy tag, either from the Actions tab (the Run workflow button; choose the tag) or:

gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref v1.1.0

It first checks the locked dependencies against known vulnerabilities (just audit) and stops if it finds one. Then it builds and uploads exactly the packages whose release tag points at that commit (scripts/release.py tagged), here canvodpy, canvod-store and canvod-grids. You can create several releases before ever running this: a tag existing is not a promise that PyPI has it.

items.title: 9. Post-release
items.text:
• Monitor issues for regressions
  • Check the Zenodo record the release created: its version must be canvodpy's (Zenodo Setup)

items.title: Troubleshooting
Supported Versions
items.text:
Security fixes go into the latest 1.x release of each package. Releases before 1.0.0 get no fixes; upgrade with the upgrading guide.

Version Supported 1.x.x < 1.0.0

items.title: Reporting a Vulnerability
items.text: We take the security of canvodpy seriously. If you discover a security vulnerability, please follow these steps:

items.title: 1. Do Not Open a Public Issue
items.text: Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions, or pull requests.

items.title: 2. Report Privately
items.text:
Report security vulnerabilities via one of these methods:

Preferred: Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: - Go to https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/security/advisories - Click "Report a vulnerability" - Fill in the details

Alternative: Email the maintainer directly: - Email: support@canvodpy.eu - Include "SECURITY" in the subject line - Provide a detailed description of the vulnerability

items.title: 3. What to Include
items.text:
Please include as much of the following information as possible:

  • Type of vulnerability (e.g., buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting)
  • Full paths of source file(s) related to the vulnerability
  • Location of the affected source code (tag/branch/commit or direct URL)
  • Any special configuration required to reproduce the issue
  • Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
  • Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
  • Impact of the issue, including how an attacker might exploit it

items.title: 4. Response Timeline
items.text: canvodpy is a small, community-maintained project. We aim to respond and confirm reports as promptly as we can, and prioritize fixes by severity, but we do not guarantee specific response or fix timelines.

items.title: 5. Disclosure Process
items.text:
1. We will confirm receipt of your vulnerability report
  2. We will investigate and validate the vulnerability
  3. We will develop and test a fix
  4. We will release a security advisory and patched version
  5. We will credit you in the advisory (unless you prefer to remain anonymous)

items.title: Data Handling
items.text:
• Do not process untrusted GNSS data files without validation
  • Be cautious when reading RINEX or SBF files from untrusted sources
  • Validate input file paths to prevent directory traversal attacks

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Keep canvodpy and its dependencies up to date
  • Monitor security advisories:
  • GitHub Dependabot alerts
  • PyPI security notifications
  • uv audit in your project, which checks the locked dependencies against known vulnerabilities (experimental in uv)

  • pip-audit, run through uv, which does the same check:

    uv export --format requirements-txt --no-emit-workspace -o requirements.txt
uvx pip-audit --disable-pip -r requirements.txt

items.title: Credential Management
items.text:
• Never commit credentials to version control
  • Use environment variables or secure credential stores for:
  • API tokens and other service credentials
  • Ephemeris download credentials (if applicable)
  • Database connection strings

items.title: Secure Configuration
items.text:
• Follow the principle of least privilege for file system access
  • Use read-only mounts for input data directories where possible
  • Validate configuration files before use

items.title: 1. File Format Parsers
items.text: canvodpy parses binary formats (SBF, RINEX). While we use robust parsing libraries: - Risk: Maliciously crafted files could potentially cause crashes or unexpected behavior - Mitigation: Always validate input files from untrusted sources

items.title: 2. Dependency Chain
items.text: canvodpy depends on scientific Python packages (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, Zarr): - Risk: Vulnerabilities in dependencies could affect canvodpy - Mitigation: We monitor Dependabot alerts and update dependencies regularly

items.title: 3. Code Execution
items.text: canvodpy loads Python configuration files: - Risk: Configuration files can execute arbitrary Python code - Mitigation: Only load configuration from trusted sources

items.title: Current Implementation
items.text:
• ✅ OpenSSF Best Practices Badge (Passing level) - Project 12329
  • ✅ Automated dependency scanning (Dependabot)
  • ✅ OpenSSF Scorecard monitoring
  • ✅ SPDX license compliance (REUSE 3.3)
  • ✅ Pinned dependencies in uv.lock
  • ✅ Pre-commit hooks (ruff linting & formatting, ty type checking, conventional commits)
  • ✅ Continuous integration (GitHub Actions: tests, coverage, code quality, CodeQL, FAIR checks)
  • ✅ Static analysis (ruff, CodeQL)
  • ✅ Type checking (ty, in the pre-push hook and in CI)
  • ✅ Dynamic analysis (pytest test suite with coverage tracking)
  • ✅ Input validation framework for GNSS data files

items.title: Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
items.text:
We follow the principles of Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure:

  1. Researchers report vulnerabilities privately
  2. We work with researchers to understand and fix the issue
  3. We coordinate a public disclosure timeline
  4. Credit is given to researchers (unless anonymous preferred)

We commit to: - Responding promptly to vulnerability reports - Keeping researchers informed of our progress - Not taking legal action against researchers who follow this policy

items.text:
We would like to thank the following individuals for responsibly disclosing security issues:

(None yet - be the first!)

items.text:
For security-related questions or concerns: - Maintainer: Nicolas François Bader - Email: support@canvodpy.eu - Affiliation: Climate and Environmental Remote Sensing (CLIMERS), TU Wien

For general questions (non-security), please use: - GitHub Discussions: https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/discussions - GitHub Issues: https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/issues

items.title: Versioning strategy
items.text: Each canVODpy package has its own version (ADR 0010). A package used on its own (for example canvod-readers) changes its version only when its code changes. The umbrella package canvodpy pins every package to an exact version, so a canvodpy version names exactly the mix of packages it installs.

items.title: Why a version per package, and one umbrella?
items.text:
• Reusable packages

    A tool that needs only canvod-readers depends on canvod-readers, and its version says what changed in the readers, not elsewhere.

  • Scientific reproducibility

    uv add canvodpy==1.1.0 installs exactly the mix of packages that was tested together, so one version is enough to cite in a paper.

items.title: Semantic versioning
items.text:
Following Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, for each package on its own:

Increment Trigger Example MAJOR Breaking API changes 1.4.2 \(\rightarrow\) 2.0.0 MINOR New features, backwards compatible 1.1.0 \(\rightarrow\) 1.2.0 PATCH Bug fixes, backwards compatible 1.1.0 \(\rightarrow\) 1.1.1

Versions are written as Python writes them (PEP 440).

canvodpy's increment is at least the largest increment of the packages released with it: a minor release of canvod-store comes with at least a minor release of canvodpy.

items.title: Pre-releases
items.text:
Before a final version, a package can be released as a test version. PEP 440 defines three kinds, marked by a suffix, and sorts them before the final version:

1.0.0a1 \(<\) 1.0.0b1 \(<\) 1.0.0rc1 \(<\) 1.0.0

Stage Suffix What it says Choose it when Alpha a Incomplete Planned features are still missing Beta b Nearly complete, may still change The planned features are in, but behavior or interfaces can still change before the final version Release candidate rc The final version, unless a bug turns up Only fixes remain Final none Released A release candidate needed no further fix
  • Each stage counts from 1 (1.0.0b1, 1.0.0b2, …), and the next stage starts again at 1 (1.0.0b2, then 1.0.0rc1). A stage may be skipped.
  • A pre-release of canvodpy pins pre-releases of the packages it releases, with the same suffix: canvodpy 1.0.0b1 pins canvod-store 1.0.0b1.
  • uv and pip skip pre-releases unless asked for one: by its exact version (uv add canvodpy==1.0.0b1), or with --prerelease allow (uv) or --pre (pip). canvodpy's exact pins then bring every package at its pre-release. A notebook or script that installs canVODpy packages next to canvodpy pins each of them too: a package that nothing pins to its pre-release is installed at its last final version.
  • Tags carry the suffix (v1.0.0b1, canvod-store-v1.0.0b1), and the draft GitHub release is marked as a pre-release. Publishing to PyPI stays a separate step, as for a final version (Releasing).

items.title: Choosing a version
items.text:
For each package in a release:

  1. Choose the increment from the changes since the package's last final version (Semantic Versioning): major, minor or patch.
  2. Choose the stage (Pre-releases): a pre-release while the release is still being tested, the final version once it holds.
  3. canvodpy takes at least the largest increment of the packages, and the same stage.

items.title: Requirements between packages
items.text:
• canvodpy requires each package at exactly one version (canvod-store==1.1.0): its pins are the log of which mix a canvodpy version is.
  • A package requires another canVODpy package with a range up to the next major version (canvod-config>=1.0.0,<2). The lower bound is the version that has what the package uses; raise it by hand when the package starts to use something newer.
  • A major release of a package (for example canvod-config 2.0.0) is outside the ranges of the packages that require it: the release is refused until each of them is checked against the new version and its range widened by hand.
  • __version__ of each package is read from the installed package (importlib.metadata), never written into the code.

items.title: Tags
items.text:
Package Tag GitHub release canvodpy vX.Y.Z (for example v1.1.0) yes, drafted from CHANGELOG.md any other package <package>-vX.Y.Z (for example canvod-store-v1.1.0) no

Every package has its own CHANGELOG.md in its folder; canvodpy's is the one at the repository root, and each of its sections lists the package versions it pins.

Before per-package versions (up to 0.4.0), all packages shared one version and the tag vX.Y.Z.

items.title: Creating releases
items.text:
The maintainer chooses the packages and versions; Releasing has the steps.

just release-status                               # commits per package since its last tag
just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0    # prepare the release commit
just tag-release                                  # on the merged commit on main

items.title: Deprecation policy
items.text: Superseded public code is deprecated with the deprecated decorator of canvod-utils and removed only with the next major version (ADR 0005). The documentation describes only the code to use: guides and examples leave deprecated code out, and the API reference hides everything that carries the decorator, and every argument named by its companion deprecated_argument (scripts/griffe_hide_deprecated.py).

items.title: Citation
items.text:
@software{canvodpy2026,
  author  = {Bader, Nicolas and Contributors},
  title   = {canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis},
  version = {1.0.0},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy},
  doi     = {10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX}
}

"Analysis was performed using canvodpy v1.0.0 (Bader et al., 2026)."

Cite the canvodpy version: it fixes the version of every package.

Release Process Conventional Commits

items.title: Architecture
items.text: This page describes how canVODpy is built: the packages, the layers they form, and the path your files take through a processing run. Design principles explains the rules behind these choices.

items.title: Packages and layers
items.text:
canVODpy consists of eleven packages and the canvodpy package, which brings them together. Each package has its own pyproject.toml and can be installed on its own. The packages form six layers, and a package depends only on packages in its own layer or in the layers below it.

Layer Packages What they do Orchestration canvodpy The canvodpy command, Site and Site.pipeline(), the processing run, VOD computation for a site (VodComputer), and the tasks for Airflow Presentation canvod-viz Hemisphere plots in 2D and 3D Persistence canvod-store, canvod-store-metadata The Icechunk stores and their log books; the description of a store, with field names that follow DataCite, ACDD, and STAC; the STAC catalog and releases of all stores under a data root Computation canvod-vod, canvod-grids, canvod-ops VOD retrieval, hemisphere grids and the assignment of observations to their cells, and the optional preprocessing Data input canvod-readers, canvod-auxiliary, canvod-preflight Readers for RINEX 2 and 3, SBF, and NMEA; orbits and clocks, and the angles of each satellite seen from the receiver; the canVOD file name convention Foundation canvod-config, canvod-utils The settings and how they're loaded; dates, file hashes, the deprecation decorators, the plugin loader, and the run identifier

The arrows point from a package to the packages it declares as dependencies. canvodpy depends on all eleven and isn't drawn, nor is a dependency that another path already implies.

graph TD
    subgraph PRESENTATION["Presentation"]
        VIZ["canvod-viz"]
    end
    subgraph PERSISTENCE["Persistence"]
        STORE_METADATA["canvod-store-metadata"]
        STORE["canvod-store"]
    end
    subgraph COMPUTATION["Computation"]
        VOD["canvod-vod"]
        GRIDS["canvod-grids"]
        OPS["canvod-ops"]
    end
    subgraph DATA_INPUT["Data input"]
        READERS["canvod-readers"]
        AUXILIARY["canvod-auxiliary"]
        PREFLIGHT["canvod-preflight"]
    end
    subgraph FOUNDATION["Foundation"]
        UTILS["canvod-utils"]
        CONFIG["canvod-config"]
    end

    VIZ --> GRIDS
    STORE_METADATA --> CONFIG
    STORE --> AUXILIARY & GRIDS & STORE_METADATA & VOD
    VOD --> UTILS
    GRIDS --> UTILS
    OPS --> CONFIG & GRIDS
    READERS --> CONFIG
    AUXILIARY --> READERS
    PREFLIGHT --> UTILS
    CONFIG --> UTILS

Package dependencies lists the same dependencies, how many packages each one depends on and is depended on by, and what each package needs when you install it on its own. Optional packages, for example the Airflow integration, live in a separate repository; see Optional extensions.

items.title: One repository, many packages
items.text:
All packages live in one repository, under packages/, and share the namespace canvod:

from canvod.readers import Rnxv3Obs
from canvod.grids import create_hemigrid
from canvod.vod import TauOmegaZerothOrder
from canvod.store import open_gnss_store

Namespace packages explains how separate packages share one namespace.

The repository is a uv workspace. One uv sync installs every package in editable mode, from one lock file, so all packages are developed and tested against the same versions of their dependencies. Each package is published to PyPI on its own, all of them except canvod-preflight so far, so you can install only the parts you need:

uv add canvod-readers   # the readers only
uv add canvodpy         # everything

items.title: What a run does
items.text:
canvodpy run, Site.pipeline().run(), and the Airflow task process_day all run the same code. A run has two phases: the GNSS phase (steps 2 to 7) stores the observations of a unit of days, then the VOD phase (step 8) computes the VOD of those days. A phase is a stage of the run, not the GNSS carrier phase. process_day runs the GNSS phase only; the Airflow DAG computes VOD in its own task.

flowchart TD
    OVERLAY["Overlay file<br/>--config, optional"] -.-> SETTINGS
    RECIPE["Naming recipe<br/>canvod-filemap, optional,<br/>local file or GitHub link"] -.-> FIND
    SETTINGS["Settings<br/>canvod-settings.yaml,<br/>local folder or GitHub link"] --> FIND
    FIND["Find and check the files<br/>of every receiver"] --> PREP
    PREP["Prepare each day<br/>orbits, clocks, receiver positions"] --> READ
    READ["Read the files<br/>in parallel worker processes"] --> ANGLES
    ANGLES["Add the angles<br/>theta and phi of each satellite"] --> PRE
    PRE["Preprocessing<br/>only if set"] --> WRITE
    WRITE["Write to the GNSS store<br/>after the duplicate checks"] --> VODSTEP
    VODSTEP["Compute VOD<br/>and write it to the VOD store"]

Dashed arrows are optional inputs.

  1. Read the settings. canvod-settings.yaml is checked against the settings models of canvod-config. An unknown key or a wrong value stops the run with a message that names it. An overlay file (--config) adds or changes settings for one run without editing the file. See Configuration.
  2. Find and check the files. The run finds the files of every receiver in any folder layout. It recognizes them by their canVOD file names or through a naming recipe. It stops before it reads anything if two files have the same canVOD file name, if files overlap in time, or if one folder holds the files of more than one receiver. The reader comes from reader_format in the settings of the receiver, or is detected from the files.
  3. Prepare each day. For each day, the run gets the satellite orbits (SP3) and, if aux_data.fetch_clock is true, the satellite clocks (CLK), and interpolates them onto the epochs of the day: orbits with cubic Hermite splines, clocks piecewise linearly. Without a NASA Earthdata account in the settings, the files come from ESA; with one, from NASA CDDIS first and from ESA if that fails. For SBF files, the setting ephemeris_source: broadcast uses the satellite angles that the receiver recorded in the files instead, and skips the download.
  4. Read the files. Each file becomes an xarray.Dataset with the dimensions epoch and sid. The files of a unit of days are read in parallel, one task per group of files that share an epoch chunk.
  5. Add the angles. From the satellite positions and the receiver position, the run computes the polar angle theta and the azimuth phi of each observation.
  6. Preprocessing. Only if processing.preprocessing is set: temporal aggregation and assignment of each observation to its grid cell. The stores' log books record the preprocessing, and a store group never mixes data that was preprocessed differently. See canvod-ops.
  7. Write to the GNSS store. The run checks each file against the store and against the other files of the unit, and then writes what is new. See Design principles.
  8. Compute VOD. After a unit of days is committed, one task per VOD analysis and day reads that day of the canopy and the reference receiver from the GNSS store, keeps the epochs and signals both have, and computes VOD with the selected calculator. The GNSS phase reads nothing back for it. The zeroth-order tau-omega calculator computes the transmissivity T from the difference of the two SNR values in decibels, and VOD = -ln(T) cos(theta). The results of the unit go to the VOD store in one commit, which checks them before it writes. A day that failed in the GNSS phase gets no VOD. See canvod-vod.

items.title: Parallel work
items.text:
• Units of days. A run works in units of days: as many days as the memory budget holds, at most 31, sized by the run itself. A run of one new day, as in live operation, is a unit of one day.
  • Preparing. Each day of a unit is prepared in its own thread, while the unit before is read.
  • Reading. The files are read in a pool of worker processes (loky), which stays up from one unit to the next. --workers, or the resource settings, set the number of workers.
  • Writing. Only one process commits. In a store made of day blocks, it first adds the blocks of the unit's days in one commit, before any file is read. Then the worker processes write the files into their slots, each worker into its own fork of the unit's session, and one writer thread merges the forks of all receivers and days of the unit and commits them with the log-book rows, once per unit. If another run committed in between, the unit is planned and written again. A day that fails (no orbit products yet, or a file that can't be read) fails alone; the other days of the unit are stored. Files that share a chunk go to one worker task. A store written by appending, by versions before day blocks, is refused until canvodpy store migrate-layout moves it. On a file system, Icechunk can't detect two commits at the same time, so every commit takes the store's commit lock. A commit from another process waits for it (see How a run writes).
  • VOD. After a unit is written, its VOD is computed in the same worker processes, one task per analysis and day, each writing into its own fork of the VOD store; the main process commits the unit's VOD once. Meanwhile the units run on in a thread of their own, one unit ahead at most, so the workers read the next unit during the VOD.

See Parallel processing for the settings.

items.title: Entry points
items.text:
Entry point Use it to canvodpy run --site ... Process a period from the command line Site(name).pipeline() Process a period from Python, with the same code canvodpy.workflows.tasks (check_day, process_day) Run single days from a scheduler such as Airflow

Command line and Python lists the options.

items.title: Build system
items.text: canVODpy uses uv_build as its build backend: a modern, fast backend from the Astral ecosystem with native namespace package support.

items.title: Distribution formats
items.text:
Wheel (preferred)Source Distribution

Pre-built, installed by copying to site-packages. No build step at install time.

canvod_readers-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
└── canvod/
    └── readers/          ← namespace package (no canvod/__init__.py)
        ├── __init__.py
        └── base.py

Filename anatomy: {name}-{version}-{python}-{abi}-{platform}.whl. The py3-none-any suffix means: any Python 3, no native extensions, any platform.

canvod_readers-0.1.0.tar.gz: contains source code + metadata. Requires a build step during installation. Provided alongside wheels for PyPI.

items.title: Build configuration
items.text:
# packages/canvod-readers/pyproject.toml
[build-system]
requires      = ["uv_build>=0.13.0,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = "canvod.readers"       # dot → namespace package
include     = ["src/canvod/readers/data/*.dat"]
exclude     = ["src/canvod/readers/tests/"]

items.title: Building
items.text:
# Single package
cd packages/canvod-readers
uv build
# → dist/canvod_readers-0.1.0.tar.gz
# → dist/canvod_readers-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

# All packages at once
just dist

items.title: Publishing
items.text:
Production PyPIAutomated (CI/CD) 
uv build
uv publish

just release prepares the release commit for the packages the maintainer chose; a maintainer tags the merged commit and starts the PyPI publish of the packages tagged there. See Release process for the full release workflow.

items.title: Version management
items.text:
Each package has its own version, following Semantic Versioning; canvodpy pins every package exactly (Versioning). The maintainer chooses the versions:

just release-status                               # commits per package since its last tag
just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0    # versions, pins, changelogs, uv.lock

just release updates version of each released package, canvodpy's pins, the CHANGELOG.md files and uv.lock, and commits them on a release branch; it makes no tag (just tag-release on the merged commit).

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
ModuleNotFoundError after install

Verify module-name in pyproject.toml uses dotted notation: 

module-name = "canvod.readers"    # correct
# module-name = "canvod_readers"  # wrong: creates regular package

Wrong package structure in wheel

Run unzip -l dist/*.whl to inspect contents. The wheel must contain canvod/readers/ but not canvod/__init__.py.

Build failures

uv build --verbose    # detailed diagnostics

items.title: Package dependencies
items.text:
canVODpy is split into packages, and each package is in one layer. A package depends only on packages of its own layer or of a lower one. This page shows the dependencies between the packages, how many packages each one depends on, and what each package needs when you install it on its own. For what each layer does, see Architecture.

The page lists the dependencies that each pyproject.toml declares under [project] dependencies. Optional packages, such as canvod-filemap from canvodpy-extensions, aren't part of it.

items.title: Dependency graph
items.text:
An arrow points from a package to a package it depends on. To keep the graph readable, it leaves out canvodpy, which depends on all eleven other packages, and every dependency that another path already implies: for example, canvod-store also depends on canvod-utils, which it reaches through canvod-store-metadata and canvod-config. The tables below list every declared dependency.

graph TD
    subgraph PRESENTATION["Presentation"]
        VIZ["canvod-viz"]
    end
    subgraph PERSISTENCE["Persistence"]
        STORE_METADATA["canvod-store-metadata"]
        STORE["canvod-store"]
    end
    subgraph COMPUTATION["Computation"]
        VOD["canvod-vod"]
        GRIDS["canvod-grids"]
        OPS["canvod-ops"]
    end
    subgraph DATA_INPUT["Data input"]
        READERS["canvod-readers"]
        AUXILIARY["canvod-auxiliary"]
        PREFLIGHT["canvod-preflight"]
    end
    subgraph FOUNDATION["Foundation"]
        UTILS["canvod-utils"]
        CONFIG["canvod-config"]
    end

    VIZ --> GRIDS
    STORE_METADATA --> CONFIG
    STORE --> AUXILIARY & GRIDS & STORE_METADATA & VOD
    VOD --> UTILS
    GRIDS --> UTILS
    OPS --> CONFIG & GRIDS
    READERS --> CONFIG
    AUXILIARY --> READERS
    PREFLIGHT --> UTILS
    CONFIG --> UTILS

items.title: Coupling
items.text:
12 packages, 32 dependencies between them.

Layer Package Depends on (Ce) Depended on by (Ca) Instability Foundation canvod-utils 0 9 0.00 Foundation canvod-config 1 6 0.14 Data input canvod-readers 2 3 0.40 Data input canvod-auxiliary 3 2 0.60 Data input canvod-preflight 1 1 0.50 Computation canvod-vod 1 2 0.33 Computation canvod-grids 1 4 0.20 Computation canvod-ops 2 1 0.67 Persistence canvod-store-metadata 2 2 0.50 Persistence canvod-store 7 1 0.88 Presentation canvod-viz 1 1 0.50 Orchestration canvodpy 11 0 1.00
  • Ce: the number of packages that this package depends on.
  • Ca: the number of packages that depend on this package.
  • Instability: Ce / (Ce + Ca). A package with 0 depends on no other package; a package with 1 has no package that depends on it.

canvod-utils and canvod-config have the most dependents (Ca = 9 and 6): a change there affects the most packages.

items.title: Checks
items.text:
• just check-package-imports installs each package with only its declared dependencies and imports every module, so a dependency that a package uses but doesn't declare fails in CI.
  • just deps-report prints the tables on this page, and just deps-mermaid prints the graph. Both read the pyproject.toml files and fail if a package depends on a package of a higher layer, or if a package has no layer in scripts/analyze_dependencies.py.

items.title: canVODpy
items.text: canVODpy computes vegetation optical depth from GNSS signals received below a forest canopy and in the open, and keeps the data and results in versioned stores. These are the words the project uses; use them in code, docs, issues and messages.

items.title: Science
items.text:
GNSS-T (GNSS transmissometry): Estimating how much vegetation weakens satellite navigation signals, by comparing the same signal received below the canopy and in the open. Avoid: GNSS-IR, GNSS reflectometry (different methods)

VOD (vegetation optical depth): The attenuation of a microwave signal by vegetation along its path, normalized to a vertical path; it tracks vegetation water content and biomass. Avoid: optical depth, tau (alone)

Transmissivity: The fraction of a signal's power that passes through the canopy: the canopy signal strength relative to the reference signal strength. Avoid: transmittance

SNR: The signal strength the receiver reports for a signal, in dB-Hz; the observable VOD is computed from. Avoid: C/N0, CN0, signal power

Polar angle: The angle between the zenith and the direction to a satellite, seen from the receiver (0 overhead, 90 degrees at the horizon). Avoid: zenith angle, elevation (its complement)

Azimuth: The direction to a satellite in the horizontal plane, clockwise from north.

Signal ID (SID): One signal of one satellite: satellite, frequency band and tracking code, e.g. G01|L1|C. Avoid: signal, channel, observable

Epoch: The time of an observation, always GPS time. Avoid: timestamp, time step

Ephemeris: The orbit (and clock) of the satellites, from agency products or from the receiver's broadcast navigation data; gives each epoch's polar angle and azimuth. Avoid: aux data, orbit file (for the data itself)

Hemisphere grid: A division of the sky seen from the receiver into cells, used to aggregate observations and VOD by direction. Avoid: sky map, mesh

items.title: Sites and receivers
items.text:
Site: A place with at least one canopy receiver and one reference receiver, processed together into one GNSS store and one VOD store. Avoid: station, location

Canopy receiver: A receiver below the vegetation. Avoid: forest receiver, below-canopy receiver

Reference receiver: A receiver with an open view of the sky near the canopy receiver. Avoid: sky receiver, open-sky receiver, clear-sky receiver

VOD analysis: One pairing of a canopy receiver with a reference receiver for which VOD is computed. Avoid: pair, combination

Receiver-day: One receiver's files of one GPS day; the smallest piece of a run that succeeds or fails on its own. Avoid: day file

Unit of days: The days a run writes together and commits once to the store. The run sizes it from its memory budget, at most 31 days; a run of one new day is a unit of one day. A day in a unit still fails alone. Avoid: batch, wave

items.title: Files
items.text:
Raw archive: Where a site's receiver files are kept before canvodpy reads them; the source every store is rebuilt from. Its files may have been prepared on the way (compressed, renamed, reduced to some observables), but are not yet read by canvodpy. Avoid: input folder, data share

Completeness: The share of the files a receiver-day should have, by its cadence and file length, that are in the raw archive. Avoid: coverage, availability

canVOD file name: The file name convention that states a file's receiver identity, start time, length, sampling and type, e.g. ROSA01TUW_R_20250010000_15M_05S_AA.rnx. Avoid: canonical name (in user-facing text), standard name

Receiver identity: The first nine characters of a canVOD file name: site, receiver role, receiver number and agency. Avoid: station ID, marker name

File type: The TYPE field at the end of a canVOD file name, naming the file's format (e.g. rnx, sbf). Avoid: extension

Naming recipe: A description of how a receiver's own file names translate to canVOD file names, for files not named by the convention. Avoid: name mapping, pattern

File index: The names of the files a run found in each folder of a receiver directory, kept so a run need not list folders that hold none of the days it processes. Avoid: file cache, file list

Reader format: The setting that tells a run which reader reads a receiver's files. Avoid: file format (for the setting)

Test data: The full set of receiver and auxiliary files the tests run on. Avoid: demo data

Setting profile: A named settings folder that a reference run uses on the test data. Avoid: test config, fixture settings

Reference store: A GNSS or VOD store built from the test data with a setting profile, which new code must reproduce within the comparison tolerances. Avoid: golden store, baseline store

Demo data: The small, published set of files the demo notebooks work with: part of one day of the test data, plus reference stores built from it. Avoid: test data, example data, sample data

items.title: Processing and storage
items.text:
Run: One processing of a site's receiver-days, started from the command line, Python or a scheduler such as Airflow; all behave the same. Avoid: job, pipeline execution

Run history: The record canvodpy keeps on one machine of every run: its settings, progress, timings, machine and problems. Avoid: journal, run log, database

Preprocessing: Optional changes to the observations before they are stored (temporal aggregation, grid assignment), applied only when the settings ask for them. Avoid: filtering, cleaning

Store: An Icechunk repository holding one kind of a site's data: a GNSS store, a VOD store, or a store of an extension (geodesy, rollup, statistics). Avoid: repo, database

Store name: The name of a store's folder: its kind (gnss, vod, geodesy), or the kind, - and a suffix for a second store of that kind (vod-recompute). The store id is the site name and the store name. Avoid: store directory name, rinex (the GNSS store's name before v1.0.0)

GNSS store: A site's versioned store of the observations of all its receivers. Avoid: RINEX store, observation store

VOD store: A site's versioned store of the VOD of all its VOD analyses.

Derived store: A store computed from other stores (VOD, geodesy, rollup, statistics); it can be rebuilt from them. Avoid: secondary store, product store

Geodesy store: A site's versioned store of the geodetic products computed from its GNSS data (reflector height, multipath).

Rollup store: A site's store of VOD summed per hemisphere cell and time bin, from which the aggregate over any time window is computed quickly. Avoid: cube, rolled store, summary store

Rollup level: The length of a rollup store's time bins (hour, day, week).

Statistics store: A site's store of running statistics per hemisphere cell and signal, updated with each new day without reading the history again. Avoid: accumulator store

Group: One receiver's data (in the GNSS store) or one VOD analysis's results (in the VOD store). Avoid: table, dataset (for the stored unit)

Log book: The record a store keeps of what was written to each group: source files, their hashes, and the preprocessing applied. Avoid: metadata table, registry

Day block: The part of a group that holds one receiver-day (or one day of a VOD analysis): every possible epoch of that day at its cadence, with or without data, padded with empty epochs to whole chunks. Avoid: day chunk, partition

Cadence: The time between the epochs a day block holds: the sampling interval of the day's files, or the aggregation interval when aggregation is set. Avoid: resolution, frequency

Snapshot: One committed state of a store, which can be read again later. Avoid: version (for a store state), checkpoint

Provisional branch: A branch of a store that holds the most recent days processed with a quicker orbit product than the store's own, until those days are processed again with the store's product; the main branch never holds them. Avoid: rapid branch, test branch

Repository metadata (Icechunk's term): The description of a store that belongs to no snapshot and no branch: who made it, what it holds, where, under which license. Some of its fields never change; the others change only by amendment. Avoid: global attributes, store identity

Commit metadata (Icechunk's term): What one commit records about how it was made: software versions, environment and settings of the run that wrote it. Avoid: history, provenance (the log books hold provenance)

Snapshot summary: The description of what one snapshot holds (time coverage, receivers, counts), written in the same commit as the data it describes. Avoid: statistics, store state

Fixed field: A field of the repository metadata that never changes once the store exists, such as its id or creation date. Avoid: immutable field

Content settings: The settings that shape a store's data, such as the signals kept, the preprocessing, the orbit product and the chunking: set by whoever creates the store, fixed with it, and the same for every run that writes to it. Avoid: fingerprint, store config

Amendable field: A field of the repository metadata that changes only by amendment, such as the creator's email or the license.

Amendment: A recorded change to an amendable field: old and new value, reason, who and when. Avoid: edit, update (for repository metadata)

Metadata rule: A rule a standard sets for a metadata field, such as the license being an SPDX identifier. New metadata that breaks one is refused; a store that already breaks one still opens, with a warning, until an amendment fixes the field, or, for a value computed from the data, the next commit. Avoid: constraint, policy

Catalog: The STAC description of all stores under one data root, kept beside them: one item per store, grouped into GNSS observations and VOD. Avoid: inventory, index

Release: A named, fixed state of all stores under a data root: a tag in each store plus a catalog that pins each store's snapshot. Avoid: version (for a store state), export

Plugin: An installed package that adds a reader or a VOD calculator to runs. Avoid: extension (canvodpy-extensions are separate packages)
