items.title: What's new in v1.0.0
items.text:
Upgrading from 0.x?

Stores written with canVODpy 0.x must be migrated before a v1.0.0 run writes to them. Upgrading to v1.0.0 has the commands, the changed settings and what is deprecated.

  • A complete command line

    • canvodpy run, vod and vod-reconcile process data and compute VOD
    • canvodpy config creates, checks, shows and explains the settings
    • canvodpy store lists, inspects, maintains, migrates and amends stores
    • canvodpy stac, doctor and dashboard

    Command line

  • Runs

    • One site per run; --update-to-latest for scheduled runs
    • A memory budget sizes the workers and the units of days a run commits at once; the next unit is read while VOD is computed
    • Each file's day comes from its name, in any folder layout
    • Warnings about files a run doesn't process and incomplete receiver-days
    • Airflow tasks run the same code as canvodpy run

    Command line and Python

  • Stores

    • Day blocks: processing a day again writes only into that day's slots; no other day is touched
    • Content settings fixed when a store is created; runs with other settings are refused
    • Compare two stores within fixed tolerances
    • Migrate the stores of a 0.x site with one command
    • Stores on S3 (experimental)

    Storage

  • Metadata and catalogs

    • Store metadata after DataCite and ACDD, checked against the standards
    • A STAC catalog of all stores; releases tag every store
    • Amend a store's description, with a reason
    • record_machine: false keeps the computer out of published stores

    Store metadata

  • Settings

    • Settings and naming recipes from a GitHub link
    • canvodpy config init --from-store writes the settings of a store
    • canvodpy config validate also checks the receiver data
    • canvodpy config explain says what a setting means
    • Preprocessing is applied when set, and recorded in the store

    Configuration

  • Run history and dashboard

    • Every run records itself, its stage timings and its resource use
    • A dashboard shows each run, the sites, and compares runs

    Diagnostics

  • Extending canVODpy

    • Your own readers and VOD calculators, from installed packages
    • Interactive hemisphere selectors for notebooks
    • A public mapping between RINEX observation codes and signal IDs

    Plugins

  • Demo data

    • canvodpy.demo_data() downloads the demo day, or its stores, checked by sha256
    • Notebooks that run in the browser

    Notebooks

The full list is in Upgrading to v1.0.0 and the changelog.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
Each page records one decision about canVODpy that is hard to reverse, would surprise a reader of the code, and was a real choice between alternatives: what was decided and why. Read the ones about your change before you start; if your change contradicts one, say so in the issue or pull request rather than working around it.

New decisions are added while a change is designed (/mattpocock-skills:grill-with-docs, see Developing with coding agents), numbered in order. A decision that is reversed is not deleted: it gets a status that names the decision replacing it.

Decision 0001 Data live in versioned Icechunk stores: one GNSS store and one VOD store per site 0002 All stored epochs are GPS time 0003 The canopy and the reference receiver record the same file format 0004 Explicit over implicit: fail loudly, no hidden defaults 0005 Superseded public code is deprecated, and removed only with the next major version 0006 Preprocessing runs only when the settings ask for it 0007 What was done to stored data is recorded in the stores' log books 0008 Runs find files by their names, in any folder layout 0009 Readers and VOD calculators from other packages are plugins 0010 Each package has its own version; canvodpy pins the exact mix 0011 Only free tools 0012 Contributors develop with agents through one shared workflow 0013 Agents open pull requests; people merge 0014 A store's description lives in its repository metadata; each snapshot carries a checked copy 0015 The STAC catalog sits beside the stores; a release is a tag in each store plus a pinned catalog 0016 Each receiver-day is a day block at its own cadence; workers write forks, one commit per day 0017 The demo notebooks use only the public interface and fetch demo data by file type from Hugging Face 0018 Every run records itself in a run history, one SQLite file per machine 0019 One set of content settings per store, set by its creator; several runs may write one store 0020 A run lists the folders of the days it processes 0021 A run works in units of days, keeps its stores' state in memory, and computes VOD in a phase of its own (proposed) 0022 canvodpy stores no secrets; credentials come from the environment (proposed)

items.title: Data live in versioned Icechunk stores: one GNSS store and one VOD store per site
items.text: Every write to a store is a commit in an Icechunk repository, so any earlier state of the data can be read again, and a dataset can be cited by its snapshot. A site has one GNSS store (all its receivers' observations) and one VOD store (all its VOD analyses), not one store per receiver or per day, so a network of sites is a short list of stores to find and query.

items.title: All stored epochs are GPS time
items.text: RINEX observation files, SBF and the orbit and clock products are GPS time natively, receivers sample on whole GPS seconds and files are named by GPS day. Storing UTC would move epochs 18 s off the sampling grid and across day boundaries. Readers convert other scales on read (NMEA from UTC) and record the scale; a RINEX file that declares another time scale is refused, and so is an append to a store written without a recorded time scale.

items.title: Consequences
items.text: The leap second table ends at the last announced IERS Bulletin C and raises after it; extend it with each new bulletin.

items.title: The canopy and the reference receiver record the same file format
items.text: A site's canopy and reference receivers are always the same kind of receiver writing the same format (both SBF, or both RINEX). Mixed setups are not supported: loading such settings fails with an error, instead of a run that silently reads one receiver with the other's reader.

items.title: Explicit over implicit: fail loudly, no hidden defaults
items.text: canvodpy's users are scientists who must be able to trust that a result was computed the way they asked. A missing or wrong input stops with a message that says what to do; nothing falls back silently. A default in a signature or a documented settings model is visible and fine. Library code reading the settings file behind the caller's back, or an except that substitutes a value, is not: entry points (the command-line tool, Site) read the settings and pass them down.

items.title: Superseded public code is deprecated, and removed only with the next major version
items.text: v1.0.0 has one way to do each job, but users of earlier versions must not break without warning. Code that a better path replaces gets the deprecated decorator of canvod-utils: it warns with a FutureWarning (shown by default, unlike DeprecationWarning), says it is left over from development, names the replacement, and is removed in v2.0.0. Code that does not belong in canvodpy at all is removed outright when the maintainers decide so. The optional packages of canvodpy-extensions delete leftover code instead of deprecating it.

items.title: Preprocessing runs only when the settings ask for it
items.text: Preprocessing (temporal aggregation, grid assignment) changes the stored data, so it is never a default. When the settings file sets it, every run applies it, whichever entry point starts the run (command line, Python, Airflow), so a store never mixes data processed in different ways.

items.title: What was done to stored data is recorded in the stores' log books, not in dataset attributes
items.text: Each store keeps a log book of what was written: the source files, their hashes, and an ordered record of the preprocessing steps (operation, settings, result) with the versions of the packages whose code ran. Stored data carry no provenance attributes, so processed and unprocessed data have the same shape. A write whose preprocessing settings differ from what the store already holds is refused, and VOD is computed only from canopy and reference data processed the same way.

items.title: Runs find files by their names, in any folder layout
items.text: A file's canVOD name carries its receiver identity and start time, so a run scans each receiver's folder recursively, in any layout, and groups files by the date in their names. Files with other names need a naming recipe (canvod-filemap), which is then the truth for their identity; having canvod-filemap installed never changes discovery by itself. Each receiver needs its own folder, no two receivers may share an identity, and two files that map to the same name, or overlap in time, stop the run.

items.title: Considered options
items.text: An identity setting that would let one folder hold several receivers was rejected: sorting the data is the user's job, and an extra setting that can be wrong is a hidden source of mixed-up data.

items.title: Readers and VOD calculators from other packages are plugins, registered through entry points
items.text: A package adds a reader or a VOD calculator to canvodpy run by declaring an entry point (canvodpy.readers, canvodpy.vod_calculators); the entry point's name is the name in the settings and on the command line. Plugins must inherit the abstract base class, and are imported and checked when canvodpy is imported, so a broken plugin fails at once with its package's name instead of in the middle of a run. A name that clashes with a built-in or another plugin is an error, and reader_format: auto never picks a plugin.

items.title: Considered options
items.text: Registering classes in Python code (ReaderFactory.register) still works inside one Python session, but cannot reach canvodpy run, which starts its own process.

items.title: Each package has its own version; canvodpy pins the exact mix
items.text:
The packages (readers, auxiliary, grids, store, and others) are useful on their own, so each gets its own version and release tags <package>-vX.Y.Z. The canvodpy umbrella package pins every package to an exact version, so a canvodpy version names exactly the mix of code it runs.

How releases work (scripts/release.py, Versioning):

  • The maintainer chooses which packages to release and their versions by hand; no tool derives them from commit messages. just release-status lists the commits per package since its last tag to help.
  • canvodpy is part of every release, and its increment is at least the largest increment of the packages released with it (a minor release of canvod-store makes at least a minor release of canvodpy).
  • A package requires another canVODpy package with a range up to the next major version (canvod-config>=1.0.0,<2). A release that leaves such a range is refused until the range is checked and widened by hand.
  • canvodpy keeps the tags vX.Y.Z; only these create a GitHub release (and a Zenodo archive), whose notes list the package versions.
  • PyPI receives the packages whose release tag points at the published commit.

items.title: Only free tools
items.text: canvodpy is maintained by scientists, often without a budget for software. Building, testing, the docs and the agent tooling must not need a paid service or an API key. A tool that can call a paid service (for example graphify's language-model commands) is used only through just recipes that run its free, local commands.

items.title: Contributors develop with agents through one shared workflow: the mattpocock-skills plugin
items.text: Most contributors are scientists who develop with coding agents. A fixed workflow raises the quality of what they build: an interview before any code, recorded decisions and terms, tests first, and a review against the coding standards and the request. canVODpy adopts the open source mattpocock/skills (MIT) for this. .claude/settings.json declares its author's GitHub marketplace and enables the plugin; just agent-skills installs or updates it. Its configuration for canVODpy lives in docs/agents/, the decisions in docs/adr/, the terms in GLOSSARY.md, the rules it reviews against in CODING_STANDARDS.md.

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Copying the skills into the repository would pin them and allow editing, but every contributor would carry a fork that no longer follows its author's fixes. canVODpy-specific steps stay in canVODpy's own files and skills instead.
  • The official Claude marketplace lists the same plugin, but lags behind its releases (in October 2026 it served 1.2.3, which still named the glossary CONTEXT.md).

items.title: Agents open pull requests; people merge
items.text:
Every change reaches main through a pull request. An agent may push its feature branch and open the pull request; it never merges or approves one, never pushes main or a tag, never force-pushes, and never bypasses a check (--no-verify, skipped hooks, changed protection or settings). A person reviews every change, merges it and is responsible for it. The rules are in CODING_STANDARDS.md (Git and GitHub) and hold for every contributor's agent.

They are enforced in two places. On GitHub, a ruleset on main requires a pull request and passing checks, and only maintainers can create, move or delete release tags (v*); this is the only boundary that holds for every tool. For Claude Code, .claude/settings.json adds deny rules and a hook, scripts/agent_git_guard.py, that blocks the forbidden commands before they run, also in modes that skip permission prompts.

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Letting agents merge once the checks pass would be faster, but the checks cannot tell whether a change is scientifically right; a person has to have looked at it.
  • Forbidding agents to push at all would leave "an agent opens the pull request" impossible, since GitHub needs the branch first.
  • Local settings alone cannot be enforced: a developer can edit or turn off anything on their own machine. They catch the agent's mistakes; the GitHub ruleset is what holds.

items.title: A store's description lives in its repository metadata; each snapshot carries a checked copy
items.text:
A store's metadata has three parts, each kept where Icechunk keeps that kind of information:

  • Repository metadata (Icechunk's repository-level metadata, on no branch and in no snapshot) is the source of truth for what describes the store as a whole: identity, creator, publisher and license, site and position, receivers or VOD analyses, references. It is written once, by the call that creates the store. Its fixed fields (id, UUID, store type, source format, naming authority, creation date) never change. The id is {site}-{gnss|vod|geodesy}, from the site name made lowercase and checked; the UUID is generated when the store is created; the naming authority (reverse DNS) is required then (ADR 0015), and so are a description of the site's stores (set per site), the publisher (DataCite) and the license (STAC). Its amendable fields change only by amendment: one explicit command (canvodpy store amend, or amend_metadata in Python) that needs a reason and records the old and new value, the reason, who and when.
  • The snapshot summary (time coverage, per-receiver counts, ranges and position, constellations, variables, size) describes what one snapshot holds. It is computed when data is written and stored in the root group in the same commit, so it cannot disagree with the data. A commit that writes no data rows (the day-block grow) carries the previous snapshot's summary, checked against a recompute by test.
  • Commit metadata (Icechunk's per-commit metadata) records how a commit was made: software versions, environment, the settings and their hash, and the hash of the uv.lock in use. The text of uv.lock and pyproject.toml is stored once per distinct hash, in the group environments inside the reserved group canvod, in a commit of its own before the first commit that uses it (ADR 0019).

The root group carries a lossless copy of the repository metadata in standard form (flat CF and ACDD global attributes, featureType = "timeSeries", zarr_conventions for cf, proj:, license, uom and stac, whose stac:link points to the store's item in the catalog, ADR 0015), with the fields that have no standard name under the canvod: prefix, plus the snapshot summary. Every commit goes through one commit function that generates this copy from the current repository metadata and refuses the commit if the copy differs. Each snapshot therefore shows its store as it was when it was committed, also after an amendment, on every branch, and to every tool that reads only the Zarr metadata of the root group.

A run that writes a receiver (GNSS store) or a VOD analysis (VOD store) not listed in the repository metadata is refused; the error names the amend command that adds it. A failed metadata write fails the commit and the run (ADR 0004), with a message that says how to fix it. Existing stores are moved to this form by one explicit command; a store not yet moved is refused with a message naming that command. Snapshots from before the move keep the old single canvod_metadata attribute and are read as such until v2.0.0. The run history is read from the commit log; the stored summaries.history is deprecated (ADR 0005).

Amended 2026-10-19 (#456). The id is {site}-{store folder}. A store's folder is named by its kind (gnss, vod, geodesy), optionally with a suffix for a second store of that kind (vod-recompute), so two stores of one site never share an id. A default store keeps the id it had ({site}-gnss, {site}-vod). Since the id is fixed, a store whose folder no longer matches its id is refused for writing.

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Root group attributes only, as before. They are part of every snapshot, so each branch carries its own copy, nothing stops a later write from changing the store's identity, and checking against the first snapshot fails once old snapshots expire.
  • Repository metadata only. xarray, compliance-checker, zarr-cm and the Zarr STAC convention read only the Zarr metadata of the root group, so the standard forms would be invisible.
  • Never changeable. Typos happen, and new publications with their DOI appear; with no recorded way to change them, people would edit stores by hand. Icechunk cannot make repository metadata immutable anyway (it can be replaced); canVODpy refuses changes and Icechunk's operations log keeps a backup of every change.
  • Snapshot summary computed on read. Always current, but every read scans the coordinates of every group, and standard tools see nothing.
  • The lockfile text in the metadata of every commit. About 160 KB compressed per commit, read with every snapshot; stored once per hash, the hash of each commit points to text that its own snapshot holds.
  • Reading both the old and the new form until v2.0.0 for whole stores. Two readers for one job, and a store's state would depend on which one ran; one explicit migration keeps a single form.

items.title: The STAC catalog sits beside the stores; a release is a tag in each store plus a pinned catalog
items.text:
All stores under one data root (the stores_root_dir of the settings) are described by one static STAC catalog, written as JSON files at that root: beside the stores, never inside a store. The catalog has three collections, gnss-observations, vod and gnss-geodesy (the stores of a geodesy extension), with one item per store. An item has the site as its point geometry, the time range of the store, and one asset per stored dataset (a receiver's observations, its SBF metadata, its log book; a VOD analysis and its log book). Every asset points at the store and says which group to open. All links and href values are relative, so the same files work on a local disk and on S3, and the whole data root can be copied or moved.

The catalog is derived: it is written only on request (write_catalog in Python, --write-catalog on a run, or the catalog command), and each write replaces the previous one, rebuilt from every store. If any store cannot be read, nothing is written and one error lists every such store (ADR 0004). Links go from the catalog to the stores; a store records no catalog location except one fixed, relative stac:link to where its own item is.

A store has two identifiers, both fixed fields (ADR 0014): a readable id {site}-{gnss|vod|geodesy}, which with the required naming authority gives a network-unique item id such as org.middle-earth.fangorn-vod, and a UUID generated when the store is created. The UUID is in the item, so opening a store from an item can refuse a store that was replaced behind the same path.

Amended 2026-10-19 (#456). The readable id is {site}-{store folder} (ADR 0014). A site may have a second store of a kind (vod-recompute); it is a second item in that kind's collection.

A release is an Icechunk tag with the same name in every store plus one catalog under releases/<tag>/ that pins each store's tag and snapshot id. Tags never move, so a release catalog stays valid as long as its tags exist, and it is never rewritten. The catalog written without a release describes main as it was at writing time and records the snapshot ids too. A release covers every store under the data root; releasing part of the data is issue #200.

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• The catalog inside each store (a STAC collection file in the store directory, as before). An Icechunk repository directory is not a place for other files, nothing links the stores of a network, and a release of several stores has nowhere to live.
  • The catalog in a separate place, with absolute href values. The catalog would need to know every store's location and each store every catalog's location; moving the data breaks it. Absolute URLs for a copy published elsewhere can be added later as an option.
  • A STAC API. A server to run and keep alive; a static catalog is read by pystac, STAC Browser and xpystac and can be loaded into an API later.
  • One collection per site. Sites differ in receivers, not in what they produce; grouping by product (observations, VOD) is what users search by, and a related link joins a site's two items.
  • One asset per store. A receiver group holds several datasets (observations, SBF metadata, log book) with different dimensions; one asset could not describe them.
  • Writing the catalog after every run. A run would fail or slow down because of another site's store; writing on request keeps runs independent.
  • A release as a catalog only, pinning snapshot ids. Snapshots expire with maintenance; a tag keeps the released state readable.
  • Readable id only, or UUID only. A readable id can come back for a new store at the same path; a UUID alone means nothing to a reader.

items.title: Each receiver-day is a day block at its own cadence; workers write forks, one commit per day
items.text:
A group's epoch axis is made of day blocks: one block per receiver-day (one per VOD analysis and day in the VOD store), covering the whole day at that day's cadence. The cadence comes from the sampling interval in the canVOD file names (or the aggregation interval, when aggregation is set), so a block's length and each file's place in it are known before any file is read. A day with files of different sampling takes the finest interval. Blocks are added at the end of the axis in the order days are first written; a day is found by its epoch coordinate, and loading puts the blocks in time order. There is no origin and no setting. A day that has a block reuses it, so writing a file again writes the same region and no duplicates arise.

Slots without data hold the standard missing value, set as both the Zarr fill_value and the CF _FillValue (NaN for floats, a declared value for integers). The epoch coordinate never has missing values: a slot with data holds the epoch's real time, an empty slot its grid time (00:00 plus a multiple of the cadence). An epoch goes to the nearest slot; nothing is interpolated or moved, and a file with two epochs in one slot is refused (ADR 0004). Loading returns every slot; drop_empty=True drops slots where every SNR is missing. Coverage and counts count epochs with data, never the length of the axis.

The epoch chunk stays at 180 epochs: one 15-minute file at 5 s. A day has ceil(86400 s / cadence) slots, and its block is padded to whole chunks, so days never share a chunk and every cadence is stored. Padding epochs are the last nanoseconds before the next day, hold missing values, and are dropped on load. Because a block's length no longer gives its cadence, the group keeps a block index in its attributes (day_block_index: start, stop, slots and cadence per day).

Amended 2026-10-16 (#376). The first version refused every cadence that does not divide 86400 s / 180 = 480 s, so that a day held whole chunks without padding. Existing users store such cadences (for example 15 min after aggregation), so blocks are padded instead.

A run grows the axis once per batch, in one small commit, only for the days whose ephemerides are ready, so days that cannot be processed never get a block. Workers read a file and write its region into a fork of one session. Two forks must never write the same chunk: Icechunk merges forks chunk by chunk, so the fork merged last replaces a shared chunk whole and the other's data in it are lost without an error (measured). The files whose names put them into one chunk therefore go to one task, with aggregation or without (six 15-minute files at 30 s share a chunk of 180 epochs); with preprocessing set, a time bin can span two files, so one task writes all files of a receiver-day. A file whose epochs reach beyond its task's chunks is written by the writer thread. The writer thread, not the loop that collects results, merges the forks of all receivers of a day and commits once per store and day, with the day's log-book rows (also of skipped files) and its snapshot summary, built from the numbers each worker returns. The first write of a new group, which creates it, is one session in the main process. Phase 1 of the next day and VOD of the previous day overlap with reading. commit_lock makes commits of other runs on the same machine wait; a growth commit that loses a conflict retries. A day whose commit loses a conflict is planned again on the new tip, against its log book, and its tasks run again; a commit is tried up to five times, with a growing, partly random wait in between. If the day or the growth loses every try, the run records the receiver-days as failed with the error and goes on with the next days. Several machines write one store only on S3 (ADR 0019).

Amended 2026-10-18 (ADR 0021, proposed). A run commits once per unit of days, not once per day, and computes VOD in a phase of its own; the day blocks and the forks that own whole chunks stay as described here.

Memory is a budget (max_memory_gb, in auto the available memory): the run sizes its workers and days_per_batch to fit it and fails at the start if one file alone does not fit. There is no hard limit; no portable one exists.

Existing stores are moved to this layout by one explicit command, canvodpy store migrate-layout, after migrate-metadata; a store not yet moved is refused with a message naming it. The migration (#279) takes each day's cadence from its data, the finest step between its epochs rounded to 1 ms, keeps the entry written last of an epoch stored twice, keeps the groups' attributes and metadata, fills the log book's epochs column and commits once; groups of day blocks written without a block index get it. The temporal-overlap check, deduplication on read and the overwrite branch are not needed for day blocks and are deprecated (ADR 0005). Several runs on different machines write one store on S3 (ADR 0019); this layout needs no change for them, since different days are different chunks.

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Keep appending, write only the receivers of a day in parallel. No layout change, but the files of one receiver stay serial in the main process (about 3 s per receiver-day); the gain stops at the number of receivers.
  • Appends in workers. Two appends to one group both resize the array; the second commit fails (measured).
  • A fixed origin for the axis (first day processed, or a setting). An origin needs refusing or rewriting earlier days, or a setting to get right; the time order only matters when loading.
  • One cadence per group, with aggregation to the sampling interval by default. A receiver that moves from 1 s to 5 s would be stored padded at 1 s, and aggregation would run when nobody asked for it.
  • Snapping epochs to the grid within a tolerance. It moves observation times, which changes the data.
  • One chunk per day. Zarr has one chunk size per array, so days of different cadence could not share a group, and one task would write a whole receiver-day. Its old drawback (each append rewrote the growing chunk, about 48 times the disk) is gone with day blocks.
  • Growing the axis for the whole run at once. A run usually stops before its last days because their orbit products are not out yet, which would leave empty blocks.
  • One commit per receiver-day, or per batch. Per receiver-day keeps today's commit count, which slows the store over time; per batch loses more work when one day fails.
  • Dropping empty slots on every load. Matches the old behavior but scans SNR on every read.

items.title: The demo notebooks use only the public interface and fetch demo data by file type from Hugging Face
items.text:
The canvodpy-demo notebooks are tutorials first and a showcase second: they must run, and they use only what canvodpy offers its users. They run, in this order of priority, inside a clone of canvodpy-demo, as a single downloaded file (uvx marimo edit --sandbox <file or URL>, also in VS Code or a container), and on molab. A notebook therefore imports nothing that sits next to it: none of the helper modules of the canvodpy-demo repository (paths, downloads, live store, widgets). The only file it may reference is its style sheet: marimo reads it from a local path only, so a notebook run as a single file runs without it.

Their input is demo data: a small, published subset of the test data (one day of RINEX 3.04 for both receivers of the Rosalia site, SBF from 00:00 to 02:00; no NMEA until a notebook needs it). canvodpy.demo_data() downloads only the kind of data asked for (kind: RINEX, SBF, auxiliary files), checks each against a sha256 written into canvodpy, unpacks it, caches it in the OS cache folder (canvodpy folder in it, one folder per data version), and returns the root of that folder, laid out like the test data, so settings written in code can point at it. Once cached, a notebook needs no network. It downloads with the download code of canvod-auxiliary, not a second copy of it.

The demo data sits in one public Hugging Face dataset, nfb2021/canvodpy-demo-data, uploaded and versioned by hand by the maintainers, with the same license as the test data. demo_data() names one commit of it, so the files can't change under a released canvodpy. It holds:

  1. demo input data, one zip per file type and receiver;
  2. the auxiliary data of the demo day (SP3 and CLK files and the processed Zarr store), marked as possibly out of date;
  3. reference stores: one GNSS store per input file type and one VOD store each, for tests, development, comparison, and showcasing.

The demo data must download fast: a user trying canvodpy waits for it. The dataset serves 13 to 26 MB/s (measured 2026-10-14), so all five zips (353 MB) take about 20 seconds; SBF stays at two hours for the same reason. The demo data is a subset of the test data, which is archived on Zenodo (all versions), and just demo-archives rebuilds the zips from it byte for byte, so the dataset needs no archive of its own.

SP3 and CLK files are always fetched from the agencies (ESA without an account, NASA CDDIS when an Earthdata email is set); the auxiliary zip is only the fallback, used by demo_data() and never by the pipeline. The notebooks show which source the files came from, and compute the auxiliary data themselves so users see that step. A notebook that needs a store writes its settings in code and runs Site(...).pipeline(); the store goes into the cache, not a temporary folder.

The dataset is published with the first release that uses it (rehearsal 1.0.0b1). Until canvodpy is on PyPI the notebooks pin it through git; then each canvod-* package is pinned to the released version.
path: The demo notebooks use only the public interface and fetch demo data by file type from Hugging Face

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• The test-data archive (Zenodo record 19708760). The GitHub integration archives the whole canvodpy-test-data repository as one 1.69 GB zip; every notebook downloaded and unpacked all of it to read a few files, and SBF alone is 2.3 GB of it.
  • Zenodo records for the demo data. Two were published on 2026-10-14 and dropped the same day: Zenodo served 0.07 to 1.4 MB/s, so the auxiliary zip took 18 minutes (7 seconds from Hugging Face), and a second DOI for a subset of archived test data only confused.
  • Hugging Face and Zenodo together (Hugging Face first, Zenodo as fallback): two uploads and two hashes to keep in step for every data version.
  • Raw files instead of zips on Hugging Face. Easy to browse, and per hour, but demo_data() would send hundreds of requests per call, and Hugging Face limits anonymous ones.
  • GitHub release assets or raw files from the test-data repository. Free and per file, but no DOI, and git refuses files over 100 MB.
  • Helper modules next to the notebooks. They work inside a clone only; a single file opened from a URL cannot import its neighbors, and a tutorial would teach calls users cannot make.
  • A ready-made store instead of running the pipeline. Hides the step the tutorial is about; the reference stores are offered in addition, not instead.
  • A cloud drive or object store opened from the notebook (molab's remote storage, fsspec). Google Drive needs every reader to log in; a public bucket needs a host and has no DOI; molab's file panel helps only the lowest-priority way of running.
  • The OS temp folder for the cache. Cleared at reboot or after a few days, so the data would download again; the cache folder also leaves no trace in a sandbox or container that is thrown away.
  • Zenodo as a source for the pipeline. It holds one demo day only.
path: The demo notebooks use only the public interface and fetch demo data by file type from Hugging Face

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• New public function canvodpy.demo_data(); the hemisphere selectors in demo/_widgets move to canvod-viz as canvod.viz.widgets with anywidget as an optional extra.
  • A new data version means a new commit of the Hugging Face dataset and the new commit and checksums in canvodpy, in one pull request.
  • Building the reference stores is part of the v1.0.0 release work.
path: The demo notebooks use only the public interface and fetch demo data by file type from Hugging Face

items.title: Every run records itself in a run history, one SQLite file per machine
items.text:
A run records what it does in the run history: one SQLite file per machine, in the log folder (processing.logging.log_dir), opened in WAL mode. A run writes its start (settings, canvodpy version and commit, machine facts, worker count, an optional free-text label), the receiver-days it plans, its progress per receiver-day, the time of each stage, samples of CPU, memory and free disk, its warnings and errors, and its end and result. Every entry point writes it the same way, because canvodpy writes it, not the command line, Python, or a scheduler around it. Rows are kept; nothing rotates them away.

The run dashboard (canvodpy dashboard) reads only the run history. The paper benchmark reads it too: its figures come from a script outside canvodpy that groups runs by label. The log files stay for diagnosing a run; they are no longer a data source.

The same file may hold an index of the files found per receiver folder, in tables of its own. A run takes from it only the folders that hold none of the days it processes (ADR 0020). If the index is lost or can't be read, the next run lists every folder and builds it again.
path: Every run records itself in a run history, one SQLite file per machine

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Keep reading the log files (the dashboard until now). The performance log rotates, so history disappears after a few weeks of a long run, and every refresh parses every line again.
  • One JSON-lines file per run. Easy to write, but every question across runs (all runs of a site, the repetitions of a label) reads and parses every file, and there is no query language.
  • DuckDB. Fast for analysis and works with marimo's SQL cells, but only one process may open a file for writing, and while it does, other processes cannot read it: the dashboard would be locked out of a running run.
  • The store's log book. A store records what was written to it, not how long it took or on which machine; runs that fail before writing leave nothing there.

SQLite comes with Python (no new dependency); it allows one writer and any number of readers across processes at the same time in WAL mode, and marimo's SQL cells, pandas, and DuckDB read it.
path: Every run records itself in a run history, one SQLite file per machine

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The run history must be on a local disk, because SQLite's WAL mode needs shared memory and does not work on a network drive.
  • Runs happen on one machine, so one file per machine sees every run of that machine. Runs on several machines have several run histories; since ADR 0019 that includes runs on several machines that write one store on S3.
path: Every run records itself in a run history, one SQLite file per machine

items.title: One set of content settings per store, set by its creator; several runs may write one store
items.text:
Several runs may write one store at the same time: on one machine to a local store, and on several machines only to a store on S3. A store shared by several machines through a network mount (SMB, NFS) is not supported. Icechunk's commits on a file system are not safe from more than one machine, and canVODpy's commit lock (a lock file next to the store) does not hold across machines either. Runs write stores on S3 as well as in local folders (processing.storage.stores_root_dir takes an S3 URL).

Every canVODpy commit rewrites the attributes of the root group (ADR 0014), so two commits made at the same time always conflict, also when they write different groups. On a local store commit_lock makes them wait for each other. On S3 there is no lock: Icechunk refuses the commit that comes second, and the run plans the day again on the new tip and tries again. A commit is tried up to five times, with a growing, partly random wait in between (ADR 0016). A file whose epochs are already in the store from a file with another hash stops the run, checked at the tip, so two runs that read different copies of a file never both write it. The text of uv.lock is stored in a commit of its own, before the first data commit that needs it, so two runs with a new lockfile don't both try to store it in their data commits. Two runs that create one store at the same time don't both create it: the creating commit does not rebase, and the run whose commit fails goes on with the store the other run created.

A store keeps one set of content settings: the settings that shape its data. The run that creates the store records them as a fixed field of its repository metadata. Every later run that writes to the store must have the same ones, on any machine; a run with other content settings stops, before it reads a file and again at the tip before each commit. The error lists each setting with the store's value and the run's value. There is no override: other content settings mean a new store. canvodpy config init --from-store <store> writes a settings file from a store's content settings, which is how a second machine joins a store. The same rule holds for one run after another, since the problem is not new with several writers: they only make it likelier.

The content settings are:

  • the signals kept (the SID mode, preset or list, and the resolved list);
  • the observables kept and how they are stored;
  • how files are read and paired (RINEX v3 parser, file pairing, receiver position mode, ephemeris source);
  • the orbit product (agency, product type, clock files);
  • all of the preprocessing, statistics included;
  • chunk sizes, compression method and level, inline chunk threshold and manifest splitting;
  • maintenance;
  • of each receiver: its type, reader format and paired canopies;
  • of a VOD store, also the parameters of each VOD calculator and the content settings of the GNSS store the VOD was computed from.

They are stored with the keys of canvod-settings.yaml, every default written out, with a format version, who set them and when, the canVODpy version, and a hash. Settings that only change how a run is carried out (workers, memory, caches, folders, logging, credentials, store strategies) may differ from run to run. Descriptions, creator, publisher and receiver hardware belong to the repository metadata and change only by amendment (ADR 0014). The canVODpy version is not a content setting: every commit records it.

A store moves to another orbit product only as new science, not by a setting: a store is never written with two products. A later provisional branch may hold the most recent days processed with a quicker product of the same agency (only the product type differs), for a near-real-time view. The main branch never holds those days; once the days with the store's own product are on main, the branch is reset to main's tip. Until that exists, another product is refused like any other content setting.

Stores created before content settings existed get them once, with canvodpy store migrate-metadata, from the settings recorded in the store's first commit. A setting that commit doesn't record is not guessed: the command stops and lists it. Runs refuse such a store until then.
path: One set of content settings per store, set by its creator; several runs may write one store

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Record the settings per file and allow differences (each log-book row carries the settings that made it; readers and VOD filter mixed data). Flexible for reprocessing, but a store could hold mixed data without anyone noticing, and VOD computed across the mix is wrong without a loud error.
  • The store holds the settings and runs take them from it, keeping only machine settings local. One truth and no divergence, but it changes the settings model (what does a user edit, what does config validate check?) shortly before v1.0.0. config init --from-store gives most of its benefit: a run's settings start as the store's.
  • An override flag (--allow-settings-change). Explicit, but it puts mixed data into a store with one keystroke, and nothing in the store would show it afterwards.
  • A join command that fetches a store's settings and starts a run. config init --from-store does the same and leaves a settings file that records how the machine was set up.
  • Writers on several machines through a network mount. Icechunk gives no guarantee there, and a lost commit would go unnoticed.
  • A lock on S3 as on local stores. Icechunk's conditional writes already refuse the second of two commits; a lock would need a lock service that every machine reaches. A CI test with two runs on one S3 store (RustFS, the emulator Icechunk's own CI uses) checks that nothing is lost without it.
path: One set of content settings per store, set by its creator; several runs may write one store

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Each machine keeps its own run history and file index (ADR 0018); canvodpy store maintain-due sees only the runs of its own machine. On S3, maintenance is a dry run only until maintenance with several writers is designed.
  • A new content setting in a later version is a new format of the content settings and needs a migration for existing stores.
path: One set of content settings per store, set by its creator; several runs may write one store

items.title: A run lists the folders of the days it processes
items.text: A run finds every file of the days it processes, without a flag. It lists the folders that hold one of those days, the folders without a data file (the receiver directory, year folders) and the folders not yet in the file index. Every other folder comes from the file index in the run history (ADR 0018). The scan runs once the run's range is known. A run without dates gets its range from where the stores end, so a daily run lists a few folders. The Airflow tasks use the same rule, with the task's day as the range. The data check (canvodpy config validate) lists every folder.
path: A run lists the folders of the days it processes

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• No file index. Every run lists every folder. Always right, but a cold listing on a network share costs about 50 ms per day folder: about 42 s per receiver for a few years of day folders, on every run, also for a daily run of one day.
  • The index, with folders of the last 30 days listed again (the first design, never released). Older folders came from the index, so a file added to one of them was missed without a message; canvodpy run --rescan listed every folder. It happened twice in testing: an end-to-end run found 81 and 79 of 96 files and skipped the VOD silently, and a test of a day written in forks stored 8640 of 17280 epochs. The 30 days counted from today, not from the run's range, so reprocessing an old range always hit it.
  • The index, plus each folder's modification time. A folder whose modification time changed is listed again. That needs one call per folder, which on a network share costs about as much as listing it, and a file replaced in place does not change the folder's time on every file system.
  • The index, with the folders of the run's range listed (chosen). The days a run processes are always listed, so the run sees all their files; the folders of other days, the bulk of an archive, come from the index.
path: A run lists the folders of the days it processes

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• --rescan, Site.pipeline(rescan=True) and the 30-day rule are gone. They were never released, so nothing is deprecated.
  • One case remains: a file for a day in the range, put into a folder that held only days outside it. The run takes that folder from the index and misses the file. A run whose --start/--end cover that folder's days finds it, and so does every run after the run history is deleted. The docs name this case.
  • A file replaced in place (same name, new content) is the user's responsibility: the run finds it by name and does not compare contents.
  • Reprocessing an old range lists that range's folders cold, about 18 s per receiver per year of day folders on a network share. A daily run lists only the folders of its days, and the in-process cache serves every lookup after the first.
path: A run lists the folders of the days it processes

items.title: A run works in units of days, keeps its stores' state in memory, and computes VOD in a phase of its own
items.text:
Proposed 2026-10-18 (#418). Amends ADR 0016: one commit per unit, not per day.

Measurements of a year of data at 58ee7ab8 (#418) showed that from about 16 workers on, the main process sets a run's wall time, and that its work per day grows with the days already stored. Three choices caused it: the store was the run's only memory, the day was the unit of every step, and the main process did all serial work, VOD included. Only live operation needs the day as a unit: receivers send 24 hours of data every 24 hours. A backlog (historical data, reprocessing, a new site) has no such constraint.

Work per day does not grow with the store. A step that runs per day or per unit reads only what that day or unit needs: the blocks of its days (ADR 0016), the log-book rows near its days, the commits made since it started. Reading a whole group, a whole log book or the whole summary again for each day is a defect.

A run keeps its stores' state in memory. At its start, a run reads each group's log book and block index once. It plans, checks overlaps (#351) and decides what to skip against that state, and adds to it what it commits. The summary written with each commit (ADR 0014) is updated from the rows of that commit, not rebuilt from the whole log book. Several runs may still write one store (ADR 0019): when a commit has to rebase onto commits of another run, the run reads only the rows that run added. The log book only grows at its end and numbers its rows, so these are the rows past the last number the run knows.

A run works in units of days. The days of a unit grow their blocks in one commit, are planned together, and are committed once per store. The number of days in a unit is derived, not a setting: enough that every worker gets several tasks within the memory budget, at most 31, so that a conflict or a crash loses little. A live run's unit is its one day. A unit holds only the days whose ephemerides are ready; the other days get no blocks and stay open for the next run, as before. A day fails alone, never its unit: a file that fails gets no log-book row and is tried again by the next run. A unit whose commit loses a conflict is planned again on the new tip and tried again (ADR 0016). Tasks are the groups of files that share an epoch chunk, or with preprocessing set a time bin (ADR 0016); the memory planner sizes workers by these tasks (#417).

VOD is a phase of its own. VOD is computed after the GNSS data of its days are committed, by tasks in the worker pool: one per analysis pair and day, reading the day from the GNSS store's committed snapshot and writing its region into a fork of the VOD store. The main process merges the forks and commits once per unit. A run chains the phase after its GNSS phase (a live run: one day of GNSS data, then that day's VOD), and the phase runs on its own over any range of days already in the GNSS store, for example once after a backlog. The GNSS phase no longer reads its days back.
path: A run works in units of days, keeps its stores' state in memory, and computes VOD in a phase of its own

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• Fix each growing step on its own (read-back, summary, log-book reads, planning). Each fix helps, but the next step added would read the whole store again; the rule in this decision makes that a defect to review against.
  • Speed up the summary's rebuild and keep rebuilding it. About 2.5 times faster on a year store, but it still grows with the store. Kept as the fallback where a whole rebuild is needed (summarize_store, a store's first commit in a run).
  • A fixed number of days per unit, or days_per_batch. A fixed number is wrong for most machines; the memory budget and the worker count already give the right size.
  • One unit per run (grow and commit everything at once). A conflict or a crash would lose the whole run's work, and the days without ephemerides would fail the rest.
  • A failed day fails its unit. Simpler, but days without SP3/CLK products are common at the end of a backlog, and the days with products must not wait for them.
  • Only one run writes a store at a time. It would make the in-memory state simpler, but ADR 0019 allows several writers, on S3 from several machines.
  • VOD from the data in memory instead of the store. It saves the read, but nothing checks that memory equals the store after removing duplicates and padding; with VOD in the worker pool the read is parallel and costs the same for every day.
  • Parallel commits to one branch. Icechunk serializes them on the branch tip.
  • Store maintenance as a speed-up. Compacting manifests and expiring snapshots changed none of the measured times.
path: A run works in units of days, keeps its stores' state in memory, and computes VOD in a phase of its own

items.title: canvodpy stores no secrets; credentials come from the environment
items.text:
Proposed 2026-10-20 (canvodpy-extensions #78).

canvodpy reads data that can need a credential: naming recipes in a private GitHub repository (canvodpy-extensions #78), stores on S3, and later stores on commercial S3 providers. A secret that sits in a settings file, a .env file or a store's metadata is copied with it, and stays in its history.

canvodpy never stores a secret. No settings field holds one, the settings loader reads no .env or secrets file, and no secret is written to a store, a log, a message or the run history.

Each service takes its provider's standard environment variables. canvodpy adds no variables of its own for secrets:

Service Variables Naming recipes on GitHub GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN Stores on S3 The AWS variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_PROFILE) or the shared AWS files (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.aws/config)

Where the secret lives is the user's choice. The system keychain, a password manager that starts a program with the secret in its environment (for example op run -- canvodpy run ..., bws run), or the secrets store of a scheduler (Airflow, Windmill). canvodpy works the same with each, on every operating system.

A secret goes only where it belongs. A recipe token is sent only to raw.githubusercontent.com, never to the target of a redirect. A recipe URL with a user name, password, query or fragment is refused, so no secret reaches the store's metadata through the URL.
path: canvodpy stores no secrets; credentials come from the environment

items.title: Considered options
items.text:
• A variable of our own (CANVOD_RECIPE_TOKEN). One more secret to manage, next to the GH_TOKEN that gh and CI already use.
  • A .env file or a secrets file read by the settings loader. The secret then sits in a file next to the settings, and is copied and committed with them.
  • canvodpy reads the keychain or a password manager itself. Each tool and operating system needs its own code, and a headless server usually runs no keychain. Starting canvodpy with the secret in its environment works with all of them.
  • Asking for the secret at run time. Scheduled runs (Airflow, Windmill) have no one to ask.
path: canvodpy stores no secrets; credentials come from the environment

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Public recipes and stores that need no credential work without any setup.
  • The NASA Earthdata email (CANVOD__PROCESSING__CREDENTIALS__NASA_EARTHDATA_ACC_MAIL) is no secret and stays a setting.
  • A credential for a new service follows this ADR: its provider's standard variables, or a new ADR.
path: canvodpy stores no secrets; credentials come from the environment

items.title: Domain docs
items.text:
How the engineering skills should consume this repository's domain documentation when exploring the codebase.

canVODpy is a single-context repository: its packages share one domain (GNSS-T, sites, files, stores), so there is one glossary and one set of decisions at the root, not one per package.

items.title: Before exploring, read these
items.text:
• GLOSSARY.md at the repository root: the project's words.
  • docs/adr/: read the decisions about the area you're about to work in (docs/adr/index.md lists them).
  • CODING_STANDARDS.md: the rules every change follows.
  • The AGENTS.md of every package you change: where things live, invariants, tests.

items.title: File structure
items.text:
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── CODING_STANDARDS.md
├── AGENTS.md
├── docs/adr/
│   ├── index.md
│   ├── 0001-versioned-stores.md
│   └── ...
└── packages/<package>/AGENTS.md

A new ADR takes the next free number and gets a row in docs/adr/index.md and an entry under Decisions in the nav of zensical.toml; the docs site shows them under Development > Decisions.

items.title: Use the glossary's vocabulary
items.text:
When your output names a domain concept (in an issue title, a refactor proposal, a hypothesis, a test name), use the term as defined in GLOSSARY.md. Don't drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If the concept you need isn't in the glossary yet, that's a signal: either you're inventing language the project doesn't use (reconsider) or there's a real gap (note it for /mattpocock-skills:domain-modeling).

items.title: Flag conflicts with an ADR
items.text:
If your output contradicts an existing ADR, surface it explicitly rather than silently overriding:

Contradicts ADR-0007 (provenance in log books), but worth reopening because…

items.title: Issue tracker
items.text: Issues and specs for this repository live as GitHub issues. Use the gh command-line tool for all operations.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• Create an issue: gh issue create --title "..." --body "...". Write a body of several lines to a file and pass it with --body-file.
  • Read an issue: gh issue view <number> --comments, filtering comments by jq and also fetching labels.
  • List issues: gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]' with appropriate --label and --state filters.
  • Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent: gh issue create --parent <parent> ..., or gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child> afterwards (gh 2.94+). Older gh: gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id> (database id, as in Blocking below). Without sub-issues, put Part of #<parent> at the top of the child body.
  • Comment on an issue: gh issue comment <number> --body "..."
  • Apply / remove labels: gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..." / --remove-label "..."
  • Close: gh issue close <number> --comment "..."

Infer the repository from git remote -v; gh does this automatically when run inside a clone.

items.title: Pull requests as a triage surface
items.text:
PRs as a request surface: no. (Set to yes if this repository treats external PRs as feature requests; /mattpocock-skills:triage reads this flag.)

When set to yes, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the gh pr equivalents:

  • Read a PR: gh pr view <number> --comments and gh pr diff <number> for the diff.
  • List external PRs for triage: gh api --paginate 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open' --jq '.[] | select(.author_association | IN("OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR") | not) | {number, title, author: .user.login, author_association, labels: [.labels[].name]}'.
  • Comment / label / close: gh pr comment, gh pr edit --add-label/--remove-label, gh pr close.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare #42 may be either: resolve with gh pr view 42 and fall back to gh issue view 42.

items.title: When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"
items.text: Create a GitHub issue.

items.title: When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"
items.text: Run gh issue view <number> --comments.

items.title: Operations of the wayfinder skill
items.text:
Used by /mattpocock-skills:wayfinder. The map is a single issue with child issues as tickets.

  • Map: a single issue labeled wayfinder:map, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. gh issue create --label wayfinder:map.
  • Child ticket: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (see Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put Part of #<map> at the top of the child body. Labels: wayfinder:<type> (research/prototype/grilling/task). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the person driving it.
  • Blocking: the native issue dependencies of GitHub, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>, where <blocker-db-id> is the blocker's numeric database id (gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id, not the #number or node_id). GitHub reports issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a Blocked by: #<n>, #<n> line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
  • Frontier query: list the map's open children (gh issue list --state open, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0, or an open issue in the Blocked by line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
  • Claim: gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me, the session's first write.
  • Resolve: gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>", then gh issue close <n>, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

items.text:
The skills speak in terms of five canonical triage roles. This file maps those roles to the actual label strings used in this repository's issue tracker.

Label in mattpocock/skills Label in this tracker Meaning needs-triage needs-triage Maintainer needs to evaluate this issue needs-info needs-info Waiting on reporter for more information ready-for-agent ready-for-agent Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent ready-for-human ready-for-human Requires human implementation wontfix wontfix Not acted on

items.title: DatasetMatcher
items.text:
Match auxiliary datasets to a reference RINEX dataset temporally.

Handles temporal alignment of datasets with different sampling rates using appropriate interpolation strategies. The reference dataset (typically RINEX observations) remains unchanged while auxiliary datasets are interpolated to match its epochs.

The matcher: 1. Validates all datasets have required dimensions (epoch, sid) 2. Determines relative temporal resolutions 3. Applies appropriate interpolation: - Higher resolution aux → nearest neighbor - Lower resolution aux → specialized interpolator from metadata

Examples:

>>> from canvod.auxiliary.matching import DatasetMatcher
>>>
>>> matcher = DatasetMatcher()
>>> matched = matcher.match_datasets(
...     rinex_ds,
...     ephemerides=sp3_data,
...     clock=clk_data
... )
>>>
>>> # Auxiliary datasets now aligned to RINEX epochs
>>> len(matched['ephemerides'].epoch) == len(rinex_ds.epoch)
True
>>> len(matched['clock'].epoch) == len(rinex_ds.epoch)
True

Notes

  • Reference dataset should be the RINEX observations
  • Auxiliary datasets should have 'interpolator_config' in attrs
  • If no interpolator config, falls back to nearest neighbor
  • Temporal distance is tracked for quality assessment

items.text:
Match auxiliary datasets to reference dataset epochs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default reference_ds Dataset

items.title: ECEFPosition
items.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Earth-Centered, Earth-Fixed (ECEF) position in meters.

ECEF is a Cartesian coordinate system with: - Origin at Earth's center of mass - X-axis pointing to 0° latitude, 0° longitude (Prime Meridian at Equator) - Y-axis pointing to 0° latitude, 90° East longitude - Z-axis pointing to North Pole

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x float

X coordinate in meters.

required y float

Y coordinate in meters.

required z float

Z coordinate in meters.

required

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

If any component is non-finite (NaN/inf), or the position is exactly (0, 0, 0) -- Earth's center, never a physically valid ECEF point for anything this codebase computes geometry relative to. This is deliberately a general sanity check (applies to satellite positions too, not just receivers) -- see from_ds_metadata() for the additional ground-station-specific plausibility check.

Examples:

>>> # From RINEX dataset metadata
>>> pos = ECEFPosition.from_ds_metadata(rinex_ds)
>>> print(f"X: {pos.x:.3f} m")

>>> # Manual creation
>>> pos = ECEFPosition(x=4194304.123, y=176481.234, z=4780013.456)
>>> lat, lon, alt = pos.to_geodetic()

If the position's ECEF magnitude falls outside the plausible ground-station band (_GROUND_STATION_MIN_RADIUS_M .. _GROUND_STATION_MAX_RADIUS_M, i.e. on/near the WGS84 ellipsoid) -- e.g. an unpopulated RINEX header defaulted to a position that happens to be finite and non-zero but still not a real ground station (this check is specific to this parse boundary, not a general ECEFPosition constraint -- see the class docstring).

items.title: Preprocessing
items.text:
Auxiliary-data preprocessing pipelines.

Composes the SID-space primitives from :mod:canvod.readers.preprocessing (sv->sid conversion, global SID padding, dtype/encoding normalization) into the two pipelines specific to auxiliary (SP3/CLK) data: preparing a dataset for Icechunk storage, and preparing one for interpolation.

The primitives themselves live in canvod-readers because they only depend on GNSS signal/constellation definitions (canvod.readers.gnss_specs), not on anything ephemeris- or interpolation-specific -- keeping them here made canvod-readers (which calls them from every reader's to_ds()) depend on canvod-auxiliary, which already depends on canvod-readers, a genuine import cycle that broke standalone canvod-readers installs.

items.title: prep_aux_ds(aux_ds, fill_value=np.nan, aggregate_glonass_fdma=True, keep_sids=None)
items.text:
Preprocess auxiliary dataset before writing to Icechunk.

Performs complete 4-step preprocessing: 1. Convert sv → sid dimension 2. Pad to global sid list (all constellations) or filter to keep_sids 3. Normalize sid dtype to object 4. Strip _FillValue attributes

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default aux_ds Dataset

Dataset with 'sv' dimension.

required fill_value float

Fill value for missing entries.

np.nan aggregate_glonass_fdma bool

Whether to aggregate GLONASS FDMA bands.

True keep_sids list[str] | None

List of specific SIDs to keep. If None, keeps all possible SIDs.

None

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

Fully preprocessed dataset ready for Icechunk or interpolation.

items.title: preprocess_aux_for_interpolation(aux_ds, fill_value=np.nan, full_preprocessing=False, aggregate_glonass_fdma=True)
items.text:
Preprocess auxiliary dataset before interpolation.

Converts satellite vehicle (sv) dimension to Signal ID (sid) dimension, which is required for matching with RINEX observations after interpolation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default aux_ds Dataset

Raw auxiliary dataset with 'sv' dimension.

required fill_value float

Fill value for missing entries.

np.nan full_preprocessing bool

If True, applies full 4-step preprocessing (pad_to_global_sid, normalize_sid_dtype, strip_fillvalue). If False, only converts sv → sid (sufficient for interpolation).

False aggregate_glonass_fdma bool

Whether to aggregate GLONASS FDMA bands.

True

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

Preprocessed dataset with 'sid' dimension.

Notes

This must be called BEFORE interpolation. The workflow is: 1. Load raw SP3/CLK data (sv dimension) 2. Convert sv → sid (this function) 3. Interpolate to target epochs 4. Match with RINEX data (sid dimension)

For most interpolation use cases, full_preprocessing=False is sufficient. Use full_preprocessing=True when preparing data for Icechunk storage.

Examples:

>>> # Load raw SP3 data
>>> sp3_data = Sp3File(...).to_dataset()
>>> sp3_data.dims
{'epoch': 96, 'sv': 32}
>>>
>>> # Preprocess before interpolation (minimal)
>>> sp3_preprocessed = preprocess_aux_for_interpolation(sp3_data)
>>> sp3_preprocessed.dims
{'epoch': 96, 'sid': 384}
>>>
>>> # Preprocess before Icechunk (full)
>>> sp3_preprocessed = preprocess_aux_for_interpolation(
...     sp3_data,
...     full_preprocessing=True,
... )
>>> sp3_preprocessed.dims
{'epoch': 96, 'sid': ~2000}  # Padded to all possible sids
>>>
>>> # Now interpolate
>>> sp3_interp = interpolator.interpolate(sp3_preprocessed, target_epochs)

items.title: compute_spherical_coordinates(sat_x, sat_y, sat_z, rx_pos)
items.text:
Compute spherical coordinates (r, theta, phi) in navigation convention.

Uses local ENU (East-North-Up) topocentric frame centered at receiver.

Navigation Convention: - theta: Polar angle from +z axis (zenith), [0, π] radians * theta = 0 → zenith (straight up) * theta = π/2 → horizon * theta > π/2 → below horizon (set to NaN) - phi: Azimuthal angle from North, clockwise, [0, 2π) radians * phi = 0 → North * phi = π/2 → East * phi = π → South * phi = 3π/2 → West - r: Radial distance in meters

Note

The phi convention follows geographic/navigation standards where: - 0° points North (positive Y in ENU frame) - Angles increase clockwise when viewed from above - This is computed as arctan2(East, North), giving North=0° reference - Differs from physics convention which uses East=0° reference

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sat_x ndarray

Satellite X coordinates in ECEF (meters).

required sat_y ndarray

Satellite Y coordinates in ECEF (meters).

required sat_z ndarray

Satellite Z coordinates in ECEF (meters).

required rx_pos ECEFPosition

Receiver position in ECEF.

required

Returns:

Type Description tuple[ndarray, ndarray, ndarray]

(r, theta, phi) where: - r: distances in meters - theta: polar angles in radians [0, π] - phi: azimuthal angles in radians [0, 2π)

Notes

Satellites below horizon (theta > π/2) are set to NaN.

Examples:

>>> from canvod.auxiliary.position import (
...     ECEFPosition, compute_spherical_coordinates,
... )
>>>
>>> # Receiver position
>>> rx = ECEFPosition(x=4194304.0, y=176481.0, z=4780013.0)
>>>
>>> # Satellite positions (example)
>>> sat_x = np.array([16364123.0, 10205789.0])
>>> sat_y = np.array([12123456.0, -8901234.0])
>>> sat_z = np.array([18456789.0, 21234567.0])
>>>
>>> r, theta, phi = compute_spherical_coordinates(sat_x, sat_y, sat_z, rx)
>>> print(f"Distance: {r[0]/1e6:.2f} Mm")
>>> print(f"Polar angle: {np.degrees(theta[0]):.1f}°")
>>> print(f"Azimuth: {np.degrees(phi[0]):.1f}°")

items.title: CanvodConfig
items.text:
Bases: BaseSettings

Complete canvodpy configuration.

Loaded from YAML files by ConfigLoader; individual fields can be overridden via environment variables using the CANVOD__ prefix and __ as the nested delimiter. Environment variables take priority over YAML-file values.

Examples:

Override a single nested field without touching the YAML. VAR=value must appear on the same command line as canvodpy — it only sets a variable for the current shell otherwise, and canvodpy (a separate process) never sees it::

CANVOD__PROCESSING__PARAMS__DAYS_PER_BATCH=7 canvodpy run ...
CANVOD__PROCESSING__CREDENTIALS__NASA_EARTHDATA_ACC_MAIL=me@x.com canvodpy run ...

To reuse an override across several commands, export it once instead::

export CANVOD__PROCESSING__PARAMS__DAYS_PER_BATCH=7
canvodpy config show   # confirms the override took effect
canvodpy run ...

items.title: load_config(config_dir=None, config_file=None)
items.text:
Load configuration from YAML files.

This is the main entry point for loading configuration.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config_dir Path | None

Directory containing config files. If None, automatically finds monorepo root and uses {monorepo_root}/config.

None config_file Path | None

Optional overlay YAML file applied on top of the main config. Can also be set via the CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE environment variable.

None

Returns:

Type Description CanvodConfig

Validated configuration object.

Raises:

Type Description ConfigValidationError

If configuration YAML is invalid.

FileNotFoundError

If config_file is specified but does not exist.

Notes

CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR/CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE are resolved here, before the cached call, not inside it. The actual caching happens in _load_config_cached, keyed on the fully-resolved paths. Resolving the env vars inside the cached function itself (as this used to do) made the cache key blind to them: whichever call happened first in a process -- e.g. canvodpy.logging.logging_config's module-level LOGGER = configure_logging(), which called load_config() bare at import time until 2026-10, before a CLI's --config/CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE is ever set -- would cache the config under the no-arg key, and every later bare load_config() call in that process (e.g. store-path/chunk- strategy resolution deep in canvod-store) would silently get that stale, pre-overlay config back, no matter what the env var said by then. See canvodpy/tests/test_cli_store.py's _clear_config_cache fixture for a hand-rolled workaround of the same symptom that predates this fix.

Examples:

>>> from canvod.config import load_config
>>> config = load_config()
>>> print(config.nasa_earthdata_acc_mail)
>>> print(config.processing.aux_data.agency)

items.title: EqualAreaBuilder
items.text:
Bases: BaseGridBuilder

Equal solid angle tessellation using concentric theta bands.

The hemisphere is divided into annular bands of constant width in theta. Within each band the number of azimuthal (phi) sectors is chosen so that every cell subtends approximately the same solid angle. This is the only grid type that has been validated for scientific use in this codebase.

Coordinate convention (physics / GNSS)

  • phi ∈ [0, 2π) – azimuthal angle from North, clockwise (navigation convention)
  • theta ∈ [0, π/2] – polar angle measured from zenith (0 = straight up, π/2 = horizon)

What angular_resolution means

angular_resolution (degrees) sets the width of each theta band. All bands have this same width Δθ. The azimuthal width of cells varies by band: near the zenith cells are wide in phi; near the horizon they are narrow, so that the solid angle stays constant.

Mathematical construction

  1. Target solid angle per cell is chosen equal to the solid angle of a cap of half-angle Δθ/2::

    Ω_target = 2π (1 − cos(Δθ/2))

  2. Zenith cap – a single cell covers [0, Δθ/2] in theta and the full azimuth [0, 2π).

  3. Theta bands – edges are placed at Δθ/2, 3Δθ/2, 5Δθ/2, … and a last edge at π/2 − cutoff_theta, so the grid reaches the horizon (or the cutoff). With the zenith cap of half width the last band is usually narrower than Δθ (half as wide when the cutoff is a multiple of Δθ); its phi divisions follow from its solid angle like any other band's. For each band [θ_inner, θ_outer] the band's total solid angle is::

    Ω_band = 2π (cos θ_inner − cos θ_outer)

  4. Phi divisions – the number of sectors in the band is::

    n_phi = round(Ω_band / Ω_target)

Each sector spans Δφ = 2π / n_phi. The cell center is placed at the geometric midpoint of its (phi, theta) rectangle.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default angular_resolution float

Theta-band width in degrees. Controls both the radial resolution and (indirectly, via the equal-area constraint) the azimuthal resolution.

2 cutoff_theta float

Minimum elevation above the horizon in degrees. The last band ends at θ = 90° − cutoff_theta; the sky below that elevation gets no cells. In GNSS terms this is the satellite elevation mask angle.

0 phi_rotation float

Rigid rotation applied to all phi coordinates after grid construction, in degrees.

0

items.title: EqualAngleBuilder
items.text:
Bases: BaseGridBuilder

Equal angular spacing in both theta and phi (NOT equal area).

Every cell is a rectangle of the same angular size Δθ × Δφ in the (theta, phi) parameter space. A cell's solid angle is Δφ · (cos θ_min − cos θ_max) ≈ Δφ · Δθ · sin θ, so cells near the zenith subtend less solid angle than cells near the horizon. A statistic that weights every cell equally therefore gives the sky near the zenith more weight than its share of the hemisphere. Not recommended for scientific analysis – use EqualAreaBuilder instead.

Coordinate convention (physics / GNSS)

  • phi ∈ [0, 2π) – azimuthal angle from North, clockwise (navigation convention)
  • theta ∈ [0, π/2] – polar angle from zenith

What angular_resolution means

angular_resolution (degrees) is used as both the theta-band width and the phi-sector width. The number of phi divisions is the same in every band but the zenith cap::

n_phi = floor(2π / Δθ)

so the sectors are wider than Δθ when Δθ does not divide 360°.

Mathematical construction

  1. A zenith cap cell covers [0, Δθ/2] × [0, 2π).
  2. Theta band edges are placed at Δθ/2, 3Δθ/2, … and a last edge at π/2 − cutoff_theta, so the grid reaches the horizon (or the cutoff); the last band is usually narrower than Δθ.
  3. Within every band, the full azimuth is split into n_phi sectors of equal width Δφ = 2π / n_phi.
  4. Cell centers are at the midpoint of each (phi, theta) rectangle.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default angular_resolution float

Angular spacing in degrees, applied identically in both theta and phi.

2 cutoff_theta float

Elevation mask angle in degrees. The last band ends at θ = 90° − cutoff_theta; the sky below that elevation gets no cells.

0 phi_rotation float

Rigid azimuthal rotation applied after construction, in degrees.

0

items.title: EquirectangularBuilder
items.text:
Bases: BaseGridBuilder

Simple rectangular grid in (theta, phi) space.

The hemisphere is divided into a regular rectangular array: a constant number of theta bands, each containing the same constant number of phi sectors. Every cell is a rectangle of the same angular size in (theta, phi), except the last band and the last sector, which are narrower when Δθ does not divide their range. It differs from EqualAngleBuilder at the zenith: EqualAngleBuilder makes the innermost half band a single zenith cap and puts its band edges half a band off, while this builder starts the first band at the zenith with the same number of sectors as every other band.

A cell's solid angle is Δφ · (cos θ_min − cos θ_max) ≈ Δφ · Δθ · sin θ, so cells near the zenith subtend less solid angle than cells near the horizon. A statistic that weights every cell equally therefore gives the sky near the zenith more weight than its share of the hemisphere. Not recommended for scientific analysis – use EqualAreaBuilder instead.

Coordinate convention (physics / GNSS)

  • phi ∈ [0, 2π) – azimuthal angle from North, clockwise (navigation convention)
  • theta ∈ [0, π/2] – polar angle from zenith (0 = straight up, π/2 = horizon)

What angular_resolution means

angular_resolution (degrees) is used as both the theta-band width and the phi-sector width::

n_theta = ceil((π/2 − cutoff) / Δθ)
n_phi   = ceil(2π / Δθ)
total cells = n_theta × n_phi

Mathematical construction

  1. Theta edges are placed at 0, Δθ, 2Δθ, … up to π/2 − cutoff_theta (the last edge is clamped exactly to π/2 − cutoff_theta rather than overshooting it).
  2. Phi edges are placed at 0, Δθ, 2Δθ, … and a last edge at 2π; the last sector is narrower when Δθ does not divide 360°.
  3. Every (theta_band, phi_sector) combination produces one cell. The cell center is the midpoint of the rectangle.
  4. No special zenith cap is created; the band nearest the zenith has the same number of phi sectors as all other bands.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default angular_resolution float

Angular spacing in degrees, applied identically in both theta and phi.

2 cutoff_theta float

Elevation mask angle in degrees. The last band ends at θ = 90° − cutoff_theta; the sky below that elevation gets no cells.

0 phi_rotation float

Rigid azimuthal rotation applied after construction, in degrees.

0
