items.title: canvodpy store log
items.text:
Show the commit history as a graph, or the store operations with --ops.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store log [OPTIONS] [site]

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml. Omit when using --path.

Options:

  • --store gnss|vod: Store of the site to open. Default: gnss. Not with --path.
  • --path STORE: Open the store at this local path or s3://bucket/prefix instead of a site's store, for example a copy. Needs no settings file.
  • --branch <str>: Show the history of this branch only. Default: all branches.
  • --ops: Show the operations on the store instead of the commit graph.
  • --limit <int>: Number of operations that --ops shows. [default: 50]
  • --svg FILE: Write the commit graph to this SVG file instead of printing it.
  • --plain: Draw the commit graph without colors, for a file or a CI log.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store maintain
items.text:
Expire old snapshots of one site's store and collect garbage.

Without --execute, this is a dry run: it reports what garbage collection would delete and how many snapshots of the main branch are older than the cutoff, and changes nothing. With --execute, it asks for confirmation, expires the old snapshots and, unless you pass --no-gc, collects garbage.

Don't run it while a canvodpy run writes to the same store.

On a store on S3, maintenance is a dry run only: a store there may be written by several machines, so --execute is refused (exit 1) and only the report is printed.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store maintain [OPTIONS] {site}

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml [required]

Options:

  • --store gnss|vod: Store to open. [default: gnss]
  • --expire-days <int>: Keep the snapshots of this many past days. Use weeks to months, not hours. [default: 90]
  • --gc / --no-gc: Run garbage collection [default: gc]
  • --execute: Expire snapshots and collect garbage, after you confirm. Without this flag the command only reports and changes nothing.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store maintain-due
items.text:
Run only the store maintenance that's due, without prompting.

Use this command, not maintain, in scheduled jobs such as cron: it never asks for confirmation, and it exits with status 0 when nothing is due. It reads processing.storage.maintenance in canvod-settings.yaml and does nothing unless both of these hold:

  • maintenance.enabled or maintenance.manifests_enabled is true. Both are false by default. Before you set them, run canvodpy store maintain SITE, which is a dry run, on your store and check its report.
  • No canvodpy run is active on this computer.

maintenance.enabled allows snapshot expiry and garbage collection. Expiry is due when the last one ran more than maintenance.expire_interval_days ago, or never ran. Garbage collection is due maintenance.gc_delay_days after an expiry, once per expiry. maintenance.manifests_enabled allows manifest compaction, which is due when the store holds at least maintenance.manifest_count_threshold manifest files.

While maintenance.dry_run_until_confirmed is true, the default, a store that's due is only reported, not changed. Set it to false once the reports look right.

On a store on S3, maintenance is a dry run only: a store there may be written by several machines, so a due store is always reported, never changed, and this command still exits 0 (a cron job does not fail overnight).

Usage:

$ canvodpy store maintain-due [OPTIONS] [site]

Arguments:

  • site: Site name. Omit when using --all-sites.

Options:

  • --all-sites: Run for every site in canvod-settings.yaml.
  • --store gnss|vod|both: Store to maintain. [default: both]
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store migrate-metadata
items.text:
Move a store written before repository metadata to the current form.

Writes the store's description into its repository metadata, gives it a new store id, made of the site name in lowercase and the store kind, and a UUID, and keeps the old id in the migration record. Snapshots from before stay readable.

The migrated store must pass the standards checks: fields the store lacks, such as its description, are given with --set, otherwise the migration is refused and lists them. In a VOD store, the attributes of VOD are replaced with the current ones: older versions copied the attributes of SNR and theta to VOD, among them the valid range of theta. A VOD store also lists each VOD analysis it holds a group of, with its receivers from the settings. The migration record keeps who migrated the store, the initials set in processing.metadata.initials.

Fields the store lacks and the settings hold are taken from them: the site's store_description, the publisher and license, the site's latitude and longitude. A value given with --set wins.

canVODpy 0.x stored epochs without recording their time scale. The epochs of groups read from RINEX files are GPS time and are recorded as such; a VOD store's, when its site's GNSS store holds RINEX epochs only. A group read from SBF or NMEA files holds UTC epochs: the command stops, and the store is rebuilt from the raw files.

A GNSS or VOD store also gets its content settings (ADR 0019), also when it was moved to repository metadata before: the settings that shape its data, taken from the settings recorded in its first commit. A setting that commit does not record is not guessed: the command stops and lists it, to be given with --set by its key in canvod-settings.yaml. A setting the data show (the preprocessing, store_delta_snr, store_radial_diff, store_radial_distance) is read from the data: canVODpy 0.x recorded settings its runs didn't follow.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store migrate-metadata [OPTIONS] {site}

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml [required]

Options:

  • --store gnss|vod: Store to migrate. [default: gnss]
  • --naming-authority <str>: Your institution's domain in reverse order, for example org.middle-earth. Default: the store's own, if it is a reverse DNS name; otherwise processing.metadata.naming_authority in the settings.
  • --set field.path=value: A field or content setting the store lacks, for example identity.description=Beech forest site, or sites.my_site.receivers.reference_01.paired_canopies=[canopy_01]. Repeat for more.
  • --yes: Migrate without asking.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store migrate-layout
items.text:
Move a store written by appending files to day blocks (ADR 0016).

Runs write day blocks only, so a store whose groups were written by appending has to be moved first. Each such group is written again, day by day: every day gets a block of slots at its cadence, the finest step between its epochs. An epoch stored more than once keeps the entry written last. The groups keep their attributes, log books and other metadata, and get the chunks of the settings (processing.icechunk.chunk_strategies).

Shows what it will do and asks first. Everything goes into one commit; snapshots from before stay readable. A store written before repository metadata is moved with canvodpy store migrate SITE.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store migrate-layout [OPTIONS] {site}

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml [required]

Options:

  • --store gnss|vod: Store to move. [default: gnss]
  • --yes: Move without asking.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store amend
items.text:
Change the description of a site's store, with a reason.

Fixed fields (the store id, UUID, store type, source format, naming authority and creation date) never change. Each changed field is recorded with its old and new value, the reason, who and when, and a new commit carries the new description. Who is the initials set in processing.metadata.initials.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store amend [OPTIONS] {site}

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml [required]

Options:

  • --store gnss|vod: Store to amend. [default: gnss]
  • --set field.path=value: New value of a field, for example identity.title=Rosalia GNSS observations. Repeat for more fields.
  • --add-receiver name: Add a receiver of the site's settings to the store, so runs may write it.
  • --add-vod-analysis name: Add a VOD analysis of the site's settings to the VOD store.
  • --update-recipe name: Record a receiver's naming recipe of the settings and its sha256 in the GNSS store, after the recipe changed on purpose.
  • --from <path>: YAML file with the keys reason, set (field paths and values), and the lists add_receivers, add_vod_analyses and update_recipes.
  • --reason <str>: Why the fields change; recorded with each one.
  • --yes: Amend without asking.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy store migrate
items.text:
Move a site's stores from canVODpy 0.x to the current form, in one go.

  1. Folders: a store's folder is named by its kind (gnss, vod), with an optional suffix (vod-recompute). The GNSS store's old folder rinex is moved to gnss; any other folder whose name is not a kind is moved to the name given with --rename. The store id is taken from the new folder name.
  2. The GNSS store, then the VOD store: their metadata (migrate-metadata), and their groups to day blocks (migrate-layout).
  3. A GNSS store made with CLK files loses its clock variable and records fetch_clock: false; since v1.0.0 runs read no CLK files by default, and VOD doesn't use the clock. The VOD store records the GNSS store's new content-settings hash.

Shows the plan and asks once. Each step that is done already is skipped, so the command can run again after a step failed; migrate-metadata and migrate-layout rerun single steps. Snapshots from before stay readable in the store's history. Stores on S3 need no migration: canVODpy writes stores to S3 since v1.0.0 only.

Usage:

$ canvodpy store migrate [OPTIONS] {site}

Arguments:

  • site: Site name, as defined under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml [required]

Options:

  • --rename OLD=NEW: The new name of a store folder whose name is not its kind, for example vod_2024=vod-2024. rinex is moved to gnss without it. Repeat for more.
  • --naming-authority <str>: As for migrate-metadata: your institution's domain in reverse order.
  • --gnss-set field.path=value: A field or content setting the GNSS store lacks (migrate-metadata --set). Repeat for more.
  • --vod-set field.path=value: A field or content setting the VOD store lacks (migrate-metadata --set). Repeat for more.
  • --yes: Migrate without asking.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy stac
items.text:
Write the STAC catalog of every store under the data root, or a release.

Usage:

$ canvodpy stac [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

Commands:

  • write: Write the latest catalog of every store...
  • release: Publish a release: tag every store under...

items.title: canvodpy stac write
items.text:
Write the latest catalog of every store under the data root.

If a store cannot be described, nothing is written: the command lists every such store with its reason and exits with code 1.

Usage:

$ canvodpy stac write [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --root <path>: Data root to catalog. Default: storage.stores_root_dir in the settings.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: canvodpy stac release
items.text:
Publish a release: tag every store under the data root and write its catalog.

TAG becomes an Icechunk tag on the current main of every store, and releases/TAG/ gets the catalog of that tag, each asset pinned to the tag and its snapshot. A release catalog is never changed afterwards. Nothing is tagged if a store cannot be described or already has the tag; if every store has the tag but the catalog is missing, only the catalog is written.

Usage:

$ canvodpy stac release [OPTIONS] {tag}

Arguments:

  • tag: Release tag, for example v2026.1; no '/'. [required]

Options:

  • --root <path>: Data root to catalog. Default: storage.stores_root_dir in the settings.
  • -c, --config-dir <path|url>: Configuration directory, holding canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the URL of a settings file in a GitHub repository, fetched by each run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com////.../canvod-settings.yaml). Default: $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, else config/ of the canvodpy checkout, else ~/.config/canvodpy.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

items.title: In the terminal
items.text:
canvodpy --help-all lists every command with its options on one screen; canvodpy COMMAND --help describes one command.

canvodpy without a command, canvodpy --version and canvodpy run start with the canVODpy logo, the website, the version, the support address, the author and the licence. The logo is shown only in an interactive terminal at least 81 columns wide, never when the output goes to a file, a pipe or a cron job. To turn it off, for example to save the second it takes at the start of a run, set CANVODPY_NO_BANNER=1.

The colours of the help, the messages and the progress bars follow the terminal's background, dark or light. canVODpy asks the terminal for it, which most current terminals answer, and otherwise reads COLORFGBG or takes dark. If it picks the wrong one, set CANVODPY_TERMINAL_THEME=dark or CANVODPY_TERMINAL_THEME=light. The colours avoid red and keep apart with red-green colour blindness, and every status comes with its symbol: ✓ done, ⚠️ needs attention, ❌ failed. NO_COLOR=1 turns the colours off. Log lines written to a file or a pipe carry no colour codes.

After canvodpy --install-completion, the command prints how to load the completion in the open terminal (for example exec zsh), so you don't need to open a new one.

items.title: Development guide
items.text: Quick reference for day-to-day canVODpy development.

items.title: Initial setup
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git
cd canvodpy
git submodule update --init --recursive   # test data + demo data
uv sync                                    # install all packages (editable)
just hooks                                 # install pre-commit hooks
just test                                  # verify everything works

Submodules

Two data repositories are pulled as submodules:

  • packages/canvod-readers/tests/test_data: falsified/corrupted RINEX files for validation tests
  • demo: clean real-world data for demos and documentation

Tests that depend on these datasets are automatically skipped if submodules are not initialized.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Two tools must be installed outside uv:

Tool Install Purpose uv brew install uv Python + dependency management just brew install just Task runner 
just check-dev-tools   # verify both are present

Full installation guide

items.title: Configuration management
items.text:
canVODpy uses three YAML files in config/:

Section Purpose processing: Processing parameters, NASA Earthdata credentials, storage strategies, Icechunk settings sites: Research sites, receiver definitions, data root paths, VOD analysis pairs sids: Signal ID filtering: all, a named preset, or a custom list

All three sections live in a single config/canvod-settings.yaml. Template: config/canvod-settings.yaml.example, a copy of the template the package ships (packages/canvod-config/src/canvod/config/templates/); edit that one and copy it.

First-time setupDaily use 
canvodpy config init                # scaffold canvod-settings.yaml from template
# edit config/canvod-settings.yaml (or: canvodpy config init --interactive)
canvodpy config validate            # check for errors
canvodpy config show                # print resolved config

just config-validate    # after editing
just config-show        # inspect current values
canvodpy doctor         # environment + config diagnostics when something's off

items.title: Testing
items.text:
just test                            # all tests
just test-package canvod-readers     # specific package
just test-coverage                   # with HTML coverage report
just test-network                    # tests that reach the download servers

Tests live in packages/<pkg>/tests/. Integration tests are marked @pytest.mark.integration and excluded from the default run.

Network tests are marked @pytest.mark.network and skipped unless just test-network runs them; GitHub CI never does. They check every product of the registry on the FTP servers, download the COD final orbits and clocks of 2025-001 and compare them with the test data, and run a day of the test data that downloads its own orbits and clocks. Run them before a release and after changing the product registry. NASA CDDIS is checked only when the settings hold credentials.nasa_earthdata_acc_mail.

items.title: Code Quality
items.text:
just check          # lint + format + type-check (run before committing)
just check-lint     # ruff linting only
just check-format   # ruff formatting only
Tool Purpose ruff Linting + formatting (replaces flake8, black, isort) ty Type checking (replaces mypy) pytest Testing with coverage

items.title: Type checking (ty)
items.text:
ty check must pass with zero diagnostics. It blocks git push (local pre-push hook) and runs again in CI (type_consistency job). There's no budget or ratchet; if you introduce a diagnostic, fix it before pushing.

Most real diagnostics mean the annotation is actually wrong: fix the annotation, not the checker. Suppress with a targeted comment only when the code is correct and a limitation of ty is the real issue (for example, a runtime-built enum.StrEnum, a deliberately dynamic attribute set on a function object, a third-party stub that's too strict for a legitimately partial dict):

_excepthook._logger_holder = logger_holder  # ty: ignore[unresolved-attribute]

Always include the specific rule name in brackets (uv run ty check prints it in the diagnostic, for example error[invalid-return-type]). A bare # type: ignore (mypy syntax) does not suppress ty diagnostics, since ty matches on its own rule codes.

items.title: Logging: add it generously
items.text:
canvodpy runs unattended on remote machines. When something goes wrong there, whatever you logged is the only evidence there is: there's no attaching a debugger to a cron job after the fact. Log more than feels necessary, especially around: file I/O, external calls (downloads, Icechunk writes), anything with a fallback/degraded path, and any place a silent skip could hide data loss. See docs/guides/diagnostics.md for the full picture (the log files, run_id, the failure events, stage_timer, the performance dashboard). This section is the short version: how to add a log line.

Which logger to use: every module, in every package, gets its logger directly from structlog:

import structlog

log = structlog.get_logger(__name__)

Only canvodpy configures logging; the canvod-* packages never do. configure_logging() installs structlog's processor chain globally, so any structlog.get_logger() call anywhere in the process, regardless of which package it's in, automatically gets routed through the two-track logging setup (human/agent files) with run_id injected, with zero per-call-site wiring. Never reach for print() or the standard library logging directly.

Event style: first positional argument is a short snake_case event name, everything else is a structured keyword, not string interpolation:

# Good
log.info("rinex_preprocessing_started", file=str(rnx_file.name), site=site_name)
log.warning("sids_dropped_no_ephemeris", count=len(dropped), sids=sorted(dropped))

# Avoid: loses structure, can't be grepped/filtered on a field
log.info(f"Started preprocessing {rnx_file.name} for {site_name}")

Timing: use stage_timer()/timed_stage() from canvod.utils.logging rather than hand-rolling t0 = time.perf_counter(); ...; duration = ...: it emits the canonical stage_timing event the performance dashboard reads, and still emits (with status="error") if the block raises.

from canvod.utils.logging import stage_timer

with stage_timer("icechunk.write", group=group_name, size_mb=size_mb):
    to_icechunk(dataset, session, group=group_name)

When one block has several sequential checkpoints, each a dashboard stage of its own, measure them yourself and emit each with record_stage_timing(stage, seconds, ...) (see _preprocess_file in processor.py). Checkpoints that are not dashboard stages belong in one specific, well-named event with their own rich context (see _preprocess_aux_data_with_hermite in processor.py), which is more useful than forcing everything through one generic name.

Only the main process adds stages to the run_summary; stages timed in a worker process reach the log and the dashboard only.

items.title: Colours in the terminal
items.text:
The CLI's colours come from one module, canvodpy.cli.theme; its docstring gives the rules and the reasons. In short: structure (commands, names, descriptions, borders) uses the brand's greens by lightness, and status uses three added colours, each always with its symbol. There is no red, and the colours keep apart with red-green colour blindness.

In a command, print through the shared console and use the roles, not colour names:

from canvodpy.cli.theme import console

console.print(f"[canvod.ok]✓ Wrote {path}[/canvod.ok]")
console.print("[canvod.warning]⚠️ No recipe for canopy_01[/canvod.warning]")
console.print(f"[canvod.error]❌ File not found: {path}[/canvod.error]")
Role For canvod.ok, canvod.done done, valid, written (✓); done in bold, for the end of a run canvod.warning needs attention, skipped, not set (⚠️, ⊘) canvod.error failed, invalid, refused (❌) canvod.danger before a step that can't be undone canvod.heading, canvod.name headings; names and values canvod.text descriptions canvod.border panel borders

test_cli_theme.py fails on a colour name ([red], style="green") or an unknown role in a CLI module, and checks each colour's contrast to the background and the distance between the colours as seen with red-green colour blindness. To change a colour, change PALETTES in theme.py and keep those tests passing for both backgrounds.

The logo of the banner (canvodpy.cli.banner) is drawn from the SVG in docs/assets/logo by scripts/render_logo.py. When the logo changes, draw its frames again:

uv run scripts/render_logo.py docs/assets/logo/canvodpy_logo_dark_mode.svg \
    canvodpy/src/canvodpy/cli/logo_frames.txt.gz

items.title: Keeping your fork in sync
items.text:
If you are working from a fork (rather than a direct clone), periodically pull updates from the upstream repository:

git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
git push origin main

# Then update your feature branch:
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main

If upstream is not configured, add it once:

git remote add upstream git@github.com:TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git

Detailed fork sync guide

items.title: Pre-commit hooks
items.text: just hooks installs Git hooks that run automatically on every commit. If any hook fails, the commit is rejected: your changes stay staged but no commit is created.

items.title: What runs
items.text: Hook Stage Effect ruff check --fix pre-commit Lints and auto-fixes Python code ruff format pre-commit Formats Python code uv-lock pre-commit Verifies uv.lock matches pyproject.toml trailing-whitespace pre-commit Strips trailing whitespace check-added-large-files pre-commit Blocks large files from being committed detect-private-key pre-commit Prevents accidental secret commits end-of-file-fixer pre-commit Ensures files end with one newline commitizen commit-msg Validates Conventional Commits format

items.title: When your commit is rejected
items.text:
# Most common: ruff auto-fixed your code. Stage the fixes and retry:
git add -u && git commit -m "feat(readers): your message"

# If commitizen rejects your message, use the correct format:
git commit -m "type(scope): description"
# types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci
# scopes: readers, aux, grids, vod, store, viz, utils, naming, ops, docs, ci, deps

# If uv-lock is out of date:
uv sync && git add uv.lock && git commit -m "feat(readers): your message"

Full troubleshooting guide

items.title: Contributing workflow
items.text:
git checkout -b feature/my-feature
# … make changes in packages/<pkg>/src/ …
# … add tests in packages/<pkg>/tests/ …
just check && just test
git add packages/<pkg>/src/... packages/<pkg>/tests/...
git commit -m "feat(readers): add RINEX 4.0 support"
git push origin feature/my-feature
# → open pull request on GitHub

items.title: Conventional commit scopes
items.text: readers · aux · grids · vod · store · viz · utils · naming · ops · docs · ci · deps

items.title: Continuous Integration
items.text:
Every push and PR triggers GitHub Actions workflows:

Workflow Checks Code Quality ruff lint, ruff format, ty type-check, lockfile consistency Test with Coverage pytest \(\rightarrow\) coverage.lcov \(\rightarrow\) Coveralls Platform Tests Multi-OS, multi-Python-version test matrix

Coverage reports are posted as PR comments and tracked on Coveralls over time. To run coverage locally:

just test-coverage    # generates HTML report

items.title: Private or local add-on packages
items.text:
You may want to develop an add-on package alongside canVODpy that is not part of the public repository, for example a private algorithm, a site-specific extension, or an experimental module you are not yet ready to publish.

The recommended pattern keeps the public workspace and lock file clean while letting you use the package locally without friction.

items.title: The pattern
items.text:
1. Place the package inside packages/

packages/
  canvod-myprivatepackage/
    pyproject.toml
    src/
      canvod/myprivatepackage/

2. Add it to .gitignore (so it is never accidentally committed)

packages/canvod-myprivatepackage

3. Exclude it from the uv workspace in the root pyproject.toml

[tool.uv.workspace]
members  = ["packages/*", "canvodpy"]
exclude  = ["packages/canvod-myprivatepackage"]

This keeps uv.lock identical for everyone else. CI never sees the directory, so it resolves the same 240 packages with or without your local copy.

4. Install locally with uv pip install

uv pip install -e packages/canvod-myprivatepackage/

uv pip install installs directly into the virtual environment. It does not modify pyproject.toml or uv.lock. After a fresh uv sync, re-run the command to restore your local install.

items.title: Upgrade path
items.text:
When the package is ready to become public:

  1. Remove it from .gitignore and from the exclude list.
  2. Commit the package directory.
  3. Run uv lock and commit the updated uv.lock.

It becomes a first-class workspace member and appears in the lock for everyone.

items.title: Why not git submodules?
items.text: You could also host the private package in its own repository and add it as a git submodule. actions/checkout@v4 does not initialize submodules by default, so CI would still see an empty directory. The trade-off is that the uv.lock would diverge between users who have initialized the submodule and those who have not, requiring everyone to keep the exclude in place anyway. For a single-developer private add-on the simpler approach is preferred.

items.title: All just commands
items.text:
just                     # list all commands
just check               # lint + format + type-check
just test                # run all tests
just sync                # install/update dependencies
just clean               # remove build artifacts
just hooks               # install pre-commit hooks
canvodpy config init     # scaffold canvod-settings.yaml from template
just config-init-interactive  # scaffold canvod-settings.yaml via guided wizard
just config-validate     # validate configuration
just config-show         # view resolved configuration
just doctor              # environment + config diagnostics
just store-list          # list every site's gnss/vod stores + status
just store-info SITE     # branches/groups/stats for one site's store
just store-log SITE      # commit history graph for one site's store
just store-migrate-metadata SITE  # move an older store to repository metadata
just store-migrate-layout SITE    # move a store written by appending to day blocks
just docs                # preview documentation (opens the browser)
just docs-lint           # language check of the docs (Vale, Google style)
just docs-links          # link check of the built docs (lychee)
just build-all           # build all packages
just deps-report         # dependency metrics report
just deps-mermaid        # mermaid dependency graph

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
No module named 'canvod.X'

Run uv sync to install/reinstall packages in editable mode.

Command not found: just

Install just: brew install just (macOS) or see contributor-setup.

Tests fail after dependency changes 
uv sync --all-extras
uv.lock needs to be updated; CI fails but local works

An untracked directory inside packages/ is being picked up by the packages/* workspace glob and included in the lock. CI does not have the directory and therefore resolves fewer packages, causing a mismatch.

Identify the culprit:

git ls-tree HEAD packages/   # shows only committed packages
ls packages/                 # shows all local packages (including untracked)

Any directory present locally but absent from the git ls-tree output is the source of the divergence. Follow the Private or Local Add-on Packages pattern to exclude it and regenerate the lock.

items.title: How the release infrastructure works
items.text:
This page documents the release chain, from commit message to PyPI upload. The steps to follow are in Releasing; the rules behind the versions are in Versioning.

  • Conventional Commits

    Structured commit messages (feat, fix, docs and others), checked by commitizen on every commit. They fill the changelogs.

    Details

  • Versions per package

    Each package has its own version, chosen by the maintainer; canvodpy pins every package exactly. scripts/release.py checks the choice and writes versions, pins, changelogs and uv.lock.

    Details

  • GitHub Releases

    The canvodpy tag starts a workflow that drafts a GitHub release from canvodpy's CHANGELOG.md section and waits for the maintainer.

    Details

  • PyPI Publishing

    publish_pypi.yml, started by hand and never by a tag, publishes the packages whose release tag points at the commit.

    Details

  • OIDC Authentication

    Short-lived tokens from GitHub, no stored API keys.

    Details

items.title: 1. Conventional commits
items.text:
Format: 

<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

<footer>


feat(readers): add RINEX 4.0 support
fix(vod): correct tau calculation
docs: update installation guide

The commit-msg hook (installed by just hooks, .pre-commit-config.yaml) runs commitizen's check and rejects other messages (fixed bug, WIP). The [tool.commitizen] section of the root pyproject.toml configures only this check; commitizen does not bump versions here.

The types sort the changelog lines (feat \(\rightarrow\) Feat, fix \(\rightarrow\) Fix, perf, refactor, everything else \(\rightarrow\) Other; type!: \(\rightarrow\) BREAKING CHANGES). They do not decide the version: the maintainer does.

items.title: 2. Versions and changelogs
items.text:
scripts/release.py, through three recipes:

Recipe What it does just release-status For each package: version, last release tag, and the commits since that tag that touched the package's folder just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0 Runs the tests, checks the choice, writes the versions, canvodpy's pins, the changelogs and uv.lock, commits them on release/v1.1.0 just tag-release On the merged commit on main: tags every package version without a tag; does not push

Checks before anything is written (a refused release names every problem and changes nothing):

  1. canvodpy is part of the release (it pins every package).
  2. Each version goes up and has no tag yet.
  3. canvodpy's increment (patch, minor, major) is at least the largest increment of the packages released with it.
  4. Every package that requires a released package (canvod-config>=1.0.0,<2) admits the new version; a major release needs the ranges widened by hand first.
  5. The release files (pyproject.toml files, uv.lock, CHANGELOG.md files) have no uncommitted changes.

Changelogs. Every package has a CHANGELOG.md in its folder; canvodpy's is the one at the repository root. A release inserts a section after the <!-- insertion marker --> line of each released package, built from the commits since its last tag that touched its folder (git log <tag>..HEAD -- <folder>). canvodpy's section lists its own commits and every pinned package version, marking the new ones. The sections can be edited in the release pull request.

Tags. <package>-vX.Y.Z for the packages (canvod-store-v1.1.0), vX.Y.Z for canvodpy. A package without a tag of its own (before per-package versions) counts from the last vX.Y.Z tag, when all packages were released together. Versions are written as Python normalizes them, so a pre-release is 1.1.0rc1, tagged v1.1.0rc1.

items.title: 3. Draft releases
items.text:
.github/workflows/release.yml runs when a canvodpy tag (v*.*.*) is pushed. Package tags (canvod-store-v1.1.0) do not match and get no release of their own, so Zenodo archives one version per canvodpy release.

  1. Checks out the tagged commit.
  2. Takes canvodpy's CHANGELOG.md section for the tag (from ## v1.1.0 ( to the next ##) as the release notes; fails if there is none.
  3. Creates a draft release (a pre-release for a, b and rc versions) and waits for the maintainer to publish it.
Maintainer                          GitHub Actions               GitHub
    | just release ..., PR, merge         |                           |
    | just tag-release, git push tags     |                           |
    |----------------------------------------------------------------->|
    |                                     | v1.1.0 pushed             |
    |                                     |<--------------------------|
    |                                     | notes from CHANGELOG.md   |
    |                                     | draft release             |
    |                                     |-------------------------->|
    | review the draft, "Publish release" |                           |
    |----------------------------------------------------------------->|

items.title: 4. PyPI publishing
items.text:
Workflow Runs on Publishes to publish_pypi.yml by hand only: gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref v1.1.0 PyPI

It checks out the tagged commit with all tags and build exactly the packages whose release tag points at that commit (scripts/release.py tagged): for the v1.1.0 example, canvodpy and canvod-store, nothing else. Tagging and publishing to PyPI are separate decisions: a tag is not a promise that PyPI has the version.

PyPI (Python Package Index) hosts wheels and source distributions. A pre-release (1.0.0b1) goes to PyPI too, through the same workflow; uv and pip install it only when asked for it. Uploads to PyPI are permanent: a version can never be uploaded twice, so a broken release is fixed by the next patch version.

items.title: 5. Trusted Publishing with OIDC
items.text:
The workflow authenticates to PyPI with OpenID Connect instead of stored API tokens:

  1. GitHub issues the workflow run a short-lived token (JWT) saying which repository, workflow, and environment it is.
  2. The publish job sends it to PyPI (uv publish, permission id-token: write, given only to the publish job; the build job has no upload permission).
  3. PyPI checks the signature and that repository, workflow, and environment match a trusted publisher configured for the project. It then returns a PyPI API token that is valid for 15 minutes and only for the projects with a matching publisher.
  4. uv publish uploads the packages with that token (OIDC trusted publishing explained).

Each project on PyPI (every package is its own project) needs the trusted publisher once:

Owner:             TUW-GEO
Repository name:   canvodpy
Workflow name:     publish_pypi.yml
Environment name:  pypi

The GitHub environment pypi (Settings \(\rightarrow\) Environments) can require a reviewer and a wait timer before the upload runs.

New package: a package that isn't on PyPI yet has no project to add the publisher to. Add a pending publisher instead, under Publishing in your PyPI account settings. It takes the package name and the four fields of the preceding block. The first upload creates the project and turns the pending publisher into a normal one. PyPI can refuse a second pending publisher while one is pending; then upload that package first.

Why OIDC: no secret to store or rotate; the PyPI token is valid for 15 minutes and only for the projects whose publisher matches this repository, workflow, and environment.

items.title: Complete example
items.text:
Releasing a fix in canvod-grids and a feature in canvod-store:

git switch main && git pull origin main
just release-status
# canvod-grids 1.0.0 (since canvod-grids-v1.0.0: 1 commits)
#     1a2b3c4 fix(grids): ...
# canvod-store 1.0.0 (since canvod-store-v1.0.0: 3 commits)
#     ...
just release canvod-grids=1.0.1 canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0
git push -u origin release/v1.1.0
gh pr create --title "bump: canvodpy 1.1.0 (canvod-grids 1.0.1, canvod-store 1.1.0)" --body "..."
# merged once CI passes, then on main:
git switch main && git pull origin main
just tag-release
git push origin v1.1.0   # on its own: it starts the draft release
git push origin canvod-grids-v1.0.1 canvod-store-v1.1.0
# draft release v1.1.0 appears: review, publish
gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref v1.1.0

Users then install uv add canvodpy==1.1.0 (the whole tested mix) or uv add canvod-store==1.1.0 on its own.

items.title: Commit message rejected
items.text: Commit message does not follow conventional commits format: write type(scope): subject, for example git commit --amend -m "fix(vod): correct tau calculation".

items.title: Release refused
items.text: just release prints Not released: and one line per problem; nothing was written. See Releasing.

items.title: Draft release missing
items.text: The tag must be a canvodpy tag (v1.1.0), and CHANGELOG.md must have a section ## v1.1.0 (...) on the tagged commit.

items.title: PyPI workflow publishes nothing
items.text: No package's release tag points at this commit: run it with --ref <canvodpy tag> after just tag-release and pushing the tags.

items.title: OIDC upload failing
items.text: The workflow is not configured for publishing: check that the project on PyPI has the trusted publisher described earlier (each package separately), with the same workflow file and environment name, and that the workflow has id-token: write.

items.title: How OIDC trusted publishing works
items.text:
Summary

OIDC lets GitHub Actions publish to PyPI without passwords or stored tokens. The workflow proves its identity with a signed token from GitHub, and PyPI answers with an API token that is valid for 15 minutes.

items.title: Stored API tokens versus OIDC
items.text:
Stored API token

  • Long-lived: valid until someone revokes it
  • Kept in GitHub secrets, from where it can leak
  • Rotated by hand

Trusted publishing (OIDC)

  • No secret stored anywhere
  • The API token PyPI issues expires after 15 minutes
  • Bound to one repository, workflow file, and environment

In the words of the PyPI docs, "PyPI's normal API tokens are long-lived." "Trusted Publishing avoids this problem because the tokens minted expire automatically."

items.title: The flow
items.text:
OIDC (OpenID Connect) is an identity layer on OAuth 2.0. GitHub issues a signed token (a JWT) that says which repository, workflow, and environment a job runs in; PyPI checks it against the trusted publishers registered for a project.

┌──────────────────────┐
│ Maintainer           │
│ gh workflow run      │
│ publish_pypi.yml     │
│ --ref v1.0.0         │
└──────┬───────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ GitHub Actions workflow                                 │
│                                                         │
│ 1. Builds the packages                                  │
│ 2. Requests a JWT from GitHub's OIDC provider           │
│ 3. Sends the JWT to PyPI                                │
└──────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PyPI                                                    │
│                                                         │
│ ✓ Verifies the JWT signature (GitHub's public key)      │
│ ✓ Matches the claims against the trusted publishers:    │
│     • repository: TUW-GEO/canvodpy                      │
│     • workflow file: publish_pypi.yml                   │
│     • environment: pypi                                 │
│ → Issues an API token (15 minutes) for every project    │
│   with a matching publisher                             │
└──────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ The workflow uploads the packages with that API token   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

items.title: 1. Registration (one-time setup)
items.text:
You register a trusted publisher for each project on PyPI. It says, in effect, that GitHub Actions in repository TUW-GEO/canvodpy, workflow publish_pypi.yml, environment pypi, may publish canvod-readers.

No secrets are exchanged. This only tells PyPI what to expect.

items.title: 2. Workflow run
items.text:
A maintainer starts the workflow on a release tag (gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref v1.0.0). Its publish job has:

permissions:
  id-token: write  # ← may request an OIDC token

items.title: 3. The token GitHub issues
items.text:
GitHub's OIDC provider issues a JWT with claims like these (shortened):

{
  "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "sub": "repo:TUW-GEO/canvodpy:environment:pypi",
  "aud": "pypi",
  "repository": "TUW-GEO/canvodpy",
  "repository_owner": "TUW-GEO",
  "repository_owner_id": "<numeric owner id>",
  "workflow": "Publish to PyPI",
  "job_workflow_ref": "TUW-GEO/canvodpy/.github/workflows/publish_pypi.yml@refs/tags/v1.0.0",
  "environment": "pypi",
  "ref": "refs/tags/v1.0.0"
}

GitHub signs it with its private key. Anyone can verify the signature with GitHub's public keys at https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/jwks.

items.title: 4. Exchange and upload
items.text:
uv publish --trusted-publishing always:

  1. Gets the JWT from GitHub's OIDC provider
  2. Sends it to PyPI, which verifies it and returns a short-lived API token
  3. Uploads the packages with that token

items.title: 5. What PyPI checks
items.text:
From PyPI's internals page:

  • The signature, "to ensure that it's actually coming from the expected provider"
  • The claims against the registered publishers: repository, workflow file, and environment
  • The repository_owner_id claim, which PyPI always checks for GitHub publishers

If the claims match, PyPI issues "a short-lived (15 minute) PyPI API token," which "is scoped to every project with a matching Trusted Publisher." If nothing matches, the upload is refused.

items.title: Scope of a publisher
items.text:
Each trusted publisher is bound to:

Scope Example Purpose Repository TUW-GEO/canvodpy Only this repository can publish Workflow publish_pypi.yml Only this workflow file Environment pypi Only this environment Package canvod-readers Only this PyPI project

So a JWT from another repository, workflow file, or environment gets no token, and the token a run gets works only for the projects whose publishers match.

items.title: Why several publishers?
items.text:
The publisher belongs to the project, so every package needs its own:

PyPI trusted publishers:
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────┐
│ Package          │ Repository       │ Workflow         │ Env  │
├──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────┤
│ canvod-readers   │ TUW-GEO/canvodpy │ publish_pypi.yml │ pypi │
│ canvod-auxiliary │ TUW-GEO/canvodpy │ publish_pypi.yml │ pypi │
│ canvod-grids     │ TUW-GEO/canvodpy │ publish_pypi.yml │ pypi │
│ ...              │ ...              │ ...              │ ...  │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────┘

If you only register canvodpy, the workflow can't publish canvod-readers.

items.title: Deployment environment
items.text:
environment: pypi  # ← Why this matters
  • Protection rules: the environment can require a reviewer's approval before the job runs, and limit which branches or tags may deploy to it.
  • History: the repository lists every deployment to the environment and who approved it.
  • OIDC scope: the JWT names the environment, so a publisher registered for environment pypi matches no run in any other environment.

items.title: 1. Mismatched environment name
items.text:
Workflow says: 

environment: pypi

PyPI registered with: 

Environment: py-pi  # ← Note the dash!

Result: no publisher matches, and the upload is refused.

items.title: 2. Mismatched workflow file
items.text:
Workflow filename: 

.github/workflows/publish-pypi.yml  # ← Note the dash!

PyPI registered with: 

Workflow: publish_pypi.yml  # ← Note the underscore!

Result: no publisher matches, and the upload is refused.

items.title: 3. Package not registered
items.text:
You set up a publisher for canvodpy but forgot canvod-readers.

Result: canvodpy publishes, canvod-readers fails.

items.title: Further reading
items.text:
• PyPI trusted publishers documentation
  • OpenID Connect
  • GitHub OIDC documentation
  • GitHub JWKS endpoint

Questions? Open an issue or a discussion.

items.title: DOI and Citations Setup (Zenodo)
items.text: Make canvodpy properly citable with a permanent DOI for academic papers using Zenodo + CITATION.cff.

items.title: Zenodo
items.text:
Zenodo is a research data repository operated by CERN.

  • Automatic DOI

    Each GitHub release automatically gets a permanent DOI (10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX). No manual uploads.

  • Permanent Archival

    CERN guarantees 20+ years of preservation. Every release is archived forever, so it stays reproducible.

  • FAIR Compliant

    Findable · Accessible · Interoperable · Reusable. Searchable by researchers worldwide, indexed by Google Scholar.

  • GitHub Integration

    Link your repository once. Every subsequent GitHub release triggers automatic archival and DOI minting.

items.title: 1. Initial setup (once)
items.text: You link your GitHub repository to Zenodo: - Zenodo watches for new releases - No manual uploads needed

items.title: 2. Every release
items.text:
just release canvod-store=1.1.0 canvodpy=1.1.0   # release commit on release/v1.1.0: open a PR, merge it
# then, on the merged main:
just tag-release
git push origin v1.1.0   # on its own: it starts the draft release
git push origin canvod-store-v1.1.0

Only the canvodpy tag (v1.1.0) creates a GitHub release, so Zenodo archives one version per canvodpy release; package tags get none.

Zenodo takes the version and date of the record from CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json at the tag. just release writes canvodpy's version and the release date into both (and into codemeta.json), so the record carries the version of the release.

Automatic workflow: 1. GitHub creates release v0.1.0 2. Zenodo detects new release 3. Zenodo archives the release 4. Zenodo mints DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX 5. Zenodo creates citation metadata

items.title: 3. Users cite your work
items.text:
Researchers can cite: 

Bader, N. F. (2026). canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis (v0.1.0).
Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX

A DOI for each version: - v0.1.0 \(\rightarrow\) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12345 - v0.2.0 \(\rightarrow\) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12346 - Concept DOI \(\rightarrow\) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.12344 (always latest)

items.title: Step 1. Create CITATION.cff (done)
items.text:
CITATION.cff enables the "Cite this repository" button on GitHub, exports to BibTeX/APA/EndNote, and provides metadata for Zenodo.

Add your ORCID iD

Edit CITATION.cff line 14 and add your ORCID identifier. Get one at orcid.org/register; it links your publications to your researcher profile.

items.title: 2.1. Create a Zenodo account
items.text:
1. Go to: https://zenodo.org
  2. Click "Sign up"
  3. Important: sign up with GitHub.
  4. Click "Log in with GitHub"
  5. This enables automatic integration

items.title: 2.2. Enable the repository on Zenodo
items.text:
1. After logging in, go to: https://zenodo.org/account/settings/github/
  2. Find TUW-GEO/canvodpy in the list
  3. Toggle ON the switch next to it
  4. Zenodo now watches for releases.

items.title: 2.3. Verify the connection
items.text:
• Should see: "✓ Enabled" next to canvodpy
  • Zenodo archives the next release

items.title: Option A. Test with a beta release
items.text:
git tag -a v0.1.0b2 -m "Test Zenodo DOI creation"
git push origin v0.1.0b2
  • Zenodo creates DOI
  • You can test the process safely

items.title: Option B. Production release
items.text:
just release canvodpy=0.1.0 canvod-readers=0.1.0 ...   # open a PR, merge it
# then, on the merged main:
just tag-release
git push origin v0.1.0   # on its own: it starts the draft release
git push origin canvod-readers-v0.1.0 ...
  • Creates the GitHub release; PyPI follows with gh workflow run publish_pypi.yml --ref v0.1.0
  • Zenodo creates DOI
  • This is the "real" first citable version

items.title: After the release
items.text:
1. Go to: https://zenodo.org/account/settings/github/repository/TUW-GEO/canvodpy
  2. You'll see your release listed
  3. Click to view the DOI
  4. Copy the DOI badge markdown

Example DOI badge: 

[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.12345.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12345)

items.title: Step 4. Add the DOI badge to the README
items.text:
Add to README.md (after other badges):

[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX)

Replace XXXXX with your actual Zenodo ID.

Tip: use the "concept DOI" (always points to latest version)

items.title: Step 5. Update the documentation
items.text:
Add citation section to README.md:

## Citing canvodpy

If you use canvodpy in your research, please cite:

Bader, N. F. (2026). canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis (v0.1.0).
Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX

BibTeX:
\`\`\`bibtex
@software{bader2026canvodpy,
  author       = {Bader, Nicolas François},
  title        = {canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis},
  year         = 2026,
  publisher    = {Zenodo},
  version      = {v0.1.0},
  doi          = {10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX},
  url          = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXX}
}
\`\`\`

items.title: For researchers using the package
items.text:
From GitHub: 1. Click "Cite this repository" (top right) 2. Choose format (APA, BibTeX, etc.) 3. Copy citation

From Zenodo: 1. Visit Zenodo DOI link 2. Click "Export" \(\rightarrow\) Choose format 3. Copy citation

items.title: For papers
items.text:
Researchers cite specific versions:

Correct:

"VOD was calculated with canvodpy v0.1.0 (Bader, 2026)."

Reference:

Bader, N. F. (2026). canvodpy v0.1.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12345

Why version-specific? - Reproducibility: v0.1.0 code is archived forever - Transparency: readers know exactly what was used - FAIR principles: the exact version is findable

items.title: Concept DOI and version DOI
items.text:
Concept DOI (10.5281/zenodo.12344): - Always points to latest version - Use for: general citations, badges

Version DOI (10.5281/zenodo.12345): - Points to specific version (v0.1.0) - Use for: research papers (reproducibility)

items.title: Benefits
items.text: Category What you get Academic recognition Citable software output; the DOI is trackable in citations ORCID integration Links code releases to your researcher profile FAIR compliance Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable Permanent archival CERN preserves every release indefinitely Trusted repository Used by CERN, NASA, and ESA; accepted by all journals

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Repository not visible on Zenodo
  1. Ensure you logged in with GitHub (not email)
  2. Check the repository is public: Zenodo only indexes public repositories
  3. Log out and back in; sync can take a few minutes
No DOI created for a release
  1. Verify the toggle is ON at Zenodo's GitHub settings
  2. Ensure the GitHub release is published (not a draft)
  3. Check your Zenodo email for error notifications
How to update citation metadata?

Update CITATION.cff, then create a new release. Zenodo reads the updated file for the new DOI automatically.

Do old releases get a DOI?

No. Zenodo only archives releases created after the integration was enabled. You can create new patch/beta releases to archive historical code states.

items.text:
Cite button: 

[Cite this repository ▼]
├── APA
├── BibTeX
└── More formats...

Methods section:

References:

Bader, N. F. (2026). canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis (v0.1.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12345

items.title: .zenodo.json
items.text:
For advanced metadata customization, create .zenodo.json:

{
  "title": "canvodpy: GNSS Vegetation Optical Depth Analysis",
  "description": "Python package for VOD calculation from GNSS SNR data",
  "creators": [
    {
      "name": "Bader, Nicolas François",
      "affiliation": "TU Wien",
      "orcid": "0000-0000-0000-0000"
    }
  ],
  "keywords": ["GNSS", "VOD", "vegetation", "remote sensing"],
  "license": "Apache-2.0",
  "communities": [
    {"identifier": "canvodpy"}
  ]
}

communities adds every archived release to the canVODpy community on Zenodo. canvodpy, canvodpy-extensions and canvodpy-test-data all set it.

Note: CITATION.cff is usually enough.

items.text:
• Get ORCID iD (if you don't have one)
  • Update CITATION.cff with your ORCID
  • Create Zenodo account (log in with GitHub)
  • Enable canvodpy on Zenodo settings

items.title: Developing with coding agents
items.text:
canVODpy is developed with coding agents, mostly Claude Code. The repository carries instructions for them, so that an agent works by the same rules as a person and knows the science and the traps before it changes code. You don't need an agent to contribute: the same files are a compact summary of the project's conventions for people too.

Everything here works with free tools only. No step needs a paid service or an API key.

items.title: The instruction files
items.text:
File What it holds AGENTS.md (root) Scientific context, packages, the one way to process data, data contracts, the development workflow, guardrails, and the reading order of these docs canvodpy/AGENTS.md, packages/<package>/AGENTS.md Per package: where things live, invariants and decisions, tests .claude/skills/<task>/SKILL.md Step-by-step guides for recurring tasks: run the pipeline, add a reader or constellation, deprecate code, store safety, the Icechunk 2 API, the link to canvodpy-extensions, releasing CLAUDE.md files One line, @AGENTS.md. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, other agents read AGENTS.md CODING_STANDARDS.md The rules every change follows and the checklist for each change; reviews check against it GLOSSARY.md The project's words, and the words to avoid (Glossary) docs/adr/ The decisions behind canVODpy and why they were made (Decisions) docs/agents/ How the workflow skills below use GitHub issues, triage labels, and the glossary .claude/settings.json Enables the workflow plugin; blocks merging, pushing main or tags and bypassing checks (with scripts/agent_git_guard.py)

Claude Code loads the root file at the start of a session, a package's file when it works in that package, and a task guide when the task fits its description. Other agents read the same Markdown files.

The files describe what cannot be seen quickly in the code: decisions, invariants, where the truth lives. They point at the code instead of copying it, so they go out of date less often.

items.title: Kept correct by a check
items.text: Every path and just recipe named in these files must exist. just check-agent-docs verifies this; it runs in just check, as a pre-commit hook and in CI. Paths in canvodpy-extensions are written extensions:<path> and checked at the extensions commit canvodpy is locked to. A change that makes a statement wrong updates the file in the same pull request.

items.title: The development workflow
items.text:
Contributors develop with one shared workflow: the open source mattpocock/skills, a set of skills for Claude Code. Each step guards against a typical failure of agent-written code: the agent building something other than what you meant, inventing its own words for things, leaving no record of why, writing code without tests, or ignoring the project's rules.

Claude Code loads the skills when it is started in the canvodpy folder, and calls them only by their full name, /mattpocock-skills:<skill>; a short /grill-with-docs is an unknown command, and a short The plain /code-review command is the review built into Claude Code.

Situation Start with What happens An idea or a change to design /mattpocock-skills:grill-with-docs The agent asks you questions in rounds, each with its recommended answer, until every decision is settled. New terms go to the glossary, decisions that are hard to reverse to docs/adr/. A change too big for one session /mattpocock-skills:to-spec, then /mattpocock-skills:to-tickets The settled design becomes a GitHub issue (the spec), split into small tickets that each work on their own. One ticket, or a change that fits one session /mattpocock-skills:implement Test first (/mattpocock-skills:tdd): a failing test, then the code that makes it pass. It ends with /mattpocock-skills:code-review. Review a branch or pull request /mattpocock-skills:code-review Two separate reviews: against CODING_STANDARDS.md, and against the issue the change was made for. Something is broken /mattpocock-skills:diagnosing-bugs First a command that shows the bug, then hypotheses, then the fix with a regression test. After a session that went wrong /mattpocock-skills:retro Suggests checks and rules so the same mistake can't happen again. Not sure which /mattpocock-skills:ask-matt Recommends the skill for your situation.

The full flow is meant for real changes; a typo needs none of it. The domain guides of canVODpy (add a reader, deprecate code, store safety and the others) still apply inside any of these steps. Some skills run helper agents in parallel (/mattpocock-skills:code-review, /mattpocock-skills:implement-spec), which uses more of your agent's quota.

items.title: The code graph
items.text:
just graph builds a graph of the code with graphify: every module, class and function, and who calls, imports, or subclasses whom. It is built from the syntax tree on your machine in about ten seconds, needs no API key, and is never committed (.graphify/). Git hooks rebuild it in the background after each commit, merge and checkout.

just graph-affected add_cell_ids_to_ds_fast   # everything that uses it
just graph-explain VodComputer                # its neighbors, both directions
just graph-path VodComputer TauOmegaZerothOrder

Agents use it before changing or deprecating anything (to find every caller) and before writing new code (to find an existing implementation). Connections marked INFERRED are guesses; check them in the code.

graphify can also call paid language-model services. The just recipes use only its free, local commands, and remove API keys from its environment. Don't run other graphify commands (its output suggests graphify cluster-only, which can call a paid service) or install its assistant skill.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
just sync          # dependencies and git hooks (including the graph rebuild)
just graph         # first build of the code graph
just agent-skills  # the workflow skills (Claude Code plugin); rerun to update
claude             # in the repository root

Start the agent in the repository root: it reads its instructions from there. .claude/settings.json declares the plugin's marketplace and enables the plugin, so Claude Code takes it from there once you trust the repository folder; just agent-skills installs and updates it explicitly. For other coding agents, npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills installs the same skills.

items.title: Guidelines for agent-assisted contributions
items.text:
1. Review all output. A person reviews every change before it is merged and is responsible for it.
  2. Run the checks. just check and the tests of the changed packages (just test-package <package>).
  3. Check scientific claims. Agents can invent references, formulas or values. Compare with primary sources (IGS formats, interface control documents, the literature).
  4. Attribution. Commits with substantial agent help say so in a Co-Authored-By: line.
  5. Agents don't merge. An agent may push its feature branch and open a pull request; it never merges or approves one, never pushes main or tags, never force-pushes and never bypasses a check (--no-verify, skipped hooks, changed settings). Claude Code blocks these through .claude/settings.json and scripts/agent_git_guard.py; don't turn that off. See the Git and GitHub section of CODING_STANDARDS.md.
  6. No secrets. Never give an agent credentials or private data. Hosted agents send what they read to their provider.

items.title: Command line and Python
items.text:
canVODpy runs from Python or from the command line. Both run the same code: canvodpy run creates a Site and processes the days with Site.pipeline(), so the stores hold the same data either way. Use Python to script runs, for example in a notebook, or in a loop over sites; use the command line for scheduled runs.

This page lists the options of both. For a first run, start with Retrieve VOD.

items.title: Process a period
items.text:
PythonCommand line 
from canvodpy import Site

site = Site("ExampleSite")
with site.pipeline() as pipeline:
    for unit in pipeline.run("2025001", "2025007"):
        print(sorted(unit.days), unit.vod.written)

canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --start 2025001 --end 2025007

Dates are YYYYDDD: the year and the day of year, for example 2025032 for February 1, 2025.

Command line Python Meaning --site ExampleSite Site("ExampleSite") Site name under sites: in canvod-settings.yaml. One site per run; see Several sites. --start, --end run(start, end) First and last day, both included; see Which days a run processes. --update-to-latest run(update_to_latest=True) Instead of --start and --end: the days from the last stored day up to the latest day with files; see Update to the latest files. --no-vod run(start, end, vod_analyses=()) Write the observations to the GNSS store and compute no VOD. --vod-calculator run(start, end, calculator=...) The VOD calculator, tau_omega by default. --dry-run pipeline.preview(start, end) or pipeline.preview(update_to_latest=True) List the days, receivers and files a run would process, without processing them. --write-catalog write_catalog(stores_root_dir) after the run After a successful run, write the STAC catalog of every store under the data root. Without it, a run writes no catalog. --label site.pipeline(label=...) Free-text label stored with the run in the run history, for example to group the repetitions of a benchmark. --workers site.pipeline(n_workers=...) Number of worker processes. --config-dir, -c CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR Folder that holds canvod-settings.yaml and recipes/, or the link of a settings file in a GitHub repository; see Where canVODpy finds the settings. --config CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE Overlay file applied on top of canvod-settings.yaml. --ephemeris-source processing.params.ephemeris_source in the settings final (orbit and clock products of an analysis center) or broadcast (the satellite angles an SBF file holds); see Ephemeris sources. --vod-calculator VodComputer(site, calculator=...) VOD calculator; tau_omega unless a plugin adds others. --dashboard None; run canvodpy dashboard Start the performance dashboard for the run's logs. --dashboard-host and --dashboard-port set its address. It stays up after the run until its button shuts it down; --dashboard-stop-at-end stops it with the run.

Options you leave out take their values from the settings file. In Python, set CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR and CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE before you create the Site:

import os

os.environ["CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR"] = "/path/to/config"

canvodpy run --help lists every option.

canvodpy run exits with code 0 when every receiver-day is written or skipped, or when --update-to-latest finds nothing new, and with 1 when it stops, for example on an error in the options or the settings. When it finishes but a receiver-day failed, it names the failed receiver-days and exits with 3; What the run does when something fails lists the reasons. A receiver-day that is written though some of its files failed counts as written. In Python, pipeline.failed_receiver_days lists the failed receiver-days.

Try it in a notebook

Open Site pipeline, Running the pipeline from the command line in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: Which days a run processes
items.text:
A run processes the days you give it. There is no default: a run without --start or --update-to-latest stops with an error, and so does a run with --update-to-latest and --start or --end.

  • --start and --end give the first and last day. Without --end, the run ends today; in Python, run(start) without end ends on the last day with files. The run processes every day in the range. With the default gnss_store_strategy: skip, files that are already in the store are skipped, so running a day twice doesn't duplicate data, and a file that arrived late for a stored day is added.
  • --update-to-latest processes the days from the last stored day on; see below.

In Python, run(start, end) and run(update_to_latest=True) work the same way and raise a ValueError for the same mistakes. process_date processes one day, process_range the days from start to end.

items.title: Update to the latest files
items.text:
canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --update-to-latest

The run chooses the dates and then runs as a run with --start and --end does:

  • Start: the earliest last stored day in the site's GNSS store, counting only the receivers with new files: files after their own last stored day, or files on that day that the store's log book doesn't hold. So a day stored while its files were still arriving, for example by a run at 03:00, gets the rest of its files on the next run; the files already stored are skipped. A receiver whose last day is completely stored and that sends no more files, for example one that was retired, doesn't hold the start back. A receiver with nothing stored yet counts from its first day with files.
  • End: the latest day on which a receiver has files.

It prints the dates it chose, for example update: 2026293 to 2026298. If no receiver has new files, it says so and exits with code 0. If the site's GNSS store holds nothing yet, it stops and asks for --start: the first run of a site names its first day.

A receiver whose files arrive a few days after the others sets the start, so its days are processed when they arrive. A file that arrives late for a day before a receiver's last stored day is not in the range; process that day again with --start and --end.

In Python, pipeline.update_range() returns the dates run(update_to_latest=True) would process, or None if nothing is new.

items.title: Several sites
items.text:
A run processes one site. For several sites, run canvodpy run once per site, for example in a shell loop:

for site in ExampleSite OtherSite; do
    canvodpy run --site "$site" --update-to-latest
done

In Python, create one Site per site and run its pipeline.

items.title: The Site object
items.text:
Site("ExampleSite") reads the settings of one site.

Attribute What it gives you site.receivers All receivers of the site, from the settings site.active_receivers The receivers a run processes: those not set to active: false site.vod_analyses The receiver pairs under vod_analyses site.gnss_store The GNSS store: observations and satellite angles site.vod_store The VOD store site.gnss_store_path, site.vod_store_path Where the stores are, from the settings; read-only site.vod Computes VOD; see Compute VOD site.pipeline() Creates a Pipeline for this site

Both stores are Icechunk repositories; see Storage.

A run creates a site's stores when it first writes data. Before that, site.gnss_store and site.vod_store raise a FileNotFoundError; the paths tell you where a run puts them.

items.title: The Pipeline object
items.text:
A Pipeline reads the files, adds the satellite angles, and writes the GNSS store. Use it in a with block, which closes it at the end.

Method What it does run(start, end=None, update_to_latest=False, vod_analyses=None, calculator="tau_omega") What canvodpy run does: stores the days from start to end (or, with update_to_latest=True, the days of Update to the latest files) in units of days, then computes the VOD of each unit's days from the GNSS store. Yields one RunUnit per unit: days (each day stored, with the groups that stored it), vod (the days with VOD written, already stored, or missing and why, per analysis) and vod_error (why the VOD of the unit failed, if it did). vod_analyses=() computes no VOD. process_date(date) Processes one day and reads it back from the GNSS store. Returns one dataset per receiver. process_range(start, end) Processes the days from start to end and reads each one back. Yields (date, datasets) for one day at a time. Use it to work with the data in Python; run reads nothing back and is faster. preview(start=None, end=None, update_to_latest=False) Returns the days, receivers and files a run would process. Without dates, it covers every day it finds data for. update_range() The first and last day a run with update_to_latest=True processes, or None if no receiver has new files. failed_receiver_days The receiver-days of this pipeline that failed, as (receiver, date) pairs. Empty when every one is written or skipped. close() Ends the pipeline. The with block calls it for you. The worker processes stay for reuse; see Parallel processing.

The datasets are xarray Datasets, keyed by store group: canopy_01 for a canopy receiver, and reference_01_canopy_01 for the data of a reference receiver paired with that canopy receiver.

The arguments of site.pipeline() override the matching settings under processing.params for this pipeline. Setting n_workers turns off the automatic choice of resource_mode: auto:

Argument Meaning n_workers Number of worker processes threads_per_worker Threads that numerical libraries use in each worker keep_vars Observation variables to keep, such as ["SNR"]

The workers' CPU cores and priority come from the settings file; Parallel processing explains them.

items.title: Compute VOD
items.text:
pipeline.run() computes the VOD of the days it stores. site.vod computes VOD for the receiver pairs under vod_analyses on its own.

From the datasets of one day, without writing:

with site.pipeline() as pipeline:
    for date, data in pipeline.process_range("2025001", "2025007"):
        vod = site.vod.compute_day_all(data, write=False)  # every pair
        # or one pair:
        # vod = site.vod.compute_day(data, "canopy_01_vs_reference_01", write=False)

Writing VOD this way (write=True, write_day) is deprecated; see Upgrading.

From observations already in the GNSS store, for example after you change the VOD settings, computed and written in the worker pool:

PythonCommand line 
from datetime import date, timedelta

report = site.vod.compute_days(
    [date(2025, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(31)],
    ["canopy_01_vs_reference_01"],
)
report.missing  # the days without VOD, and why

Each day of each pair is one task in the worker pool, which reads only that day from the GNSS store, so a day takes as long in a large store as in a small one. Without the list of analyses, every pair is computed. A day whose VOD the store already holds from the same GNSS files is not computed again (report.stored), so running it twice adds nothing. A day without data in the canopy or the reference group gets no VOD and is listed in report.missing.

To get the VOD of a time range back as one dataset, use site.vod.compute_bulk:

from datetime import datetime

vod = site.vod.compute_bulk(
    "canopy_01_vs_reference_01",
    start=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    end=datetime(2025, 1, 31, 23, 59, 59),
)

It runs site.vod.compute_days for the days of the range, then reads the VOD from start to end back from the VOD store. start and end are times, both included: datetime(2025, 1, 31) alone would end at midnight at the start of January 31. With write=False, it reads the range into memory and computes the VOD there, without the worker pool, and writes nothing. site.vod.compute_bulk_all computes every pair.

canvodpy vod --site ExampleSite --analysis canopy_01_vs_reference_01 \
    --start 2025001 --end 2025031

The command runs site.vod.compute_days for whole days, from --start to --end; without them, for every day of the GNSS store. It lists the days without VOD.

A day can end up in the GNSS store but not in the VOD store, for example when writing the VOD failed. canvodpy run warns about such days. To list them and compute their VOD:

canvodpy vod-reconcile --site ExampleSite --analysis canopy_01_vs_reference_01
canvodpy vod-reconcile --site ExampleSite --analysis canopy_01_vs_reference_01 --execute

The VOD package page describes the VOD model and its output.

Try it in a notebook

Open VOD retrieval in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: What only the command line does
items.text:
canvodpy run adds a few steps around Site.pipeline():

  • It ends on today when you leave out --end; see Which days a run processes.
  • Before processing, it stops if a VOD store group holds VOD computed from data with other preprocessing settings. In Python, site.vod makes the same check when it writes.
  • It warns about days that are in the GNSS store but not in the VOD store.
  • If the VOD of a unit of days fails, it says which days are left without VOD and continues. pipeline.run() does the same and reports the error in RunUnit.vod_error.
  • It shows the progress per receiver.

items.title: Scheduled runs
items.text:
To process new data every day, schedule canvodpy run with --update-to-latest, for example with cron at 03:00:

0 3 * * * /path/to/canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --update-to-latest --config-dir /path/to/config

For several sites, add one line per site, or call a script with the loop of Several sites.

Cron runs with a minimal environment, so give the full path to canvodpy (which canvodpy prints it) and to the settings folder. A scheduler can check the exit code: 3 means some receiver-days failed.

For Apache Airflow, check_day and process_day in canvodpy.workflows.tasks run the code of canvodpy run for one site and day. process_day raises an error when a receiver-day failed, so Airflow retries the task. Ready-made Airflow DAGs are an optional extension; see Optional extensions.

Try it in a notebook

Open API overview in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

Next in the trail: configuration · parallel processing · architecture

items.title: Configuration guide
items.text:
canVODpy reads its settings from one file, canvod-settings.yaml. The file holds what canVODpy cannot know on its own:

  • Where your data is. Paths differ on every machine.
  • Who you are. Your name, institution, and ORCID go into the metadata of each store.
  • How much of the machine to use. By default, canVODpy sizes the workers to the machine; you can set limits.

Everything else, such as the signals to keep or the chunk sizes, has a default that you can change.

canVODpy checks the file with pydantic-settings when it loads it. A misspelled field name, or text where a number belongs, stops the load with the location of the error.

items.title: Configuration commands
items.text:
canvodpy config init        # create canvod-settings.yaml from the template
canvodpy config edit        # open canvod-settings.yaml in $EDITOR
canvodpy config validate    # check the settings and the receiver data of all sites
canvodpy config show        # print the settings canVODpy uses
canvodpy config explain processing.storage.stores_root_dir  # what a setting means
canvodpy doctor             # show which settings file canVODpy found
