Every setting is described in the Settings reference, and the template links each setting to its entry there. canvodpy config explain prints the same entry in the terminal; it takes the setting's path, or its end (gnss_store.epoch), and names a site or receiver as in your file (sites.my_site.receivers.reference_01.directory). In canvodpy config init --interactive, answer ? to a question to see the entry of the setting it asks for.

canvodpy config show prints the settings after the overlay file is applied, so a value set there appears instead of the value in canvod-settings.yaml.

items.title: Overlay file
items.text:
To change settings for one machine, such as the store path on a cluster, use an overlay file instead of editing canvod-settings.yaml.

Pass --config to any command that accepts it:

# Validate or inspect with an overlay applied
canvodpy config validate --config cluster-overlay.yaml
canvodpy config --config cluster-overlay.yaml show

# Run the pipeline with an overlay
uv run canvodpy run --site mysite --start 2025001 --end 2025028 \
    --config cluster-overlay.yaml

canvodpy config also takes --config before its command, for every command: canvodpy config --config cluster-overlay.yaml validate works too.

Only the fields present in the overlay are changed; everything else is read from the main file. A list in the overlay, such as sids.custom_sids, replaces the list of the main file as a whole; its entries are not added to the main file's.

items.title: An overlay can add and change settings, not remove them
items.text:
The overlay is merged on top of the base canvod-settings.yaml; it can add new keys or override existing ones, but it cannot remove a key that exists in the base file. If your base file defines a site (or any other field) that isn't mentioned in the overlay, that entry stays in the settings canVODpy uses, no matter what the overlay contains.

Rename the template site

The template from canvodpy config init contains a site my_site under sites:. Rename it to your site. If you add your site next to it, my_site stays, with paths such as /path/to/your/gnss/data/my_site, and canvodpy config validate and canvodpy run fail on it. An overlay can't remove it; remove it from canvod-settings.yaml. To start over, run canvodpy config init --force, which overwrites the file.

items.title: Where canVODpy finds the settings
items.text:
canVODpy looks for canvod-settings.yaml in the first of these folders that exists:

  1. $CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, or the folder passed with --config-dir
  2. config/ of a canVODpy clone
  3. ~/.config/canvodpy

The same folder holds the naming recipes, in recipes/. CANVOD_CONFIG_FILE names an overlay file, like --config.

items.title: Settings from a GitHub repository
items.text:
--config-dir and CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR also take the raw link of a settings file in a GitHub repository, at a commit, a tag or a branch:

canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --start 2025001 --end 2025007 \
  -c https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<repo>/refs/tags/<tag>/config/canvod-settings.yaml
  • A receiver's recipe: name is read from the same repository at the same commit, tag or branch, from recipes/<site>/<name>.yaml next to the settings file, as in a local folder. A recipe: that is a URL is read from that URL.
  • Every run downloads the files again, into a folder of the run that only you can read. A run is a canvodpy command, a new Site in Python (also the second one in the same notebook) or an Airflow task. The folders are removed when the process ends: the command, the notebook kernel or the Airflow worker. A run needs network access.
  • Each Airflow task is a run of its own, so the tasks of one DAG run read the link again; they read other settings if the branch moved in between.
  • canvodpy doctor names the link and the sha256 of the settings file.
  • The link is not recorded. Stores keep the settings, the run history keeps the settings of each run, and both name a recipe URL by its file name only.
  • A private repository needs a GitHub token in GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN, for example export GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token).
  • The folders of your machine (stores, auxiliary files, logs) go into an overlay file with --config, so one settings file serves every machine.
  • canvodpy config init and canvodpy config edit write the settings file, so they need a local folder; change settings from a link in their repository.

Settings come from these sources, the first one wins: overlay file, canvod-settings.yaml, package default. Write only the fields you want to change.

canVODpy rejects unknown field names. The error names the closest allowed field and lists all allowed fields; canVODpy never corrects a name by itself:

processing.icechunk.chunk_strategies.vod_stores
  Unknown key 'vod_stores'. Did you mean 'vod_store'? Allowed keys: gnss_store, vod_store

items.title: Minimal working example
items.text:
A canvod-settings.yaml that can create stores needs only these fields; the rest have defaults:

processing:
  metadata:
    author: Jane Scientist
    email: jane.scientist@example.edu
    institution: Example University
    naming_authority: edu.example
    publisher: Example University
    license: CC-BY-4.0

  storage:
    stores_root_dir: /data/stores

  logging:
    log_dir: /data/logs

sites:
  mysite:
    gnss_site_data_root: /data/mysite
    store_description: GNSS-T observations below a beech canopy

    receivers:
      reference_01:
        type: reference
        directory: 01_reference
        paired_canopies: all
      canopy_01:
        type: canopy
        directory: 02_canopy

    vod_analyses:
      canopy_01_vs_reference_01:
        canopy_receiver: canopy_01
        reference_receiver: reference_01

items.title: Content settings: fixed for each store
items.text:
Some settings shape the data a store holds: which signals are kept, how the files are read, the orbit product, the preprocessing, the chunk sizes and the compression. These are the store's content settings. The run that creates a store records them in it, and every later run that writes to the store must have the same ones, also a run on another computer. Data written with other content settings would sit next to the old data in one store without anything showing the difference.

A run compares its settings with the store's twice: when it starts, before it reads a file, and again just before each commit, because another run may have created the store or written to it meanwhile. On a difference the run stops and lists each setting with the store's value and its own. You then have two options:

  • use the store's settings: canvodpy config init --from-store <store> writes a settings file from them, or
  • write to a new store: set processing.storage.gnss_store_name to the kind plus a suffix (for example gnss-recompute, see Store folders), or set another stores_root_dir.

There is no option to write anyway. A store's content settings never change; to process with other settings, create a new store.

Content setting Where The signals kept sids.mode, sids.preset, sids.custom_sids, and the list of signals they give Observables and how they are stored processing.params.keep_gnss_observables, aggregate_glonass_fdma, store_radial_distance, store_delta_snr, store_radial_diff, store_sbf_raw_observables, store_sbf_metadata How files are read and paired processing.params.rinex_v3_parser, file_pairing, receiver_position_mode, ephemeris_source The orbit product processing.aux_data.agency, product_type, fetch_clock Preprocessing all of processing.preprocessing, statistics included Store layout processing.icechunk.compression_algorithm, compression_level, inline_chunk_threshold_bytes, manifest_splitting_enabled, manifest_splitting_epoch_range, chunk_strategies.gnss_store Maintenance all of processing.storage.maintenance Each receiver type, reader_format, paired_canopies

A VOD store keeps its own content settings too. It has no SIDs, receivers or site entries of its own; it records the settings that shape the VOD output and the content-settings hash of the GNSS store it was computed from (gnss_content_hash), so a run that computes VOD from a GNSS store with other content settings stops.

VOD content setting Where The VOD output options processing.params.store_delta_snr, store_radial_diff Store layout processing.icechunk.compression_algorithm, compression_level, inline_chunk_threshold_bytes, manifest_splitting_enabled, manifest_splitting_epoch_range, chunk_strategies.vod_store Maintenance all of processing.storage.maintenance Where the VOD came from gnss_content_hash (the GNSS store's content-settings hash)

The calculator and its parameters are recorded per VOD group ({calculator}/{analysis}) when the group is first written, and every later write compares them: a group never holds results computed with other calculator parameters. On a difference the run stops and names each parameter with both values; use a new analysis name (canvodpy store amend --add-vod-analysis) or a new VOD store.

Every other setting may differ from run to run: the resources (resource_mode, n_max_threads, memory), the Icechunk cache and concurrency settings, aux_data.ftp_timeout_s, logging, folders, credentials, the store strategies, keeper_tags, netcdf_compression, and a receiver's directory, naming and recipe. The metadata (processing.metadata, processing.references, descriptions, receiver hardware and antenna) is written into the store when it's created and changes only with canvodpy store amend.

canvodpy store info <site> shows when and by whom a store's content settings were set, and their hash. In Python, show_metadata(store_path, section="content") from canvod.store_metadata lists them in full. A receiver added to a store with canvodpy store amend --add-receiver brings its own three content settings from the settings file.

A store created before canVODpy kept content settings is refused by runs until it has them. canvodpy store migrate-metadata <site> takes them from the settings recorded in the store's first commit. A setting that commit doesn't record, such as the paired_canopies of a reference receiver, isn't guessed: the command stops, lists it, and you give the value the data was written with, for example --set sites.mysite.receivers.reference_01.paired_canopies=[canopy_01]. A setting the data show, such as processing.preprocessing or store_delta_snr, is read from the data, since canVODpy 0.x recorded settings its runs didn't follow (Move an older store).

ADR 0019 records why (Decisions).

items.title: Join or reproduce a store
items.text:
A store's content settings are what a second machine must match to write into that store. canvodpy config init --from-store <store> writes a settings file from them, which is how a fresh worker joins a store, and how anyone reproduces the processing of a store they can open (a published one, or a copy):

canvodpy config init --from-store /data/stores/fangorn/gnss
canvodpy config init --from-store s3://my-bucket/fangorn/gnss

<store> is the store's directory, or its s3://bucket/prefix URL. The written file keeps:

  • the store's content settings, unchanged. They must stay as they are: other settings mean a different store (see Content settings);
  • the site and its receivers as the store describes them (the site name, description, coordinates, the store's description, and each receiver's description, recipe and recorded data directory as the default);
  • processing.storage.stores_root_dir and gnss_store_name, taken from the store argument: <root>/<site>/<name>;

and writes TODO for the values the run owner fills in: the folders of their computer, which stores never record (gnss_site_data_root, aux_data_dir, shared_aux_cache_dir, log_dir), each receiver's directory, and processing.metadata.author, email and institution. Interactive (the default) asks for each and offers the store's recorded receiver directory as the default; --no-interactive keeps the TODO values.

Credentials are never written. At the end the command prints the environment variables to set instead: the NASA Earthdata one for CDDIS, and the AWS_* ones for a store on S3. An existing settings file is not overwritten, also with --force.

canvodpy config validate lists every TODO value with its dotted key and exits with code 1, so a settings file written this way is easy to finish. A store without content settings (created before canVODpy kept them) is refused, naming canvodpy store migrate-metadata.

items.title: processing:
items.text:
Metadata, resources, storage, and ephemeris products.

processing:
  metadata:
    author: Your Name
    email: your.email@example.com
    institution: Your Institution
    naming_authority: org.example  # your domain in reverse; required to create a store
    publisher: Example University  # required to create a store
    license: CC-BY-4.0  # SPDX identifier, or "other"; required to create a store
    initials: JD  # who set a new store's content settings or changed its metadata; required to amend or migrate
    # optional: orcid, institution_ror, department, research_group,
    # website, publisher_url, license_uri (required when license is "other")

  credentials:
    nasa_earthdata_acc_mail: null

  aux_data:
    agency: COD          # SP3/CLK analysis center code
    product_type: final  # final or rapid; the agency must publish it
    # fetch_clock: false # true adds the CLK files; VOD does not use them

  params:
    keep_gnss_observables: [SNR]   # observables to keep (SNR, Pseudorange, Phase, Doppler)
    rinex_v3_parser: validated     # 'unvalidated_fast' is DANGEROUS: no checks, your responsibility
    store_radial_distance: false   # store satellite distance (r)
    receiver_position_mode: shared # or per_receiver
    file_pairing: complete         # or paired
    ephemeris_source: final        # or broadcast (SBF only)

    # --- Resource management ---
    resource_mode: auto            # auto or manual
    # n_max_threads: 4             # required if manual
    # cpu_affinity: [0, 1, 2, 3]  # CPU cores (manual only; not on macOS)
    # nice_priority: 10            # manual only; 0=normal, 19=lowest priority

  # Optional; nothing is applied unless set (see Preprocessing)
  # preprocessing:
  #   temporal_aggregation:
  #     freq: "1min"               # divides one day
  #     method: median             # mean or median (floating-point variables)
  #     integer_method: first      # first, last or middle (integer flags)
  #   grid_assignment:
  #     grid_type: equal_area
  #     angular_resolution: 2.0    # degrees

  netcdf_compression:              # NetCDF files written by the RINEX readers
    zlib: true
    complevel: 5

  icechunk:
    compression_level: 3
    compression_algorithm: zstd
    inline_chunk_threshold_bytes: 512
    chunk_strategies:
      gnss_store:
        epoch: 180    # epochs per file (15 min at 5 s sampling)
        sid: -1
      vod_store:
        epoch: 180    # as gnss_store
        sid: -1

  storage:
    stores_root_dir: /path/to/stores
    gnss_store_strategy: skip         # skip, overwrite, or unsafe_append; see the warning below

  logging:
    log_dir: /path/to/logs            # required for a run

items.title: Key fields
items.text:
Field Values Description params.keep_gnss_observables list GNSS observables to retain (default [SNR]). With the validated parser, only the fields of these observables are read and checked, so a malformed field of a left-out observable doesn't drop its epoch. params.rinex_v3_parser validated, unvalidated_fast How RINEX v3 files are parsed. validated (default) checks every epoch and drops (and logs) epochs that fail. unvalidated_fast is dangerous: no checks, corrupted records can enter the store, and the results are entirely your responsibility; every use emits an UnvalidatedParserWarning. Both give the identical dataset for a valid file. params.receiver_position_mode shared, per_receiver shared uses canopy receiver position for all receivers (enables 1:1 SNR comparison). per_receiver uses each receiver's own position. params.file_pairing complete, paired complete ingests all files per receiver independently. paired only processes dates where both receivers have data. params.ephemeris_source final, broadcast final computes satellite positions from agency SP3/CLK products. broadcast uses the satellite angles the receiver computed from the broadcast ephemeris (SBF SatVisibility blocks; almanac-based angles are not used; SBF only, no SP3/CLK download, faster but less accurate). aux_data.fetch_clock true, false Whether to download and interpolate CLK clock-correction files alongside SP3 (only applies to ephemeris_source: final). Default false: VOD does not use clock data. true adds each satellite's clock correction to the GNSS store as the variable clock. params.days_per_batch 1–30 Deprecated, removed in v2.0.0; prints a FutureWarning. Only caps the days per unit, which the run sizes from the memory budget (Parallel processing). Leave it out. params.resource_mode auto, manual auto starts one worker per physical CPU core and leaves at least two CPU threads free for the operating system. manual uses the limits you set (n_max_threads is then required); use it on shared servers. params.store_radial_distance true, false Whether to store satellite radial distance in the output. params.store_sbf_raw_observables true, false SBF only: add the pre-correction observables (SNR_raw, Pseudorange_unsmoothed, Pseudorange_raw, Phase_raw) to the observations. Default true. params.store_sbf_metadata true, false SBF only: store the per-file metadata dataset sbf_obs (SatVisibility geometry, MeasExtra, PVT, DOP, receiver status) under {group}/metadata/sbf_obs, in the same commit as the observations. Default true. storage.stores_root_dir folder or S3 URL Where the stores are, one folder per site: a local folder, or s3://bucket/prefix to write the stores on S3, experimental (Stores on S3). Credentials, region and endpoint of S3 come only from the environment. Other URLs are refused. storage.gnss_store_strategy skip, overwrite, unsafe_append What to do when a file already exists in the store. skip (default) is the normal case. See warning below before ever using unsafe_append. logging.log_dir folder Folder of the log files. Required: a run stops if it is not set. Diagnostics describes the files.

Parallel processing explains resource_mode, n_max_threads, max_memory_gb and the other resource settings.

gnss_store_strategy: unsafe_append writes duplicate epochs

skip, the default, leaves a file that is already in the store alone, so a second run over the same files changes no data; the log book gets a row per file it saw, with action set to skipped. A run finds the days whose files are all stored by the files' hashes, before it downloads auxiliary data or reads a file, writes their rows in one commit and passes the days on to the VOD phase, which computes only VOD that is missing. overwrite deletes the stored epochs of the file's time span and writes the file again. Use it after a fix in canVODpy, such as in a reader, to recompute stored data. The VOD of those days stays as it was: the rewritten files are the same files, so their VOD results are skipped. For VOD of the recomputed data, write it to a new VOD store (set storage.vod_store_name to another name, such as vod-recompute).

unsafe_append writes the file again on top of the stored data, without checking for epochs that are already there. The store then holds each of these epochs twice, and the extra chunks stay in the store. The pipeline and Site.vod.compute_bulk(..., write=False) remove the duplicates when they read; MyIcechunkStore.read_group() does not. On duplicated epochs, .sel() can fail or return several matches, and aligning canopy and reference data multiplies the rows. Don't use unsafe_append unless you need it.

items.title: Ephemeris data sources
items.text:
canVODpy downloads SP3 and CLK products from ESA GSSC, which needs no account. If you set credentials.nasa_earthdata_acc_mail to the email address of a (free) NASA Earthdata account, canVODpy downloads from NASA CDDIS first and falls back to ESA GSSC when that download fails.

aux_data.agency and aux_data.product_type must name a product of the product registry, which also lists the GNSS each product covers; a run and canvodpy config validate stop on any other combination and name the closest products. Ultra-rapid products are not supported.

items.title: sites:
items.text:
Your sites, their receivers, and the receiver pairs to compute VOD for. Each key under sites: is the name of a site.

sites:
  my_site:
    gnss_site_data_root: /data/my_site
    description: null        # optional free-text description
    country: null            # ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, e.g. AT
    latitude: null           # WGS84 decimal degrees
    longitude: null
    altitude_m: null         # meters above WGS84 ellipsoid

    receivers:
      reference_01:
        type: reference
        directory: 01_reference
        reader_format: auto           # auto, rinex3, rinex3_stripped, rinex2, sbf, nmea, or a reader plugin
        paired_canopies: all          # 'all' or list of canopy receiver names
      canopy_01:
        type: canopy
        directory: 02_canopy
        reader_format: auto

    vod_analyses:
      canopy_01_vs_reference_01:
        canopy_receiver: canopy_01
        reference_receiver: reference_01

items.title: Receiver fields
items.text:
Field Default Description type -- reference or canopy. directory -- Subdirectory under gnss_site_data_root holding this receiver's files. reader_format auto Reader for the receiver's files: rinex3, rinex3_stripped (signal strengths only, faster), rinex2, sbf, nmea, or the name of an installed reader plugin (Your Own Readers and VOD Calculators). auto detects it per day, never choosing a plugin: SBF and NMEA by file type, and the RINEX version from the header. A day whose files need different readers stops the run with an error; then set the reader, or keep each format in its own directory. A canopy receiver and its reference must record the same file format (rinex3 and rinex3_stripped both read RINEX 3); mixed formats are rejected when the settings load, or, with auto, by canvodpy config validate and at the start of a run. paired_canopies -- Which canopy receivers this reference is paired with: all or a list of canopy receiver names. Required for reference receivers, must not be set for canopy receivers. receiver_hardware -- Optional: manufacturer, model, serial_number and firmware of the receiver. Copied into the GNSS store's metadata when the store is created or the receiver is added to it. antenna -- Optional: manufacturer, model and radome (IGS names), serial_number, height_m (meters), choke_ring (true or false) and polarization (RHCP, the standard, LHCP or dual-pol) of the antenna. Copied into the GNSS store's metadata like receiver_hardware.

Leave out the receiver and antenna details you don't want to disclose; every field in them is optional.

items.title: sids:
items.text:
The signals (signal IDs, SIDs) to keep. There are three modes:

Mode Behavior all Keep every SID in the file preset Use a named built-in list (see below) custom Keep only the SIDs you list explicitly Default presetAll signalsCustom list

canVODpy has one preset, default: 271 SIDs of MEO satellites of GPS, Galileo, BeiDou, and GLONASS. It leaves out:

  • GEO satellites, which stand still in the sky, and IGSO satellites, which cover only a narrow track;
  • SBAS, IRNSS, and QZSS;
  • GPS L2W: semi-codeless tracking gives a less precise SNR and higher, more variable VOD (Bader et al., 2026, Remote Sensing of Environment 345, 115580).

The list names PRNs, and PRNs are reassigned to other satellites over time. BeiDou C13 and C16 are left out: both were IGSO satellites until 2026-04-18 (IGS satellite metadata), and C13 is a MEO satellite from 2026-04-19 on. For data from 2026-04-19 on, add the C13 SIDs with mode: custom if you want them. SatelliteCatalog shows which satellite held a PRN on a given day (Satellite Catalog). All are RINEX 3 signals. RINEX 2 band-only SIDs (e.g. L1|u) are not included and must be selected explicitly, see RINEX v2.11 Parsing.

sids:
  mode: preset
  preset: default

This is the default. To keep every SID, use mode: all.

sids:
  mode: all

sids:
  mode: custom
  custom_sids:
    - "G01|L1|C"
    - "E01|E1|C"

items.title: Check the settings and the data
items.text:
canvodpy config validate checks the settings file (types, required values, unknown fields), then finds the files of each receiver exactly as canvodpy run does. It reports the days and files a run would process, the files it would skip, and the problems that would stop it, for example two files that cover the same time. A first run, and config validate, refuse to start when a setting the new store needs is missing (its description, publisher, license or naming authority). To check one site:

canvodpy config validate --site <site>

items.title: Optional: non-canonical filenames
items.text:
A run processes only files that follow the file naming convention. For a receiver whose files have other names, set a naming recipe:

sites:
  my_site:
    receivers:
      reference_01:
        recipe: my_site_reference

The recipe is read from <config dir>/recipes/<site>/<recipe>.yaml and gives each file a canonical name without renaming it on disk. Naming recipes need an optional extension; see Optional extensions. Where you can, rename the files to the convention instead.

A recipe can also be read from a raw GitHub link, so that every machine uses the same recipe from one repository; see Files that don't follow the convention.

items.title: Contributor setup
items.text:
This guide walks you through everything you need, from creating a GitHub account to running your first test, so you can start contributing to canVODpy even if you have never used Git, GitHub, or Python tooling before.

Just want to use canVODpy, not contribute?

See Retrieve VOD instead.

  • Steps 1–5   GitHub + Git

    GitHub account · Homebrew · Git install · SSH keys · Git identity

  • Steps 6–9   Tools + Repository

    Install uv + just · Fork + clone · Submodules · Development environment

  • Step 10   Configuration + First run

    Initialize canvod-settings.yaml · Set paths and credentials · Validate · Process your first day

  • Steps 11–13   Verify + Contribute

    Run tests · Quality checks · Your first pull request

items.title: 1. Create a GitHub account
items.text: GitHub is a website that hosts code and lets teams collaborate on software projects. If you don't already have an account, sign up at github.com/signup.

items.title: 2. Install Homebrew (macOS only)
items.text:
Homebrew is the standard package manager for macOS. It lets you install developer tools with a single command. Open Terminal (press Cmd+Space, type "Terminal" and press Enter) and run:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Follow the on-screen instructions. When it finishes, it tells you to run two commands to add Homebrew to your PATH: copy and run them. Then verify:

brew --version

Note

If you already have Homebrew installed, run brew update to make sure it's current.

items.title: 3. Install Git
items.text:
Git is the version-control system that tracks changes in the codebase. Install it for your operating system:

macOSLinux (Debian/Ubuntu)Linux (Fedora)Windows 
brew install git

sudo apt update && sudo apt install git

sudo dnf install git

Download and run the installer from git-scm.com. Accept the default options during installation. Afterwards, open Git Bash (installed with Git) to run the commands in this guide.

Verify the installation:

git --version

You should see something like git version 2.x.x.

items.title: 4. Set up an SSH key for GitHub
items.text: SSH keys let you securely connect to GitHub without typing your password every time.

items.title: Generate a key
items.text:
macOS / LinuxWindows (Git Bash) 
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Press Enter three times to accept the defaults (default file location, no passphrase).

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Press Enter three times to accept the defaults.

items.title: Add the key to the SSH agent
items.text:
macOSLinuxWindows (Git Bash) 
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

items.title: Copy the public key
items.text:
macOSLinuxWindows (Git Bash) 
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Select and copy the output.

clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

items.title: Add the key to GitHub
items.text:
1. Go to github.com/settings/keys.
  2. Click New SSH key.
  3. Give it a title (for example "Laptop"), paste the key, and click Add SSH key.

items.title: Test the connection
items.text:
ssh -T git@github.com

You should see: Hi <username>! You've successfully authenticated...

items.title: 5. Configure your Git identity
items.text:
Tell Git who you are (this information appears in your commits):

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your_email@example.com"

Use the same email you registered on GitHub.

items.title: 6. Install development tools
items.text:
canVODpy uses two command-line tools to manage the project:

  • uv: a fast Python package manager that handles dependencies and virtual environments.
  • just: a command runner (like a simplified Makefile) that provides shortcuts for common tasks.

items.title: Install uv
items.text:
macOSLinuxWindows 
brew install uv

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

items.title: Install just
items.text:
macOSLinux (any distribution)Linux (Ubuntu 23.04+ / Debian 13+)Windows 
brew install just

This works on all Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Mint, Fedora, etc.):

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://just.systems/install.sh | bash -s -- --to ~/.local/bin

Make sure ~/.local/bin is on your PATH. Add this to your ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc if needed:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

sudo apt install just

Warning

This does not work on Linux Mint or older Ubuntu versions. Use the "Linux (any distro)" tab instead.

winget install Casey.Just

items.title: Verify both tools
items.text:
uv --version
just --version

items.title: 7. Fork and clone the repository
items.text: A fork is your own copy of the project on GitHub. You make changes in your fork and then propose them back to the original project via a "pull request."

items.title: Fork on GitHub
items.text:
1. Go to github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy.
  2. Click the Fork button in the top-right corner.
  3. GitHub creates a copy at github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/canvodpy.

items.title: Clone your fork
items.text:
git clone git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/canvodpy.git
cd canvodpy

Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your actual GitHub username.

items.title: Add the upstream remote
items.text:
This lets you pull in updates from the original repository later:

git remote add upstream git@github.com:TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git

Verify your remotes:

git remote -v

You should see origin (your fork) and upstream (the original).

items.title: 8. Initialize submodules
items.text:
The repository uses two Git submodules that contain test data and demo data. Initialize them after cloning:

git submodule update --init --recursive

This pulls:

  • packages/canvod-readers/tests/test_data: validation test data (falsified/corrupted RINEX files for testing)
  • demo: clean real-world data for demos and documentation

If you skip this step, tests that require these datasets are skipped.

items.title: 9. Set up the development environment
items.text:
From inside the canvodpy directory, run:

# Verify required tools are available
just check-dev-tools

# Install all Python dependencies and the git hooks (code checks before
# each commit, code graph rebuild after each commit)
just sync

# First build of the code graph (free, local; see "Developing with coding agents")
just graph

items.title: 10. Configure and run
items.text: Follow Retrieve VOD to initialize canvod-settings.yaml, validate it, and process your first day of GNSS data.

items.title: 11. Verify everything works
items.text:
Run the test suite:

just test

Run code-quality checks (linting, formatting, type checking):

just check

If both commands complete without errors, your environment is ready.

items.title: 12. Keeping your fork up to date
items.text: The upstream repository (TUW-GEO/canvodpy) receives regular updates. To incorporate these into your fork, you need to fetch from upstream and merge into your local branch. This section explains every step.

items.title: Why this is necessary
items.text: When you forked the repository, GitHub created a snapshot of main at that moment. Any commits pushed to the upstream main after your fork was created are not automatically reflected in your fork. If you work on a feature branch for several days, the upstream main may have moved ahead, and your branch falls behind it. Merging upstream changes prevents conflicts from accumulating and ensures you are building on the latest codebase.

items.title: One-time setup (already done if you followed step 7)
items.text:
Verify that you have the upstream remote configured:

git remote -v

You should see two remotes:

origin    git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/canvodpy.git (fetch)
origin    git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/canvodpy.git (push)
upstream  git@github.com:TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git (fetch)
upstream  git@github.com:TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git (push)

If upstream is missing, add it:

git remote add upstream git@github.com:TUW-GEO/canvodpy.git

items.title: Update your local main branch
items.text:
Every time you want to sync with the latest upstream changes:

# 1. Switch to your local main branch
git checkout main

# 2. Fetch all new commits from the upstream repository
git fetch upstream

# 3. Merge upstream/main into your local main
#    This is a fast-forward merge (no merge commit) if you have not
#    committed directly to your local main, which you should not do.
git merge upstream/main

# 4. Push the updated main to your fork on GitHub
git push origin main

After these four commands, your fork's main branch on GitHub is identical to the upstream main.

items.title: Update your feature branch
items.text:
If you are working on a feature branch, incorporate the freshly updated main:

# Switch to your feature branch
git checkout feature/my-feature

# Rebase your feature branch onto the updated main
git rebase main

Rebasing replays your commits on top of the latest main, producing a linear history. If Git reports a merge conflict during rebase, it pauses and shows you which files conflict. Resolve each conflict by editing the file, then:

git add <resolved-file>
git rebase --continue

If you want to stop the rebase and return to the state before:

git rebase --abort

Force push after rebase

Rebasing rewrites commit history. If you have already pushed your feature branch to your fork, you will need to force-push after rebasing:

git push --force-with-lease origin feature/my-feature

--force-with-lease is safer than --force because it refuses to overwrite commits that someone else may have pushed to the same branch.

items.title: Quick reference
items.text:
# Full sync sequence (run periodically):
git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
git push origin main
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main

items.title: 12b. Working in teams
items.text: During collaborative sprints, each team works on its own topic (often aligned with a package such as canvod-grids or canvod-readers). A shared develop branch acts as the integration point: no one commits to it directly. Instead, each team gets its own team branch.

items.title: Branch structure
items.text:
main
└── develop/sprint-2026              ← integration branch (shared by all teams)
    ├── team-grids/                  ← Team A
    │   ├── (direct commits)         ← Workflow A
    │   └── team-grids/add-new-grid   ← Workflow B feature branches
    ├── team-readers/                ← Team B
    └── team-vod/                    ← Team C

items.title: Set up the team branch
items.text:
The team lead creates the branch once:

git checkout develop/sprint-2026
git checkout -b team-grids
git push -u origin team-grids

All other team members fetch and switch to it:

git fetch origin
git checkout team-grids

From here, choose the workflow that fits your team:

Workflow A, push to the team branch directlyWorkflow B, feature branches with pull requests

Best for small teams (2–3 people) or when members work on separate files.

Everyone commits and pushes to the team branch:

# Make your changes, then:
git add <files you changed>
git commit -m "feat(grids): add new grid type"
git push origin team-grids

If someone else pushed before you, pull first:

git pull --rebase origin team-grids
git push origin team-grids

Best for larger teams or when you want lightweight review within the team.

Create a feature branch off the team branch:

git checkout team-grids
git checkout -b team-grids/add-new-grid

Work, commit, and push your feature branch:

git add <files you changed>
git commit -m "feat(grids): add new grid tessellation"
git push -u origin team-grids/add-new-grid

Then open a pull request on GitHub targeting team-grids.

To stay up to date with teammates' merged work:

git checkout team-grids
git pull origin team-grids
git checkout team-grids/add-new-grid
git rebase team-grids

items.title: Merge the team's work into the develop branch
items.text: When your team's feature is ready, open one pull request from team-grids into the develop branch on GitHub. This is where the maintainer reviews the team's combined work.

items.title: Make your changes
items.text: Edit files with your favorite text editor or IDE.

items.title: Run quality checks
items.text:
just test
just check

items.title: Stage and commit
items.text:
git add <files you changed>
git commit -m "feat(grids): add new grid type"

Commit messages follow the Conventional Commits format: type(scope): description. Common types: feat, fix, docs, test, refactor.

items.title: Push
items.text: Push to your team branch or feature branch (see Working in teams).

items.title: Open a pull request
items.text:
1. Go to your fork on GitHub. You'll see a banner suggesting to open a pull request.
  2. Click Compare & pull request.
  3. Set the base branch to your team branch (or the develop branch, depending on your workflow).
  4. Add a title and description, then click Create pull request.

items.title: 14. Pre-commit hooks and why your commit may be rejected
items.text:
When you ran just sync in step 9, a set of pre-commit hooks was installed into your local .git/hooks/ directory. These hooks run automatically every time you execute git commit. If any hook fails, the commit is aborted: your changes remain staged but no commit is created.

This is intentional: it prevents code that does not meet the project's quality standards from entering the Git history. The hooks are defined in .pre-commit-config.yaml at the repository root.

items.title: What runs on every commit
items.text:
The following checks execute automatically in sequence. If any one fails, the commit is rejected.

Hook When it runs What it checks Typical failure reason ruff check pre-commit (before commit is created) Python linting: unused imports, undefined names, style violations, type annotation issues You have an unused import or a linting rule violation ruff format pre-commit Python formatting: consistent code style (indentation, line length, quote style, trailing commas) Your code is not formatted according to the project style uv-lock pre-commit Lockfile consistency: verifies uv.lock matches pyproject.toml You changed a dependency in pyproject.toml but did not run uv sync trailing-whitespace pre-commit Removes trailing whitespace from all files A line ends with invisible spaces or tabs check-added-large-files pre-commit Blocks files larger than the threshold from being committed You are trying to commit a large binary, dataset, or log file detect-private-key pre-commit Scans for accidentally staged private keys (SSH, PGP) You are about to commit a secret: do not override this end-of-file-fixer pre-commit Ensures every file ends with exactly one newline A file is missing its final newline or has extra blank lines at the end check-agent-docs pre-commit Every path and just recipe named in AGENTS.md files and task guides exists You moved or renamed a file or recipe that an instruction file names commitizen commit-msg (after you write the message) Validates that your commit message follows the Conventional Commits specification Your message does not match the type(scope): subject format ty type check pre-push (before git push) Type checking of the whole workspace with ty A type error; the push is aborted

CI also runs just check-package-imports (too slow for a hook, about two minutes): it installs each package with only the dependencies its own pyproject.toml declares and imports every module. It fails when a package imports a library it does not declare, which the shared .venv hides. Run it after you add an import of a new library to a package.

After a commit, merge or checkout, the code graph hook rebuilds the code graph in the background (.graphify/, log in .graphify/build.log). To move demo and the test data to their latest commits, run just update-submodules on a feature branch; it commits the new pointers there, and they reach main through a pull request.

items.title: How to fix a rejected commit
items.text:
When a hook fails, read the error output carefully. The most common scenarios:

ruff linting or formatting failurecommitizen message validation failureuv-lock mismatchLarge file blocked

ruff will often auto-fix the issue. After the commit is rejected:

# The hook already ran ruff --fix, so files may have been modified.
# Check what changed:
git diff

# If the changes look correct, stage them and commit again:
git add -u
git commit -m "feat(readers): your original message"

If ruff cannot auto-fix (e.g., an undefined variable), you must edit the code manually, then stage and commit again.

Your commit message does not follow the Conventional Commits format. The error will say something like:

commit validation: failed!
please enter a commit message in the commitizen format.

The required format is:

type(scope): subject

Where type is one of: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci, build, style

And scope is one of: readers, aux, grids, vod, store, viz, utils, naming, ops, docs, ci, deps

Examples of valid messages:

git commit -m "feat(readers): add RINEX 4.0 parser"
git commit -m "fix(store): handle empty epoch arrays"
git commit -m "docs: update installation guide"
git commit -m "test(vod): add tau-omega edge cases"

Examples of invalid messages (will be rejected):

git commit -m "added new feature"           # no type prefix
git commit -m "feat: add stuff"              # too vague (but technically valid)
git commit -m "FEAT(readers): add parser"    # type must be lowercase
git commit -m "feat(readers) add parser"     # missing colon after scope

You modified a pyproject.toml (added or changed a dependency) but the lockfile is out of date:

uv sync          # regenerates uv.lock
git add uv.lock
git commit -m "feat(readers): your original message"

You are trying to commit a file that exceeds the size threshold (typically data files, .zarr stores, or log files). These should not be in the Git repository. Remove the file from staging:

git reset HEAD <large-file>
echo "<large-file>" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: update gitignore"

items.title: Bypassing hooks (emergency only)
items.text:
In rare situations where you need to commit despite a hook failure (for example, you are certain the failure is a false positive), you can skip hooks:

git commit --no-verify -m "fix(store): emergency hotfix"

Use --no-verify with extreme caution

Skipping hooks defeats their purpose. The CI pipeline on GitHub runs the same checks: your pull request will fail if the code does not pass ruff, formatting, and commit message validation. Only use --no-verify when you fully understand why the hook is failing and are certain the failure is not a genuine code quality issue.

items.title: 15. Continuous integration and test coverage
items.text: Every push to a branch and every pull request triggers automated checks on GitHub Actions. These are the same checks that run locally via just check and just test, but they execute in a clean environment to ensure reproducibility.

items.title: CI pipelines
items.text:
Workflow Trigger What it does Code Quality Every push and PR, weekly Checks lockfile consistency, runs ruff linting, checks formatting, runs type checking with ty, checks the agent instruction files Test with Coverage Push to main, all pull requests, weekly Runs uv run pytest (coverage is on by default in pyproject.toml), uploads results to Coveralls, posts a coverage summary comment on the PR Platform Tests Every push and PR, weekly Runs the test suite on Linux, macOS, and Windows with Python 3.14 S3 Tests Every push and PR Runs the tests of stores on S3 against an S3 emulator (RustFS) on Linux; elsewhere these tests are skipped Docs Quality Push to main, every pull request, weekly, or started by hand Checks the language of the docs pages a pull request changes with Vale, and the links of the built site with lychee: links between our pages on every push and pull request, external links too in the weekly run, which opens an issue when one fails Deploy Docs A published release, or started by hand Builds and deploys the documentation site

No CI workflow checks out the test-data submodule (packages/canvod-readers/tests/test_data): the tests that need it skip there, and the S3 Tests leave out the two S3 tests that read it (canvodpy/tests/test_s3_run.py, canvodpy/tests/test_s3_two_runs.py). Run them on your machine before you open a pull request that touches the readers, the stores or the pipeline (git submodule update --init packages/canvod-readers/tests/test_data, then just test). The end-to-end runs take their settings from config/canvod-settings.yaml.example, not from your settings file, so they run the same on every machine.

items.title: Test coverage with Coveralls
items.text:
The project uses Coveralls to track test coverage over time. After each test run in CI:

  1. pytest generates a coverage report in LCOV format (coverage.lcov)
  2. The report is uploaded to coveralls.io/github/TUW-GEO/canvodpy
  3. A coverage summary is posted as a comment on the pull request, showing which lines are covered and which are not

Coverage is not a gate (low coverage does not block your PR), but it is visible to reviewers. When adding new code, include tests. This is both good scientific practice (every computation should be verifiable) and a courtesy to future contributors who need to understand what the code does.

To measure coverage locally before pushing:

just test-coverage
# Opens an HTML report in your browser showing line-by-line coverage

items.title: 16. Common commands cheat sheet
items.text:
Print this

Command What it does just test Run all tests just check Lint, format, and type-check all code just sync Install dependencies and git hooks just hooks Install the git hooks only just graph Rebuild the code graph (free, local) just check-dev-tools Verify uv, just, and python3 are installed just config-init Scaffold canvod-settings.yaml from template just config-validate Validate the current configuration just config-show Show the resolved configuration just config-check-data <site> Check a site's data files as a run reads them just docs Preview documentation locally just docs-lint Check the language of the docs (Vale) just docs-lint-changed Vale on the pages changed since origin/main just docs-links Check every link of the built docs (lychee) just cli-docs Write the command-line reference from --help just cli-docs-check Check that reference against the --help texts just test-coverage Run tests with coverage report just clean Remove build artifacts and caches uv sync Install/update Python dependencies 17. Troubleshooting "command not found" for uv, just, or git The tool is not installed or not on your PATH. Re-run the installation step and, if needed, open a new terminal window so your shell picks up the updated PATH. "Permission denied (publickey)" when pushing or cloning Your SSH key is not set up correctly. Go back to step 4 and make sure the key is added to both the SSH agent and your GitHub account. uv sync fails with a Python version error canVODpy requires Python 3.14. Install a supported version with uv python install 3.14 and try again. Pre-commit hook fails on commit Run just check. It will auto-fix most linting and formatting issues. Stage the fixed files and commit again. "push rejected" or "failed to push"

Your branch is behind the remote. Pull the latest changes first:

git pull --rebase origin my-feature
Windows: just says "could not find the shell" or "system cannot find the path"

The Justfile expects Git Bash at C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe (the default Git for Windows location). If Git is installed elsewhere, find its location by running in PowerShell:

where.exe bash

Then update the path in the first lines of the Justfile:

set windows-shell := ["C:/YOUR/ACTUAL/PATH/TO/bash.exe", "-c"]

Warning

Do not commit this change: it's specific to your machine. The default path works for most installations and for CI.

Windows: uv install fails with "execution of scripts is disabled"

PowerShell's default execution policy blocks scripts. Use the bypass flag:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Windows: line ending warnings (LF will be replaced by CRLF)

Configure Git to keep Unix-style line endings:

git config --global core.autocrlf input

Next in the trail: configuration · API levels · architecture · AI development

items.title: Diagnostics
items.text: A scheduled canvodpy run often runs on a server where nobody watches it. Its log files are then the only record of what happened. This page explains where the logs go, what each file holds, how to find the cause of a failure, and how to see where a run spends its time.

items.title: Where the logs go
items.text:
Set the log folder under processing.logging in canvod-settings.yaml:

processing:
  logging:
    log_dir: /path/to/logs

A run needs log_dir: without it, canvodpy run and site.pipeline() stop before they process anything, with a message that names the setting.

Importing canVODpy writes no log files. Until a run starts, warnings and errors go to the terminal only. File logging starts when a pipeline is created, by canvodpy run or by site.pipeline() in Python, so the log folder comes from the settings of that run, including --config-dir and --config. To write the log files without a pipeline, for example when you use a reader or a store directly, call canvodpy.setup_logging(), or canvodpy.setup_logging(log_dir=...) for another folder.

The terminal shows warnings and errors in every case.

items.title: The log files
items.text:
The logs use structlog: each entry is an event with a name, such as task_failed, and fields, such as the date and the receiver. The log folder holds these files:

File What it holds When a new file starts Old files kept human/main.log Information, warnings, and errors, one readable line each Every midnight 30 human/errors.log Errors only, with the full traceback At 50 MB 5 machine/agent.json Every event, including debug messages, one JSON object per line At 100 MB 150 machine/performance.json Timing events: stage_timing and every event with a duration_seconds field At 50 MB 60 component/processor.log Events of the file processing Every midnight 7 component/auxiliary.log Events of the orbit and clock data Every midnight 7 component/icechunk.log Events of the store writes Every midnight 7

Older files get a number or a date at the end of the name, for example agent.json.1 or main.log.2026-10-09.

machine/agent.json always records every event, debug messages included. A failure on a remote server can't be run again with more logging, so the detail has to be there already. A timing event is therefore in both machine/agent.json and machine/performance.json: to count or sum timings, read only machine/performance*.json.

Each worker process writes its own set of files, with its process ID in the name, for example machine/agent.12345.json. Files can't be shared safely between processes. A worker creates a file only when it logs to it. New workers get new process IDs, so these files don't rotate like the files of the main process. Instead, a run deletes worker files that haven't changed for 30 days when its file logging starts. To keep them longer or shorter, set worker_log_retention_days:

processing:
  logging:
    log_dir: /path/to/logs
    worker_log_retention_days: 90

items.title: What the run does when something fails
items.text:
Most failures don't stop a run. The run logs an error event and goes on:

Event What failed What the run does task_failed Reading one file Writes the other files of that receiver and day worker_pool_broken A worker process died, for example because the machine ran out of memory Writes the other files of that receiver and day receiver_all_tasks_failed Every file of one receiver and day Writes nothing for that receiver and day batch_all_tasks_failed Every file of one batch Goes on with the next batch icechunk_write_failed Writing one receiver and day to the GNSS store Goes on with the next receiver read_back_failed Reading a written day back from the GNSS store Goes on with the next receiver vod_failed Computing the VOD of one receiver pair and day (canvodpy run only) Goes on with the next pair

These events carry the date (date or date_key) and the receiver, and human/errors.log holds their tracebacks.

After receiver_all_tasks_failed, icechunk_write_failed and read_back_failed, the receiver-day counts as failed: canvodpy run names it at the end and exits with code 3, and process_day raises an error.

When a store write or read fails with a file system or Icechunk error, for example because a network drive lost its connection, the run tries again up to four times, after 5, 15, 45, and 90 seconds. Each retry logs a store_op_retry warning. Only when the last try fails does the run log the error. An object store's server error (an S3 "500 Internal Error") is retried the same way. If the error comes while a unit of days is committed, the run plans the unit's days again and writes them again (op is write_unit); in the VOD phase it computes the unit again (op is vod_unit, with the unit's first and last day). So one such error does not lose the days of a unit. Errors that would fail the same way again are not retried: no permission, a missing file or folder, a full disk or quota, and a read-only file system.

A conflict, when another commit changed the store first, is not a lost connection: the run tries again on the new state of the store, up to five tries in all, and logs a store_conflict_retry warning (for a day of a store made of day blocks, forked_unit_conflict_retrying) with the number of the retry and the seconds it waited. The wait doubles with every retry, from about 1 second, and has a random part, so two runs that collided don't try again at the same moment. When the last try loses too, the run logs a store_conflict_lost error: another writer committed to the store first every time, so what this step would have written isn't in the store. It names the step (op, for example write_unit for a unit of days), the days (date, or first and last for vod_unit) and the number of tries, with a hint to run those days again. For commit_skipped_files only the log-book rows of the skipped files are missing; the days' data is in the store. After a lost unit of days, the run goes on with its other days and records the unit's days as failed.

Other errors stop the run:

  • run_crashed: canvodpy run logs this event when an error ends the processing of a site. It names the step the run was in (stage, for example pipeline_process or vod_store) and the last day that was processed completely (last_good_date_key). Then the run stops.
  • uncaught_exception: any error that would end Python is logged with its traceback before Python ends, in canvodpy run and in your own scripts once file logging has started.

At the end of a run, also after a crash, canvodpy run logs a run_summary event with the number of days processed (days), the VOD results written (vod_results), and per step the number of times it ran, its total time, and its errors (stages). stages covers the steps of the main process, such as planning, writing (the GNSS store), vod_calc, and vod_store. The reading steps run in the worker processes; their times are in the log files and in the dashboard.

items.title: Missing files and days without VOD
items.text:
Before it processes anything, a run checks the files of each of its receiver-days. A receiver-day is complete when it has as many files as its file length gives for a whole day: 96 files of 15 minutes (15M in the name), 24 of an hour, one daily file. For each receiver-day with fewer files, the run prints one line and logs a receiver_day_incomplete warning with the receiver, the day, the files found (files_found) and the files expected (files_expected):

  incomplete: canopy_01 has 81 of 96 files on 2025001

The run still processes that day, with the files it has. Today is not checked, because its files are still arriving.

A day on which one receiver of a pair has files and the other has none is not processed, so it gets no VOD. The run prints one line per receiver that lacks files and logs a days_without_vod warning:

  no VOD on 2 days, reference_01 has no files: 2025002, 2025003

When the VOD of a processed day is skipped because the data of a receiver is missing, for example because that receiver-day failed, the run prints which data is missing and logs a vod_skipped warning; the log says why the receiver-day failed:

  VOD canopy_01_vs_reference_01: skipped, no data of canopy_01 on 2025001 (the log says why)

In Python, site.pipeline(on_incomplete_day=..., on_days_without_vod=...) receives the same findings: (receiver, day, files_found, files_expected) for each incomplete receiver-day, and a receiver with its days without VOD.

items.title: Search the logs
items.text:
Each line of machine/agent.json is one JSON object, so you can search it with grep or jq:

cd /path/to/logs

# The errors that stopped a run
grep -E '"event": "(run_crashed|uncaught_exception)"' machine/agent.json

# Every failed file, with its date and receiver
jq -c 'select(.event == "task_failed") | {timestamp, date, receiver}' machine/agent*.json

# Everything one run logged, in the main process and the workers
grep -h '"run_id": "ExampleSite-20261010-030000-3f9a1c"' machine/agent*.json

The worker processes write to their own files, so search machine/agent*.json to include them. Add the older files (machine/agent*.json*) to search further back.

items.title: The run ID
items.text:
canvodpy run gives each run, which is one site, a run ID: the site name, the start time in UTC and six random characters, for example ExampleSite-20261010-030000-3f9a1c. The random part keeps the run IDs of two machines apart when both start a run in the same second. In Python, site.pipeline() sets one in the same way; it applies until the pipeline is closed, at the end of the with block. Every event of the run carries it in the run_id field, in the main process, and in the workers, so one search finds everything a run logged.

The run ID also goes into the message of each commit the run makes to the stores, as (run=ExampleSite-20261010-030000-3f9a1c). To see which run wrote which data, list the commits:

canvodpy store log ExampleSite --store gnss

To use a run ID of your own, set it before you create the pipeline; the pipeline then keeps it:

from canvodpy import Site
from canvodpy.logging import reset_run_id, set_run_id

site = Site("ExampleSite")
token = set_run_id("ExampleSite-reprocessing-2025")
try:
    with site.pipeline() as pipeline:
        for date, data in pipeline.process_range("2025001", "2025007"):
            ...
finally:
    reset_run_id(token)

The worker processes take the run ID when they start. When the run ID changes, the run starts new workers.

items.title: The run history
items.text:
Every run records itself in the run history: run_history.sqlite in the log folder, one file per machine (ADR 0018). A run of canvodpy run, of site.pipeline() (until the pipeline is closed, at the end of the with block) and of the Airflow task process_day records:

  • its start: site, run ID, settings, canvodpy version and commit, machine (CPU, memory, operating system, Python, size and free space of the disks of the log folder and the stores), worker count, and the label of --label or site.pipeline(label=...);
  • the receiver-days it plans, and for each one it finishes: written, skipped (every file already in the store) or failed, and the size of the data written (in memory, before compression);
  • the time of each stage, with the process that ran it (see the table below);
  • every 30 seconds and once more at its end, also when it fails: the CPU use and memory use of the machine (percent) and the free space of the disks of the log folder and the stores (history.resource_samples(run_id));
  • once a data day the run finishes, on the same background thread: the on-disk size of each local store the run writes (the GNSS and VOD stores), recorded against the data day (YYYYDOY) the run had finished, so the run history shows how the store grew over the run; how long the walk took is recorded beside it (history.store_sizes(run_id));
  • its warnings and errors, in words, with their receiver and day (a receiver-day with missing files reads, for example, canopy_01 has 81 of 96 files on 2025001);
  • its end: finished, or failed with the error.

The same file holds the file index: the names found in each folder of every receiver directory, so a run need not list the folders that hold none of the days it processes.

The stages a run records, from every stage_timing event of the run:

Stage Process One per finding_files main receiver folder scanned auxiliary_data main day: downloading or reading the orbit and clock files rinex.process_file worker file: everything below, together reading, validating, augmenting worker file: reading it, checking its signals, adding positions and geometry day_block_growth main batch: giving its days a block in the GNSS store, one commit planning main day: planning which worker writes which part of the day (reads the store's day blocks and log book) writing main unit of days with workers: merging the workers' parts of all its receivers and days and committing them to the GNSS store, one commit; one record per unit, with days and the comma-joined dates; without workers: receiver-day, writing to the GNSS store assembly main receiver-day: reading the written day back from the GNSS store, in process_range and process_date only (a run reads nothing back) icechunk.write main group write of a store made before day blocks vod_day_block_growth main unit of days: giving its days a block in the VOD store, one commit vod_calc worker VOD analysis and day: reading the day from the GNSS store and computing its VOD (recorded by the main process) vod_store main unit of days: merging the VOD of all its days and analyses and committing it to the VOD store, one commit; one record per unit, with days

A run that has no end and whose process is gone shows as interrupted. A run whose run ID the run history already holds (set by the caller and used before) gets a number (ExampleSite-20261010-030000-3f9a1c-2).

Read it from Python, also while a run writes to it:

from canvodpy.run_history import RunHistory

with RunHistory.open("/path/to/logs", read_only=True) as history:
    for run in history.runs(site="ExampleSite", label="benchmark-a"):
        print(run.run_id, run.status, run.started_at, run.ended_at)
        for problem in history.problems(run.run_id):
            print(" ", problem.level, problem.day, problem.message)

The run history must be on a local disk: SQLite needs shared memory for one process to write while others read, which network drives (NFS, SMB) don't provide. A run refuses to start when the log folder (processing.logging.log_dir) is on a network drive. Errors that stop canvodpy run before processing starts (for example a settings check) are in the log files only.

items.title: See where a run spends its time
items.text:
Finding the files is the first thing a run does, before it reads a file. On a network drive it can take minutes, so the CLI says, for each receiver, Finding files of receiver <name> in <folder>... and then Found <n> files on <d> days for receiver <name> (<s> s), so you know it is working. From the second run on, the folders that hold none of the days the run processes come from the file index and the listing is much shorter; the log event files_found says per receiver how many folders were listed and how many came from the index.

Next, a run over days already in the store finds the days whose files are all stored, by hashing the files' bytes, and skips them before it downloads auxiliary data or reads a file. The log event stored_days_skipped names those days, how many files were hashed and the seconds it took; the run history counts their receiver-days as skipped. The run then writes a log-book row with action set to skipped for each of their files, all in one commit. Since no file is read, the row takes its time span, attributes and preprocessing record from the row that holds the file. skipped_files_logged names the days and the commit; skipped_files_not_logged says why the commit failed. A failed commit leaves the days stored and skipped.

canvodpy dashboard opens a marimo app that reads the run history of a log folder:

canvodpy dashboard                         # log folder from the settings
canvodpy dashboard --logs-dir /path/to/logs
canvodpy dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

To start it together with a run, use canvodpy run --dashboard. --dashboard-host and --dashboard-port set its address. The dashboard keeps running after the run ends, so you can look at the finished run, and a line at the end of the run says so. At the top, the dashboard says whether the run is still going and has a button, Shut the dashboard down, which stops the dashboard but never the run. To stop the dashboard when the run ends, add --dashboard-stop-at-end. It then stops even when the run fails or you stop the run with Ctrl-C. Whoever can open the dashboard can press the button, so with --dashboard-host 0.0.0.0 that's anyone who can reach its address.

No runs of your own yet? canvodpy.demo_data("run_history") downloads an anonymized example: nine runs of the same seven days of two receivers with 1 to 126 workers, and a warm-up run with failed orbit downloads. Open it with canvodpy dashboard --logs-dir <folder>/run_history, where <folder> is the folder demo_data returns. The demo notebook 23 · Run Dashboard shows the dashboard on it.

The dashboard reads the run history, not the log files, so nothing disappears when the log files rotate, and it knows a run's settings, machine, progress, and problems.

Site overview: one row per site: its last run, that run's status and its start and end, and the receiver-days it planned, wrote, skipped, failed and hasn't done yet.

Run page: pick a run (newest first). It shows the run's settings, the canvodpy version and commit, the machine, the workers and the label; the progress per receiver (planned, written, skipped, failed, not yet done, bytes added); an estimate of when it finishes; the last finished step; the throughput; and the run's warnings and errors in words, with their receiver and day.

The page labels the times in UTC and the three numbers above, and says how each is computed:

  • Estimate: for a running run, the mean time per finished receiver-day of this run times the receiver-days not yet done. There is no estimate before the first receiver-day finishes.
  • Last finished step: the newest recorded stage of a run (stage, receiver, day, how long ago). The run history records a stage when it ends, so this is the last finished step, not the step running now.
  • Throughput: receiver-days finished per hour and bytes added per hour over the run (so far, for a running run).

Charts: the run page also shows charts of the run, built from the run history queries only:

  • Time per stage: the median of a stage's per-day seconds (left, "Median per day") and the total seconds of each stage (right, "Total"), in the same order (by total). The median is over the seconds of a day, added up over the day's receivers; a stage that names no day (such as day_block_growth) takes the median of its records; a unit of days is split evenly over its days. A long bar is a stage that takes a lot of the run. Each bar has its value at its end, so a stage far shorter than the longest still shows on the linear axis, where its bar is too thin to see.
  • Time per day: the stage seconds of a data day, added up over all its receivers, as a line over the days so a trend over the run is easy to see. A run that works in units of days splits a unit's record evenly over its days. Receivers run in parallel, so this is not wall time; a day can show more seconds than it took. A day's time is final only after its unit's VOD phase: until then it still rises, since a unit's writing record is split over its days when the unit commits, and its VOD runs during the next unit. The x-axis is a date axis: its labels thin out to fit the page, so a year of days stays readable. The days of runs recorded with ISO dates for the VOD phase (2025-06-18) are shown under their YYYYDOY day too.
  • Store size on disk: the on-disk size of each local store (GNSS, VOD) as a line, plus a Total line, measured on the background sampler thread when the run finished a new data day (never inside a stage or a commit), so the growth of the store over the run is visible. The x-axis is the data day as a date, one point per data day the size was measured (a unit of days has one point, on its last day); the y-axis is in MB or GB, chosen from the values. How long each walk took is recorded too (history.store_sizes(run_id)).
  • CPU and memory: the percent of the CPU and memory used, sampled during the run. A line near 100 % shows what limits the run.
  • Free disk: the free space of each folder, sampled during the run. Free disk is one value per folder, so a chart has one line per folder; the y-axis is in gigabytes.
  • Throughput over time: the receiver-days finished, cumulative from the run start. The slope is the pace; a steep line is a fast run.

The dashboard is always dark, whatever the machine's or the browser's setting: the notebook's script header sets the marimo theme. The data colors fit canvodpy's colors, those of this documentation. A chart with one series is canvodpy's green. Up to four series, such as CPU and memory, get cream, blue, amber and brick red, which differ in hue and in lightness. More series, such as a comparison of eight worker counts, run from dark blue over sky blue and amber to canvodpy's cream, so they get lighter in the sorted order of their labels. Both stay readable with a red-green color vision deficiency and in grayscale.

Every chart of a duration (time per stage, time per day, the comparison) has a Time axis switch between a linear axis from zero and a logarithmic one, which spreads short and long stages apart. The free-disk chart starts its axis near the lowest value, not at zero, so a change in free space is visible. Hover over a point or a bar of any chart for its values; a day shows as YYYYDOY and as a date. The settings and the machine of a run are folded in; click to open them.

Compare runs by label: a run can take a free-text label with canvodpy run --label <text>, for example to group the repetitions of a benchmark. The dashboard groups the runs that share a label and compares them:

  • Only finished runs are compared, and a run without a label is left out.
  • Each group shows its machine, workers, version and settings, or "differs" when the group is not uniform. A group whose machine, workers, version or settings differ is not a set of repetitions of the same thing, and the dashboard says so.
  • For each stage, the median time of the group's finished runs that recorded it, with the minimum and the maximum. Per stage a run's time is the sum over its receivers and days (across its worker processes). In total, the median of the runs' wall time (ended minus started), with the minimum and the maximum. Stages run in parallel, so the stage times can add up to more than the total. The median is the middle of the sorted times; the spread is min to max.
  • A grouped bar chart shows the median time per stage: per stage one bar per label, side by side, colored as described above, in the sorted order of the labels (with zero-padded numbers, such as w001, w016, w126, that is the order of the numbers). Hover over a bar for its label and time.

Download the data: the run page and the comparison each have a download button (Download the data of this run, Download the data of this comparison). Each gives a zip with:

  • run_history.sqlite: every record of the runs shown (settings, machine, receiver-days, stage timings, resource samples, warnings and errors) and nothing of other runs.
  • One CSV file per table and chart of the view, with the rows the dashboard showed.
  • README.txt: the canvodpy version, the log folder, the runs, and what each file holds.

Unzipped, the folder opens like a log folder, so canvodpy dashboard --logs-dir <folder> shows the same runs on another machine. The zip is made when you click, so for a running run its run history can hold records newer than the page. Each table's own Export button saves just that table as CSV or JSON.

A run's status is one of:

  • Running: the run's process lives.
  • Finished: it ended and wrote a result.
  • Failed: it ended with an error.
  • Interrupted: its process is gone without an end (killed or crashed).
  • Unknown: it started on another machine, whose processes can't be checked from here.

It reloads the run history every 10 seconds by default, so you can watch a run while it runs. On a long run, pick a longer interval.

You can open the same notebook without canvodpy installed, on a machine that has a run history folder. From v1.0.0 on, canvodpy on PyPI ships the run history, and marimo run --sandbox installs canvodpy in a sandbox and takes the folder from --logs-dir after --:

uvx marimo run --sandbox \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy/main/canvodpy/src/canvodpy/cli/dashboards/performance.py \
  -- --logs-dir /path/to/logs

Read from that URL, the notebook takes the run history from the installed canvodpy (its logo comes from the installed package too), but the style sheet sits next to the notebook, so the app runs with marimo's default styling.

Try it in a notebook

Open Batch processing in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: Time your own code
items.text:
To time a step in your own code or in a plugin, use stage_timer or its decorator form timed_stage. Each writes one stage_timing event when the step ends, with the step name, the duration in seconds (duration_seconds), the status (ok or error), and the fields you pass. It also writes the event when the step fails, before the error goes on.

from canvodpy.logging import stage_timer, timed_stage

with stage_timer("my_step", receiver="canopy_01"):
    ...


@timed_stage("my_function")
def my_function(): ...

When you measure the times yourself, for example several steps from one set of checkpoints, record_stage_timing("my_step", seconds, ...) writes the same event.

The events go to machine/performance.json. The dashboard draws events that carry a date_key (YYYYDDD) and a receiver or analysis field.

Every commit to a store also writes a commit_parts event there, not a stage: the seconds it waited for the commit lock (lock_wait_seconds), opened the repository (open_seconds), checked the content settings (content_check_seconds) and the stored lockfile (lockfile_check_seconds), rebased (rebase_seconds), wrote the store metadata and snapshot summary (summary_seconds; a process's first commit to a store rebuilds the summary from the whole store, later ones update it from their own log-book rows), committed (icechunk_commit_seconds) and released the lock (lock_release_seconds), with the commit message and the number of the commit in this process (commit_number).

Next in the trail: parallel processing · configuration · architecture

items.title: Optional Extensions
items.text:
canvodpy ships as a lean core. Packages that only a subset of users need (because their receivers use non-standard filenames, or because they run a specific orchestrator) live in a separate repository so the core install stays small and dependency-free by default:

github.com/TUW-GEO/canvodpy-extensions

canvodpy works fully without any of these. canvod-filemap is used only for receivers whose settings name a naming recipe (recipe:); canvod-airflow and canvod-adapters call canvodpy, not the other way around.

items.title: Available extensions
items.text: Package Purpose Status canvod-filemap Recipe-based filename mapping for non-canonical GNSS filenames (proprietary receiver output, legacy RINEX v2 short names, custom layouts) Available canvod-airflow Airflow DAGs: one daily DAG per configured site, plus backfill; the tasks run the code of canvodpy run (canvodpy.workflows.tasks.check_day, process_day) Available canvod-adapters Data exchange between canvodpy and other GNSS-T programs (gnssvod): observations and VOD, checked against canvodpy's dataset contracts Available

items.title: Installing an extension
items.text:
Each extension is a package on PyPI, released on its own under the tag <package>-v<version> (for example canvod-filemap-v1.0.0). None has extras: each package brings what it needs.

uv add canvod-filemap
uv add canvod-airflow
uv add canvod-adapters

In a clone of this repository, canvod-filemap is the dependency group filemap:

uv sync --group filemap

The group exists only in this repository: it is not part of the canvodpy package on PyPI, so canvodpy[filemap] does not exist. Its version range is in the root pyproject.toml:

[dependency-groups]
filemap = ["canvod-filemap>=1.0.0"]

If you have both repositories cloned as sibling directories locally (common for contributors iterating on canvod-filemap itself), you can point the group at your checkout in your own uncommitted copy to pick up changes without releasing:

# pyproject.toml (local override, do not commit)
[tool.uv.sources]
canvod-filemap = { path = "../canvodpy-extensions/packages/canvod-filemap" }

Don't commit a local path source

A path-based source only works on machines that happen to have canvodpy-extensions cloned as a sibling directory. uv resolves every dependency group's sources when it locks, even groups that are not installed, so committing a local path breaks uv sync for everyone else.
