items.text: Function Purpose Input dims Output dims preprocess_aux_for_interpolation() Minimal prep for interpolation sv: 32 sid: 896 prep_aux_ds() Steps 1-4; with keep_sids, only those signals (used by runs) sv: 32 sid: 4429 map_aux_sv_to_sid() Step 1: expand sv \(\rightarrow\) sid sv: 32 sid: 896 pad_to_global_sid() Step 2: pad to all constellations sid: 896 sid: 4429 normalize_sid_dtype() Step 3: convert to object dtype Any dtype fixed strip_fillvalue() Step 4: remove _FillValue attributes Any attributes cleaned

items.title: Step 1: map_aux_sv_to_sid()
items.text:
Each satellite position is replicated across all its signal IDs:

from canvod.auxiliary.preprocessing import map_aux_sv_to_sid

sp3_sid = map_aux_sv_to_sid(sp3_data)

# G01 position is identical for every signal ID of G01
sp3_sid["X"].sel(sid="G01|L1|C")  # 12 345 678.9 m
sp3_sid["X"].sel(sid="G01|L2|W")  # 12 345 678.9 m  (same)
sp3_sid["X"].sel(sid="G01|L5|I")  # 12 345 678.9 m  (same)

Signal IDs generated for GPS G01 (28 total):

G01|L1|C  G01|L1|L  G01|L1|M  G01|L1|N  G01|L1|P  G01|L1|S  G01|L1|W
G01|L1|X  G01|L1|Y  G01|L1|p  G01|L1|u
G01|L2|C  G01|L2|D  G01|L2|L  G01|L2|M  G01|L2|N  G01|L2|P  G01|L2|S
G01|L2|W  G01|L2|X  G01|L2|Y  G01|L2|l  G01|L2|p  G01|L2|u
G01|L5|I  G01|L5|Q  G01|L5|X  G01|L5|u

Signal ID format: "{SV}|{BAND}|{CODE}", for example "G01|L1|C", "E08|E5a|Q". Uppercase codes are RINEX 3 attributes; the lowercase codes are the RINEX 2 tracking-code markers for signals whose code RINEX 2 does not record.

items.title: Step 2: pad_to_global_sid()
items.text:
Pads the Dataset to include all possible Signal IDs across all supported constellations: every \(\text{SV} \times \text{band} \times \text{code}\) in the constellation BAND_CODES (4 429 at the time of writing). Signal IDs outside that set are dropped. Required for Icechunk storage, where sequentially appended datasets must share the same coordinate space.

from canvod.auxiliary.preprocessing import pad_to_global_sid

sp3_global = pad_to_global_sid(sp3_sid)
sp3_global.sizes["sid"]  # 4429

Added SIDs are filled with NaN.

items.title: Step 3: normalize_sid_dtype()
items.text:
Converts the sid coordinate to object dtype for Zarr/Icechunk compatibility. Fixed-length Unicode string types (<U12, etc.) cause dtype conflicts when datasets from different files are concatenated and appended.

from canvod.auxiliary.preprocessing import normalize_sid_dtype

ds = normalize_sid_dtype(ds)
ds["sid"].dtype  # dtype('O')

items.title: Step 4: strip_fillvalue()
items.text:
Removes _FillValue attributes that conflict with Icechunk's internal missing-data handling. NaN is the standard missing-value marker throughout the pipeline.

from canvod.auxiliary.preprocessing import strip_fillvalue

ds = strip_fillvalue(ds)
# No variable in ds.data_vars has a "_FillValue" encoding key

items.title: Scientific note
items.text:
Replicating satellite positions across signal IDs is scientifically valid:

One position per satellite is enough for the angles

SP3 positions refer to the satellite's center of mass. The antenna phase centers of the signals sit up to a few meters from it and differ slightly between frequencies. Seen from a receiver about 20 000 km away, a few meters change \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) by about \(10^{-7}\) rad, far below anything VOD can resolve, so every signal of a satellite can use the same position.

items.title: Product registry
items.text: The product registry provides declarative configuration for 23 final and rapid SP3/CLK products from 14 analysis centers (agency codes). Products are defined in TOML; no hardcoded URLs in the processing code. Every product was checked against the file listings of ESA GSSC and NASA CDDIS (2025-001 and 2026-244, checked 2026-10-05); just check-products repeats the check (see Checking the registry).

items.title: Product types
items.text:
• Final

    Latency 14–21 days · Accuracy cm-level

    Highest quality. Use for scientific research, reprocessing campaigns, and publication-quality VOD products.

  • Rapid

    Latency 17–24 hours · Accuracy near-final (cm-level)

    Available the following day. Use for near-real-time processing when final products have not yet been released.

Type Latency Orbit accuracy Clock accuracy Final 14–21 d < 2.5 cm < 75 ps Rapid 17–24 h < 2.5 cm < 75 ps

Ultra-rapid, real-time and near-real-time products are not supported: they are issued several times a day, are partly predicted, and their file names carry the issue hour. The settings reject product_type: ultra-rapid.

items.title: Available products
items.text:
Systems: G GPS, R GLONASS, E Galileo, C BeiDou, J QZSS, read from the SP3 header of 2026-09-01. A run drops the observations of satellites the product has no orbits for (warning sids_dropped_no_ephemeris, once per file), so those signals get no VOD: choose a product that covers the systems of your signal selection, or narrow the selection.

Code Agency Final Rapid COD Center for Orbit Determination in Europe GRECJ GRE EMR Natural Resources Canada G GR ESA European Space Agency GRECJ GR GFZ GeoForschungsZentrum Potsdam GRE GRECJ GRG CNES GEC GEC IAC Information-Analytical Centre GRECJ – IGS International GNSS Service G (NASA CDDIS only) G JAX JAXA (multi-GNSS) GRECJ – JGX JAXA GRE GRE JPL Jet Propulsion Laboratory GE GE MIT Massachusetts Institute of Technology GE – NGS National Geodetic Survey G, no clocks – SIO Scripps Institution of Oceanography G, no clocks G, no clocks USN US Naval Observatory – G

canvod.auxiliary.list_products() lists them; the registry is the truth. The default, COD final, covers all five systems. Products without clock files can't be used with fetch_clock: true; a run, and canvodpy config validate, stops before any download if the configured product does not exist or has no clocks while fetch_clock is true, and names the closest products.

Several samplings per product

Agencies have changed the sampling of their files over the years (for example ESA rapid: 15 min SP3 and 5 min CLK in 2025, 5 min SP3 and 30 s CLK in 2026). The registry lists every sampling a product has been published with, and the readers try them in that order, locally and then on each server. The sampling of the file used is recorded in the sampling_rate attribute of the orbit dataset.

Servers and fallback

Products are downloaded from ESA GSSC (no account needed). NASA CDDIS is a fallback, tried when ESA fails, once credentials.nasa_earthdata_acc_mail holds the email of a free NASA Earthdata account. Products that only NASA CDDIS hosts need that account.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Look up a productIn a run 
from canvod.auxiliary import get_product_spec

spec = get_product_spec("COD", "final")
spec.prefix  # "COD0MGXFIN"
spec.sp3_samplings  # ["05M"], tried in this order
spec.clk_samplings  # ["30S"]; [] if the product has no clocks
spec.systems  # "GRECJ"
spec.sp3_filenames("2025001")  # ["COD0MGXFIN_20250010000_01D_05M_ORB.SP3"]
[s.url for s in spec.ftp_servers]  # ESA first, then NASA CDDIS

Runs pick the product from the settings; no manual lookup is needed:

processing:
  aux_data:
    agency: COD
    product_type: final
    fetch_clock: false  # true: also CLK, which VOD does not use

To add satellite geometry to a dataset in your own code, use an ephemeris provider (see canvod-auxiliary).

items.title: Registry format
items.text:
Products are declared in packages/canvod-auxiliary/src/canvod/auxiliary/products/products.toml, one [[products]] table each, with its servers in priority order:

[[products]]
agency = "COD"
type = "final"
prefix = "COD0MGXFIN"
sp3_sampling = ["05M"]
clk_sampling = ["30S"]
systems = "GRECJ"
description = "CODE final multi-GNSS"
ftp_path = "/gnss/products/{gps_week}/{file}"

[[products.ftp_servers]]
url = "ftp://gssc.esa.int"
priority = 1
description = "ESA GSSC"

[[products.ftp_servers]]
url = "ftps://gdc.cddis.eosdis.nasa.gov"
priority = 2
requires_auth = true
description = "NASA CDDIS"

type is final or rapid. Every file covers one day (01D).

items.title: Checking the registry
items.text:
just check-products                    # 2025-001 and the day three weeks ago
just check-products 2025001 2026244    # chosen days (YYYYDOY)

The recipe lists each server's GPS-week directory once per day and looks up every product's SP3 file, and CLK file if it has clocks, under each of its samplings. It prints the file found per product and day, or, for a missing product, the files of that product the servers do have, and exits with 1 if any product is missing. NASA CDDIS is checked when the settings hold credentials.nasa_earthdata_acc_mail; otherwise products hosted only there are reported as skipped. Run it after editing products.toml, and from time to time: agencies rename products, change samplings, and stop publishing.

just test-network runs the same check for 2025-001 as tests, one per product, together with a real download of the COD final files and a run that downloads its own orbits and clocks (see Testing).

items.title: canvod-config
items.text:
canvod-config reads canvod-settings.yaml and checks it with Pydantic models. Every other canVODpy package gets its settings from these models.

This page describes the Python side. To write the settings file, see the Configuration guide.

items.title: Load the settings
items.text:
from canvod.config import load_config

config = load_config()

config.processing.metadata.author
config.processing.storage.stores_root_dir
config.sites.sites["ExampleSite"].receivers["canopy_01"].directory
config.sids.mode

load_config() finds the settings file the same way the command line does; see Where canVODpy finds the settings. To load a file from another folder, pass the folder: load_config(Path("my_config")). To apply an overlay file, pass config_file=.

Fields you leave out of the file take their defaults.

items.title: The models
items.text:
load_config() returns a CanvodConfig, with one model per section of the file:

Attribute Model Holds config.processing ProcessingConfig metadata, credentials, ephemeris products, processing parameters, compression, storage, logging, preprocessing config.sites.sites dict[str, SiteConfig] one entry per site with its receivers and VOD analyses config.sids SidsConfig the signals to keep: all, a preset, or a custom list

The API reference lists every field, its type and its default.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
load_config() checks the whole file before any processing starts. A wrong field raises ConfigValidationError with the location of the error. A misspelled field name is never corrected; the error names the closest allowed name:

storage.gnss_store_stratgy
  Unknown key 'gnss_store_stratgy'. Did you mean 'gnss_store_strategy'?

From the command line, canvodpy config validate runs the same check.

Try it in a notebook

Open Configuration in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: Purpose
items.text: The canvod-grids package provides spatial grid implementations for hemispheric GNSS signal analysis. It discretizes the hemisphere visible from a ground-based receiver into cells, a prerequisite for spatially resolved VOD estimation.

items.title: Grid types
items.text:
Seven implementations are available, all inheriting from BaseGridBuilder:

  • EqualAreaBuilder (recommended)

    Cells of approximately equal solid angle. Ensures uniform spatial sampling across the hemisphere, avoiding zenith over-weighting.

  • EqualAngleBuilder

    Regular angular spacing in \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\). Cells near zenith are smaller. Use it when you want uniform angular resolution.

  • EquirectangularBuilder

    The same number of azimuth sectors in every \(\theta\) band, no zenith cap. Fast to compute; cells shrink strongly toward the zenith.

  • GeodesicBuilder

    Icosahedron subdivision. Near-uniform cell area with triangular cell boundaries.

  • FibonacciBuilder

    Fibonacci-sphere sampling: nearly uniform points, each the center of its Voronoi cell.

  • HEALPixBuilder

    Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization. All pixels of the full sphere have the same area; the hemisphere keeps the pixels whose center is at least as high as the outer edge. Requires the optional healpy dependency, which is not installed by default (see Optional dependencies below).

  • HTMBuilder

    Hierarchical Triangular Mesh. Recursive triangular decomposition of the sphere; supports efficient spatial indexing.

All builders accept angular_resolution (degrees), cutoff_theta and phi_rotation (degrees) and return a GridData object. cutoff_theta (default 0) leaves out the sky within that many degrees of the horizon. A run's grid assignment uses cutoff_theta = 0.

Where a grid ends depends on its type:

Grid type Outer edge Observations near the horizon equal_area, equal_angle, equirectangular exactly \(\theta = 90^\circ -\) cutoff_theta; the last band is narrower when the band width does not divide the range (half a band for equal_area and equal_angle at a cutoff that is a multiple of the resolution) all get a cell up to the outer edge, none beyond htm, geodesic the triangles whose center is higher than the outer edge; some extend below it all observations higher than the horizon get a cell (with cutoff_theta = 0) healpix the pixels whose center is at least as high as the outer edge; some extend below it all observations higher than the horizon get a cell (with cutoff_theta = 0) fibonacci the Voronoi cells whose lattice point is higher than the outer edge some low observations get no cell: up to about \(1^\circ\), \(3^\circ\) and \(6^\circ\) elevation at \(2^\circ\), \(5^\circ\) and \(10^\circ\) resolution

So the solid angles of the ring grids add up to the hemisphere (\(2\pi\) sr with cutoff_theta = 0); those of the triangle and pixel grids add up to somewhat more (geodesic \(1.01 \times 2\pi\) to \(1.05 \times 2\pi\), HEALPix \(1.01 \times 2\pi\) to \(1.08 \times 2\pi\) at \(2^\circ\) to \(10^\circ\)).

items.title: Optional dependencies
items.text:
HEALPix requires an explicit install

HEALPixBuilder delegates pixel geometry entirely to healpy, which is not installed by uv sync --dev, because it's declared in canvod-grids' own optional dependency group, not the workspace's dev group. Install it with:

uv sync --dev --group optional

healpy publishes no Windows wheels on PyPI (Linux and macOS only), which is the main reason it's kept optional rather than a hard dependency. Every other grid type only needs numpy/scipy, which install everywhere. Calling create_hemigrid("healpix", ...) without healpy installed raises ImportError with the same install instructions.

CI installs the optional group on Linux/macOS runners so HEALPix is covered by canvod-grids' correctness suite (test_grid_correctness_all_types.py); it's skipped on the Windows CI leg for the same wheel-availability reason.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Factory functionBuilder patterncanvodpy factory 
from canvod.grids import create_hemigrid

grid = create_hemigrid("equal_area", angular_resolution=5.0)
print(grid.ncells)  # 1051
print(len(grid.theta_lims))  # 19 θ bands

from canvod.grids import EqualAreaBuilder

builder = EqualAreaBuilder(angular_resolution=5.0)
grid = builder.build()

from canvodpy import GridFactory

builder = GridFactory.create("equal_area", angular_resolution=5.0)
grid = builder.build()
print(grid.grid.head())  # Polars DataFrame with cell geometry

All three build the same grid. create_hemigrid and GridFactory take the builder of each grid type from one table, canvod.grids.GRID_BUILDERS.

items.title: GridData
items.text:
The GridData object returned by all builders provides:

Attribute Type Description grid polars.DataFrame One row per cell: center (phi, theta), bounds (phi_min, phi_max, theta_min, theta_max), cell_id ncells int Total number of grid cells grid_type str Grid type, for example "equal_area" theta_lims, phi_lims, cell_ids arrays Band edges, azimuth edges and cell ids per \(\theta\) band get_solid_angles() np.ndarray Solid angle of each cell (sr) get_grid_stats() dict Summary: cell count, solid-angle statistics

For the Fibonacci, geodesic, HEALPix, and HTM grids the bounds are bounding boxes, not the true (curved or triangular) cell boundaries.

items.title: Grid operations
items.text:
canvod.grids.operations handles the interface between grids and xarray Datasets:

  • Cell Assignment

    add_cell_ids_to_ds_fast assigns each observation to the cell that contains it, eagerly or lazily for Dask arrays: by band and sector edges for the ring grids, by spherical triangle for HTM and geodesic, by pixel for HEALPix, by Voronoi cell for Fibonacci. Observations outside the grid get NaN (see the table in Grid types). The nearest cell center is not used: near a cell's corner it often belongs to a neighboring cell. canvodpy run uses the same function when grid assignment is set. The lookup needs the grid's full geometry, so use a grid built with create_hemigrid; a grid read back with canvod.store.load_grid works for the ring grids only.

  • Grid Persistence

    grid_to_dataset converts GridData to an xarray Dataset.

    To save a grid in a store and read it back, use store_grid and load_grid from canvod-store.

  • Aggregation

    In canvod.grids.aggregation (also importable from canvod.grids):

    aggregate_data_to_grid computes one statistic per cell.

    compute_percell_timeseries computes per-cell time series (\(\text{cell} \times \text{time}\)).

    compute_hemisphere_percell computes daily per-cell time series of the full hemisphere.

    compute_zenith_percell computes daily per-cell time series for \(\theta \leq 30^\circ\).

items.title: Analysis subpackage
items.text:
canvod.grids.analysis provides filtering, weighting, and pattern analysis:

Module Purpose filtering Global IQR, Z-score, SID pattern filters per_cell_filtering Per-cell variants of the filtering filters masking Spatial and temporal mask construction weighting Per-cell weight calculators solar Solar geometry (elevation, azimuth) temporal Diurnal aggregation and analysis spatial Per-cell spatial statistics

items.title: SIDPatternFilter
items.text:
SIDPatternFilter selects observations by GNSS system, frequency band, and tracking code. It operates on the sid dimension where SIDs have the format SV|Band|Code (for example G01|L1|C).

Slice (drop non-matching SIDs)Mask (NaN non-matching values) 
from canvod.grids.analysis import SIDPatternFilter

filt = SIDPatternFilter(system="G", band="L1", code="C")
ds_gps_l1c = filt.filter_dataset(ds)  # returns smaller dataset or None

filt = SIDPatternFilter(system="E")
ds_masked = filt.apply(ds, "SNR", output_suffix="galileo")

items.title: Storing analysis results
items.text: To store weights, masks, statistics, and per-cell time series in a VOD store, use AnalysisStorage from canvod-store.

items.title: Coordinate convention
items.text:
Angles

All grids use standard spherical coordinates:

  • phi (\(\varphi\)): azimuth from 0 to \(2\pi\) · 0 = North · \(\pi/2\) = East · clockwise
  • theta (\(\theta\)): polar angle from zenith · 0 = zenith · \(\pi/2\) = horizon

This matches the coordinate output of canvod-auxiliary, so no conversion is needed.

items.title: Role in the VOD pipeline
items.text:
flowchart TD
    A["`**Augmented Dataset**
    epoch x sid, with theta, phi`"]
    A --> B["`**Grid Assignment**
    add_cell_ids_to_ds_fast`"]
    B --> C["`**Gridded Dataset**
    + cell_id_* variable`"]
    C --> D["`**VOD per observation**
    tau-omega, carries cell_id_*`"]
    D --> F["`**Per-cell statistics**
    compute_hemisphere_percell`"]
    F --> E["`**Hemispherical Map**
    canvod-viz`"]

items.title: canvod-preflight
items.text: canvod-preflight defines the canVOD filename convention: CanVODFilename parses and builds canonical names, and find_overlaps finds files whose named time spans overlap. Runs from the command line and from Python use both to decide which files they process.

items.title: The canVOD filename convention
items.text:
Every canVOD-compatible GNSS file follows this naming format:

{SIT}{T}{NN}{AGC}_R_{YYYY}{DOY}{HHMM}_{PERIOD}_{SAMPLING}_{CONTENT}.{TYPE}[.{COMPRESSION}]

items.title: Fields
items.text: Field Width Description Example SIT 3 Site ID, uppercase FAN, ORT T 1 Receiver type: R = reference, A = active (below the canopy) R, A NN 2 Receiver number, zero-padded 01, 35 AGC 3 Data provider / agency ID INK, MEA _R 2 RINEX data-source field, always R (receiver-generated) _R YYYY 4 Year 2025 DOY 3 Day of year (001--366) 001 HHMM 4 Start time (hours + minutes) 0000 PERIOD 3 Batch duration: value + unit 01D, 15M SAMPLING 3 Data frequency: value + unit 05S, 01S CONTENT 2 User field, filled as needed (AA by default) AA TYPE 2--8 File format, lowercase; runs read rnx, sbf and nmea, and the type of each installed reader plugin rnx, sbf, nmea, ubx COMPRESSION -- Optional compression extension; runs do not read compressed files (warning compressed_files_not_processed), decompress them first zip, gz

items.title: Duration codes
items.text: Unit Meaning Example S Seconds 05S = 5 seconds M Minutes 15M = 15 minutes H Hours 01H = 1 hour D Days 01D = 1 day

items.title: Example
items.text:
FANR01INK_R_20250010000_01D_05S_AA.rnx
Part Field Meaning FAN Site Site ID FAN R Type Reference receiver 01 Number Receiver 01 INK Agency The Inklings 2025001 Date 2025, day of year 001 0000 Start 00:00 GPS time 01D Period 1-day file 05S Sampling 5-second intervals AA Content Default rnx Type RINEX observation

As in the RINEX 3 long names, the start time is in the time scale of the observations, which for canVODpy is GPS time.

Try it in a notebook

Open Naming convention in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: Which files a run processes
items.text:
A run scans each receiver's directory recursively, in any folder layout (all files in one folder, one folder per day, or deeper nesting). A file's day comes from the date in its name, not from its folder. Without a naming recipe, only files that follow the convention are processed. A run stops before reading any data if

  1. a directory holds files of more than one receiver,
  2. two files map to the same canonical name, or
  3. two files cover the same time, for example a daily file next to the 15-minute files of the same day.

items.title: Folders of other days come from the file index
items.text:
Listing a folder on a network drive is slow: about 50 ms per day folder on an SMB share, so a few years of day folders take most of a minute per receiver. A run therefore keeps a file index, the names it found in each folder, in the run history. A run lists

  • every folder that holds a day the run processes,
  • folders without a data file (for example the receiver directory itself and year folders), and
  • folders that are not in the index yet.

Every other folder comes from the index, without asking the drive. A run therefore finds every file of the days it processes, also a file added to an old folder since the previous run. A run with --update-to-latest starts where the stores end, so a daily run lists only a few folders.

One case is not seen: a file for a day the run processes, put into a folder that held only other days. Say the folder 25001 held only files of 2025-001, and a file of 2025-100 is copied into it. A run of 2025-100 takes 25001 from the index and misses the file. Run once with --start and --end covering the folder's days (here --start 2025001 --end 2025001), or delete the run history; either way the folder is listed again. The same holds for a file deleted, renamed or compressed in a folder of other days. A file replaced in place, with the same name and new content, is your responsibility: a run finds files by name and does not compare contents.

The Airflow tasks follow the same rule for their day. The data check, canvodpy config validate, always lists every folder. If the run history is deleted or its index can't be read, the next run lists every folder and writes the index again. A dry run reads the index but never writes it, so it shows the files a run would find. See ADR 0020 for the reasons.

With reader_format: auto, the reader is detected per day: SBF and NMEA by file type, and RINEX 2 or 3 by the file header. A day whose files need different readers stops the run; set reader_format, or keep each format in its own directory.

Files a run does not process (names that neither the recipe nor the convention recognizes, or a file type the receiver's reader_format does not read) do not stop it. The run processes the other files and logs one warning per receiver, files_not_processed, with the number of such files per file type and an example.

Compressed files are never processed, with or without a recipe: general compression and archives (.gz, .Z, .zip, .bz2, .xz, .zst, .7z, .tgz, .tar, and .rar) and Hatanaka-compressed RINEX (.crx, RINEX 2 .yyd). They get a warning of their own, compressed_files_not_processed. Decompress them first (for Hatanaka, crx2rnx). A receiver directory holding only compressed files fails the check below.

Check a site before processing it; the check finds the files exactly as a run does and also lists the files a run would pass over:

canvodpy config validate --site <site>

items.title: Files that don't follow the convention
items.text:
A run processes only files with canonical names. For files with other names, for example RINEX v2 short names or the names a receiver's firmware gives its SBF files, set a naming recipe on the receiver:

sites:
  my_site:
    receivers:
      reference_01:
        recipe: my_site_reference

The recipe gives each file a canonical name without renaming it on disk. Naming recipes need an optional extension; see Optional extensions.

A recipe can also be read from a URL, so that every machine uses the same recipe from one repository. The URL is the raw link of the file, at a commit, a tag or a branch:

        recipe: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<recipes-repo>/<commit>/my_site/my_site_reference.yaml

Every run downloads the recipe again, so a run needs network access. The GNSS store records each receiver's recipe, a URL by its file name only, and the sha256 of the recipe file. Every run compares them with the settings and stops if the recipe or its content changed; the message names the canvodpy store amend --update-recipe command that records a new recipe on purpose. A recipe in a private repository needs a GitHub token with read access in GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN; canvodpy never stores it (ADR 0022).

items.title: Purpose
items.text: The canvod-ops package provides a preprocessing pipeline for observation datasets. canvodpy run, the Python API and Airflow apply it before writing to the GNSS store if the processing.preprocessing setting is set (see Preprocessing during a run); without that setting the store holds the observations at the receiver's sampling interval. You can also apply the operations yourself, for example to datasets read from a store. Operations are applied as a chain: each operation receives a dataset, transforms it, and passes the result to the next.

items.title: Pipeline
items.text:
A Pipeline is an ordered sequence of operations (Op instances). It processes a dataset through each operation and collects metadata about what happened:

from canvod.ops import Pipeline, TemporalAggregate, GridAssignment

pipeline = Pipeline(
    [
        TemporalAggregate(freq="1min", method="mean", integer_method="first"),
        GridAssignment(grid_type="equal_area", angular_resolution=2.0),
    ]
)

ds_out, result = pipeline(ds_in)

# result.to_metadata_dict() → stored in dataset attrs for reproducibility

flowchart TD
    RAW["`**Raw Dataset**
    epoch, sid`"]
    RAW --> TA["`**TemporalAggregate**
    1-min mean`"]
    TA --> GA["`**GridAssignment**
    2-deg equal-area`"]
    GA --> OUT["`**Enriched Dataset**
    + PipelineResult`"]

items.title: TemporalAggregate
items.text:
Aggregates observations into regular time bins. Reduces the number of epochs by grouping into frequency buckets and computing the mean or median of the floating-point variables. Bins start at multiples of freq counted from 00:00 and are labeled with their start. Missing values (NaN, and -1 in integer variables) are ignored; a bin without any value stays missing. Integer variables (for example LLI and SSI) are flags and codes, which cannot be combined: each bin takes one of its values, the first, last or middle one in time order (integer_method, required; of an even number of values, middle takes the earlier of the two). The value of one epoch stands for the bin, so a loss of lock in another epoch of the bin is not seen. A bin keeps no count of the epochs behind it.

The result has the same variables, dimensions, data types, attributes and encodings as the input, with fewer epochs, so aggregated data cannot be told apart from unaggregated data by their structure. What was done is reported in the result of the returned OpResult instead, for example {"aggregated": true, "input_sampling_s": 5.0, "output_sampling_s": 60.0}, and kept in the stores' log books (see The preprocessing record). The aggregation runs on NumPy arrays in blocks of bins of bounded size; a day of 1 s data with 300 signals takes about one second.

SNR is averaged as stored, in dB-Hz, not as linear power. Because VOD is linear in the SNR difference in dB, the mean of the dB values gives the mean of the per-epoch VOD if the canopy and reference bins average the same epochs and \(\theta\) changes little within a bin (issue #192). The median is the same in dB and in linear power.

Measured on one day of the Rosalia test data (5 s, 271 signals), against the mean of the per-epoch VOD (mean |VOD| 0.88):

Bin \(\theta\) change in a bin (p95) VOD error from \(\theta\) (mean / p95) VOD error, receivers aggregated separately (mean / p95 / max) 30 s \(0.20^\circ\) 0.0001 / 0.0005 0.0015 / 0.009 / 0.15 1 min \(0.45^\circ\) 0.0003 / 0.0012 0.0017 / 0.009 / 0.44 5 min \(2.4^\circ\) 0.0015 / 0.0048 0.0036 / 0.012 / 0.40 15 min \(7.2^\circ\) 0.0041 / 0.013 0.013 / 0.066 / 0.59

\(\theta\) within a bin matters little up to a few minutes. The larger error comes from bins in which the canopy and the reference receiver have values at different epochs (for example a satellite tracked by one receiver for part of the bin): a run aggregates each receiver on its own, so such bins average different epochs. A bin also keeps no count of the epochs behind it, so a bin with one value weighs like a full one in later averages.

from canvod.ops import TemporalAggregate

op = TemporalAggregate(freq="1min", method="mean", integer_method="first")
ds_out, result = op(ds_in)
Parameter Default Description freq "1min" Target frequency (pandas offset alias) method "mean" Floating-point variables: "mean" or "median" integer_method required Integer variables: "first", "last" or "middle" value of the bin

If every epoch already is the start of its own bin, the operation is a no-op: it returns the dataset unchanged and reports "aggregated": false. Data at the target interval but off the bin starts (for example epochs at :02) are relabeled to the bin starts.

items.title: Per-SID independence
items.text:
TemporalAggregate groups by (time_bin, sid) before computing the aggregate. This is critical because each SID (satellite + band + code) observes the canopy from a different sky position (\(\theta\), \(\varphi\)). Mixing VOD or SNR values across satellites within a time bin conflates spatial variability (different view angles) with temporal variability, which gives a physically meaningless average.

Geometry (\(\theta\), \(\varphi\)) is aggregated per SID with the same method, so it describes where the aggregated value came from; .first() would instead assign a single observation's geometry to it. The azimuth \(\varphi\) is aggregated as an angle: each value is taken relative to the first value of its bin, so a satellite crossing north (\(\varphi = 0\)) yields north, not south.

Coordinate handling:

Coordinate type Example Aggregation Data variables VOD, SNR Mean or median per (time_bin, sid) Geometry theta Mean or median per (time_bin, sid) Azimuth phi Mean or median as an angle per (time_bin, sid) SID-only coordinates sv, band, code Preserved unchanged

Anti-pattern: naive xarray resampling

A plain ds.resample(epoch="1D").mean() preserves the sid dimension (xarray resamples along epoch only), so per-SID independence is maintained. However, it does not distinguish between data variables and geometry coordinates, and does not handle SID-only coordinates explicitly. For production use, prefer TemporalAggregate.

items.title: GridAssignment
items.text:
Assigns each observation to the grid cell that contains its direction (phi, theta); an observation outside every cell gets NaN. The grid is built with create_hemigrid and its defaults (see canvod-grids). Adds a cell_id_* variable to the dataset.

from canvod.ops import GridAssignment

op = GridAssignment(grid_type="equal_area", angular_resolution=2.0)
ds_out, result = op(ds_in)
# ds_out now has cell_id_equal_area_2.0deg(epoch, sid)
Parameter Default Description grid_type "equal_area" Grid builder name angular_resolution 2.0 Resolution in degrees

phi and theta may be data variables (as the runs write them) or coordinates, on (epoch, sid). If either is missing, the operation is skipped with a warning.

items.title: Op and OpResult
items.text:
All operations inherit from the Op abstract base class:

from canvod.ops import Op, OpResult


class MyOp(Op):
    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return "my_operation"

    def __call__(self, ds: xr.Dataset) -> tuple[xr.Dataset, OpResult]:
        # transform ds
        return ds, OpResult(
            op_name=self.name,
            parameters={...},
            input_shape=dict(ds.sizes),
            output_shape=dict(ds.sizes),
            duration_seconds=elapsed,
        )

Each OpResult records:

  • Operation name and parameters (the settings)
  • result: what the operation measured or derived (for example the input sampling)
  • Input/output dataset dimensions
  • Execution time
  • Optional notes (for example "no-op: data already at target frequency")

OpResult.step() gives the operation's entry in the preprocessing record, {"op", "settings", "result"}, and PipelineResult.record() the record of all operations in the order they ran. A new operation therefore records itself: it only has to fill parameters and result. If it runs code of another package, it names that package in packages (GridAssignment sets packages = ("canvod-ops", "canvod-grids")), so the record gives its version too.

items.title: Preprocessing during a run
items.text:
canvodpy run, the Python API and Airflow apply the operations set in the processing.preprocessing section of canvod-settings.yaml. Nothing is applied unless the section is set, and each operation runs only if its own subsection is set (and not enabled: false):

processing:
  preprocessing:
    temporal_aggregation:
      freq: "1min"      # whole number + "s", "min" or "h"; must divide one day
      method: "median"  # "mean" or "median", floating-point variables
      integer_method: "first"  # "first", "last" or "middle", integer variables
    grid_assignment:
      grid_type: "equal_area"
      angular_resolution: 2.0

The temporal aggregation runs first, then the grid cell assignment. Both run on the files of one worker task together (preprocess_files), after azimuth and elevation are computed and before the data goes to the GNSS store. A task holds the files of one receiver whose epochs share a chunk of the aggregated epochs, so a time bin that spans two files is in one task and is aggregated from the observations of both; it is stored with the file that holds its first observation. Each stored file keeps its own attributes (for example the file hash) and all sid coordinates. VOD is then computed from the aggregated data and carries the cell_id_* variables along.

items.title: The preprocessing record
items.text:
For traceability, transparency and reproducibility, every write records which preprocessing produced the data. The record is written by the operations themselves and has this form (here for one day of 5 s data):

{
  "format_version": 2,
  "software": {"canvod-grids": "1.0.0", "canvod-ops": "1.0.0"},
  "steps": [
    {
      "op": "temporal_aggregate",
      "settings": {"freq": "1min", "method": "mean"},
      "result": {"aggregated": true, "input_sampling_s": 5.0, "output_sampling_s": 60.0}
    },
    {
      "op": "grid_assign",
      "settings": {"grid_type": "equal_area", "angular_resolution": 2.0},
      "result": {"assigned": true, "variable": "cell_id_equal_area_2.0deg", "n_cells": 6563}
    }
  ]
}

format_version is the version of the record's layout, not of the software. software gives the version of every package whose code ran the operations (canVODpy packages are released separately): canvod-ops always, canvod-grids when cells were assigned. Records of format 1, written by canVODpy up to 0.4.0, name only the canvod-ops version (canvod_ops_version) and are still read. Without processing.preprocessing, steps is empty, which records that no preprocessing was applied.

The record is kept in the log books of the stores, never in the data: stored data have exactly the variables and attributes of data without preprocessing.

  • GNSS store: the preprocessing column of {group}/metadata/table holds the record of each file, written in the same commit as the file's data.
  • VOD store: the preprocessing column of the analysis group's log book holds, per receiver, the records of the GNSS data the result was computed from, for example {"canopy_01": [record], "reference_01": [record]}.
  • Store history: the commit log of the store. Each commit records its settings, among them the preprocessing, and the canVODpy version in its commit metadata; canvod.store_metadata.show_metadata lists the commits.

A store group never mixes data preprocessed with different operations or settings. Before each write, the store compares the settings of the new data with every record in the group's log book; the results may differ (for example data at 1 s and at 5 s, both aggregated to 1 min). A VOD result is computed only from canopy and reference data preprocessed with the same settings. On a mismatch, the write raises PreprocessingMismatchError and canvodpy run stops with exit code 1, since every later day would be refused the same way: keep the setting for the life of a store, or start a new store.

canvodpy run checks before it processes any data. For the GNSS store, processing.preprocessing is one of the store's content settings: the run compares it with the settings the store was created with, when it starts and again before each commit. For the VOD store, it compares the configured preprocessing with every VOD analysis group of the selected calculator. A mismatch therefore stops the run at once, also when a new GNSS store would feed an existing VOD store. canvod.ops.planned_settings(config) gives the settings a configuration records, and MyIcechunkStore.check_settings_match compares them with a group.

items.title: Adding grid cells to stored data
items.text:
Data written without grid_assignment can get their cells afterwards, for a GNSS receiver group or a VOD analysis group:

from canvod.ops import assign_grid_cells_in_store

assign_grid_cells_in_store(
    site.gnss_store, "canopy_01", grid_type="equal_area", angular_resolution=2.0
)

It runs the same operation as grid_assignment in a run on all data of the group and writes only the new cell_id_* variable; the data, the group's attributes, the log book and the other subgroups stay as they are. In a group of day blocks, the cells of each day go into the day's block, and the empty epochs that pad the block stay empty. The log book receives one row for the whole group (action add_variables, no time range) whose record holds the grid_assign step. From then on, the data already in the group count as preprocessed with that step as well:

  • A later run must set grid_assignment to the same grid_type and angular_resolution; its data then carry the cells, and the write goes through. A run without it is refused with PreprocessingMismatchError.
  • A VOD analysis group accepts only VOD computed from GNSS data with the same grid assignment: assign the cells to the receiver groups too, or compute the VOD again from them.

An append whose variables differ from the group's (for example data without the cell_id_* variable of the group) is refused in any case (GroupVariablesMismatchError, which also stops a run): the variable would no longer be as long as the others, and the group could no longer be opened.

build_default_pipeline(config) builds the same pipeline from a PreprocessingConfig; called without one, it reads the setting.

items.title: Build a reader
items.text:
This guide shows how to write a reader for a GNSS file format that canVODpy does not read yet. The result is a validated dataset that canvod-store, canvod-auxiliary, and canvod-vod accept like the output of the built-in readers.

To use the reader in canvodpy run, install it as a plugin (see Your own readers and VOD calculators). To add it to canVODpy itself, also follow Add it to canVODpy.

You should know xarray datasets, Pydantic models and Python's abstract base classes.

items.title: The reader contract
items.text:
Every reader inherits from GNSSDataReader (canvod.readers.base), a Pydantic BaseModel and an abstract base class in one. One parent is enough:

graph TD
    A["`**MyFormatReader**`"] -.inherits.-> B["`**GNSSDataReader**
    BaseModel + ABC`"]
    A --> C[DatasetBuilder]
    C --> D[SignalID]
    C --> E[SignalIDMapper]
    C --> F[validate_dataset]

A reader must:

  1. Implement the abstract members: source_format, file_hash, start_time, end_time, systems, num_satellites (properties) and iter_epochs(), to_ds() (methods). A reader that misses one cannot be created.
  2. Set the class attribute file_type: the TYPE field of the files' canVOD names, for example "rnx".
  3. Return from to_ds() a dataset that passes validate_dataset().

The base class gives every reader:

Member What it does fpath The path of the file; construction raises FileNotFoundError if it is not a file aggregate_glonass_fdma Whether GLONASS FDMA channels are merged into the bands G1 and G2 (default True); see GLONASS FDMA channels model_config arbitrary_types_allowed=True _build_attrs() The required global attributes; author and institution come from the settings file num_epochs Counts the epochs of iter_epochs(); override it if the header stores the count to_ds_and_auxiliary() Calls to_ds() and returns no auxiliary datasets; see Return auxiliary data

items.title: The output dataset
items.text:
validate_dataset(ds) checks the dataset against constants in canvod.readers.base and raises one ValueError that lists every problem it finds:

Constant Value REQUIRED_DIMS ("epoch", "sid") REQUIRED_COORDS epoch (datetime64[ns]); sid, sv, system, band, code (strings); freq_center, freq_min, freq_max (float32, MHz) DEFAULT_REQUIRED_VARS ["SNR"]; every data variable has the dimensions (epoch, sid) REQUIRED_ATTRS Created, Software, Institution, File Hash

epoch holds one entry per observation epoch, in GPS time (its attribute time_system says so). sid holds one entry per signal, written SV|band|code, for example G01|L1|C; sv, system, band and code split it up. The store uses File Hash to refuse a file it already holds, and the band overlap checks use the frequency coordinates.

DatasetBuilder produces all of this. With it, a reader only parses its format.

items.title: Create the class
items.text:
from pydantic import ConfigDict

from canvod.readers.base import GNSSDataReader


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    """Reader for .myf files."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    file_type = "myf"

    @property
    def source_format(self) -> str:
        return "my_format"

source_format names the format. A run puts it on each file's dataset as the Source Format attribute, and the GNSS store records it as its source_format (root attribute and identity.source_format of the store's metadata). A run refuses files of different formats in one store. The built-in readers return rinex3, rinex3_stripped, rinex2, sbf and nmea.

The base class does not freeze readers. frozen=True stops anyone from changing fpath or another field after construction; the RINEX readers use it, SbfReader and NmeaObs do not. @cached_property works either way.

If the format needs settings, add them as fields:

from pydantic import PrivateAttr


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    file_type = "myf"

    skip_header: bool = False  # a field, set at construction
    _cache: dict = PrivateAttr(default_factory=dict)  # not part of the model

Do not declare fpath again

fpath comes from GNSSDataReader. Declaring it again replaces the field and its check that the file exists.

items.title: Hash the file
items.text:
The store compares file_hash with the hashes of the files it already holds, so the same file must always give the same hash. Use the shared function, as every built-in reader does:

from canvod.utils.tools import file_hash


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    ...

    @property
    def file_hash(self) -> str:
        """First 16 characters of the SHA-256 of the file."""
        return file_hash(self.fpath)

It reads the file in 8 KB chunks. A reader that holds the whole file in memory anyway can call canvod.utils.tools.bytes_hash(data), which gives the same value without reading the file again.

items.title: Describe the file
items.text:
These properties summarize the file without building the dataset:

from datetime import datetime
from functools import cached_property


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    ...

    @cached_property
    def _header(self):
        return self._parse_header()  # parsed once, on first use

    @property
    def start_time(self) -> datetime:
        return self._header.start_time

    @property
    def end_time(self) -> datetime:
        return self._header.end_time

    @property
    def systems(self) -> list[str]:
        """System letters, for example ["G", "E", "R"]."""
        return self._header.systems

    @property
    def num_satellites(self) -> int:
        return self._header.num_satellites

items.title: Iterate over the epochs
items.text:
iter_epochs() yields one epoch at a time, so a large file never has to fit in memory. What an epoch looks like is up to the reader; the base class types it as object. A named tuple is enough:

from collections.abc import Iterator
from typing import NamedTuple


class MyObservation(NamedTuple):
    sv: str  # "G01"
    band: str  # "L1"
    code: str  # "C"
    snr: float


class MyEpoch(NamedTuple):
    timestamp: datetime
    observations: list[MyObservation]


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    ...

    def iter_epochs(self) -> Iterator[MyEpoch]:
        with self.fpath.open("rb") as f:
            self._skip_header(f)
            while (epoch := self._read_next_epoch(f)) is not None:
                yield epoch

items.title: Build the dataset
items.text:
DatasetBuilder (canvod.readers.builder) turns epochs and values into the output dataset:

import xarray as xr

from canvod.readers.builder import DatasetBuilder


class MyFormatReader(GNSSDataReader):
    ...

    def to_ds(self, keep_data_vars: list[str] | None = None, **kwargs) -> xr.Dataset:
        builder = DatasetBuilder(
            self,
            time_system="GPS",
            aggregate_glonass_fdma=self.aggregate_glonass_fdma,
        )
        for epoch in self.iter_epochs():
            ei = builder.add_epoch(epoch.timestamp)
            for obs in epoch.observations:
                sig = builder.add_signal(sv=obs.sv, band=obs.band, code=obs.code)
                builder.set_value(ei, sig, "SNR", obs.snr)
        return builder.build(
            keep_data_vars=keep_data_vars,
            extra_attrs={"Format Version": "1.0"},
        )
Method What it does DatasetBuilder(reader, time_system=..., aggregate_glonass_fdma=True) Starts a dataset. time_system must be "GPS"; anything else raises ValueError add_epoch(timestamp) Adds an epoch and returns its index add_signal(sv, band, code) Returns the SignalID; adding the same signal again changes nothing set_value(epoch_index, signal, variable, value) Sets one value build(keep_data_vars=None, extra_attrs=None) Builds the dataset, validates it, and returns it

build():

  1. sorts the signals by their sid string;
  2. looks up freq_center of each band with SignalIDMapper, and sets freq_min and freq_max to the center frequency minus and plus half the bandwidth, all as float32;
  3. fills every value you did not set with NaN for floating-point variables and -1 for integer ones;
  4. adds the metadata of the coordinates and of the variables it knows;
  5. adds the global attributes of _build_attrs() and extra_attrs (a run sets Source Format itself, from source_format);
  6. calls validate_dataset().

It knows these variables:

Variable Type Meaning SNR float32 Signal-to-noise ratio (dB) CN0 float32 Carrier-to-noise density (dB-Hz) Pseudorange float64 Pseudorange (m) Phase float64 Carrier phase (cycles) Doppler float32 Doppler shift (Hz) LLI int8 Loss of lock indicator SSI int8 Signal strength indicator

Other names are stored as float32, without metadata.

Unknown bands

A band that SignalIDMapper does not know gets NaN for freq_center, freq_min and freq_max, without an error. Check the frequency coordinates of your first dataset.

items.title: Epochs in GPS time
items.text:
canVODpy stores every epoch in GPS time, the time scale of the orbits and clocks. The builder stores each timestamp as given and drops its time zone without converting it. Convert other time scales before add_epoch():

from datetime import UTC

from canvod.readers.gnss_specs.leap_seconds import utc_to_gps

# UTC or local time: convert to UTC, then add the leap seconds of the date
builder.add_epoch(utc_to_gps(local_timestamp.astimezone(UTC)))

GPS time is ahead of UTC by the leap seconds since 1980, 18 seconds since 2017.

items.title: GLONASS FDMA channels
items.text:
GLONASS satellites send on their own frequency channels. With aggregate_glonass_fdma=True (the default), the builder merges them into the bands G1 and G2: the center frequency is the mean of the channels, and the band reaches across all of them. With False, the bands are G1_FDMA and G2_FDMA.

A run passes processing.params.aggregate_glonass_fdma to the reader, to the padding of the signals (pad_to_global_sid) and to the orbit data (prep_aux_ds), so the GLONASS signals of observations and orbits match. A reader that only has merged bands sets the class attribute per_channel_glonass = False (the default): the base class then refuses aggregate_glonass_fdma=False.

items.title: Return auxiliary data (optional)
items.text:
If the format holds more than observations, such as satellite angles or quality indicators, override to_ds_and_auxiliary() to read both in one pass over the file. It returns the observation dataset and a dictionary of auxiliary datasets:

def to_ds_and_auxiliary(
    self, keep_data_vars: list[str] | None = None, **kwargs
) -> tuple[xr.Dataset, dict[str, xr.Dataset]]:
    obs_ds, meta_ds = self._read_once(keep_data_vars)
    return obs_ds, {"my_format_meta": meta_ds}

SbfReader returns its metadata this way, as sbf_obs: the satellite geometry the receiver computed and its quality data of each epoch.

items.title: Signal IDs
items.text:
SignalID checks each part of a signal ID when it is created. It is frozen and hashable, so it works as a dictionary key:

from canvod.readers.base import SignalID

sig = SignalID(sv="G01", band="L1", code="C")
sig.sid  # "G01|L1|C", also str(sig)
sig.system  # "G"
SignalID.from_string("E25|E5a|I")

SignalID(sv="X01", band="L1", code="C")  # ValueError: no system X
SignalID(sv="G1", band="L1", code="C")  # ValueError: two digits needed

The satellite is a system letter, G (GPS), R (GLONASS), E (Galileo), C (BeiDou), J (QZSS), S (SBAS) or I (NavIC/IRNSS), and two digits.

Band names must be ones that SignalIDMapper knows, for example:

System Bands GPS L1, L2, L5 Galileo E1, E5a, E5b, E5, E6 GLONASS G1, G2, G3, G1a, G2a BeiDou B1I, B1C, B2a, B2b, B3I QZSS L1, L2, L5, L6

Codes are the RINEX 3 tracking codes (C, P, W, I, Q, X and others); the builder does not check them. Never guess a code your format does not record: the lowercase markers p, l and u exist for that case (see RINEX v2.11). Padding to all signals (pad_to_global_sid()) drops any other code that is not a RINEX 3 code.

items.title: Test the reader
items.text:
Keep a small sample file with the tests. Test the contract, not only the values:

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pytest

from canvod.readers.base import validate_dataset
from my_canvod_plugin import MyFormatReader

SAMPLE = Path(__file__).parent / "test_data" / "sample.myf"


@pytest.fixture
def reader():
    return MyFormatReader(fpath=SAMPLE)


def test_missing_file_refused(tmp_path):
    with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
        MyFormatReader(fpath=tmp_path / "missing.myf")


def test_file_hash(reader):
    assert reader.file_hash == MyFormatReader(fpath=SAMPLE).file_hash
    assert len(reader.file_hash) == 16


def test_dataset_passes_contract(reader):
    ds = reader.to_ds()
    validate_dataset(ds)
    assert ds.attrs["File Hash"] == reader.file_hash
    assert ds["freq_center"].dtype == np.float32
    assert not np.isnan(ds["freq_center"]).any()  # every band known


def test_keep_data_vars(reader):
    assert list(reader.to_ds(keep_data_vars=["SNR"]).data_vars) == ["SNR"]


def test_summary(reader):
    assert reader.start_time <= reader.end_time
    assert set(reader.systems) <= set("GRECJSI")
    assert reader.num_satellites > 0

Also compare a few values with what the receiver's own software shows for the same file.

items.title: Register and create
items.text:
ReaderFactory creates readers by name:

from canvodpy import ReaderFactory

ReaderFactory.register("my_format", MyFormatReader)
reader = ReaderFactory.create("my_format", fpath="data.myf")

Registering in a script makes the reader available to that script only. canvodpy run uses the readers that ship with canVODpy and installed plugins.

ReaderFactory.create_from_file(path) and detect_reader(path) pick a built-in reader from the file: NMEA by the .nmea extension or a first line starting with $, RINEX 2 or 3 by the version in the first header line. A RINEX 3 file with signal strengths only gets rinex3_stripped. Other files raise ValueError; SBF is created by name. A registered reader is never detected.

A run whose receiver sets reader_format: auto tells SBF and NMEA files by their canVOD file type, and RINEX 2 from RINEX 3 with detect_reader(). It uses the full RINEX 3 reader for stripped files too.

items.title: Add it to canVODpy
items.text:
A reader that ships with canVODpy goes into its own folder in canvod-readers:

packages/canvod-readers/
├── src/canvod/readers/
│   ├── __init__.py       # export MyFormatReader
│   └── my_format/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── reader.py
└── tests/
    ├── test_my_format_reader.py
    └── test_data/sample.myf

canvodpy run knows its built-in formats by name. A new one needs all of these; they list the formats, so keep them in step:

Where What canvodpy/src/canvodpy/__init__.py Register the reader in _register_builtin_components canvodpy/src/canvodpy/factories.py ReaderFactory._detect_format, if reader_format: auto should find it canvodpy/src/canvodpy/orchestrator/discovery.py _READER_FILE_TYPES, _ALL_FILE_TYPES packages/canvod-preflight/src/canvod/preflight/convention.py FileType, if the file type is new packages/canvod-config/src/canvod/config/models/sites.py The reader_format values and description; _FILE_FORMAT if the reader reads the files of another format (as rinex3_stripped reads RINEX 3), so a canopy and its reference count as the same format packages/canvod-store/src/canvod/store/viewer.py _FORMAT_LABELS

The built-in readers predate DatasetBuilder: each assembles its dataset itself and calls validate_dataset() at the end of to_ds(). A new reader should use the builder.

items.title: Complete example
items.text:
A reader for a made-up text format, with epochs in UTC:

"""Reader for .gnsd files (GNSS Simple Data, a made-up format).

GNSD 1.0
EPOCH 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z
G01 L1 C 42.5
E01 E1 C 40.1
EPOCH 2025-01-01T00:00:30Z
G01 L1 C 43.0
END
"""

from collections.abc import Iterator
from datetime import datetime
from functools import cached_property
from typing import NamedTuple

import xarray as xr

from canvod.readers.base import GNSSDataReader
from canvod.readers.builder import DatasetBuilder
from canvod.readers.gnss_specs.leap_seconds import utc_to_gps
from canvod.utils.tools import file_hash


class GnsdObservation(NamedTuple):
    sv: str
    band: str
    code: str
    snr: float


class GnsdEpoch(NamedTuple):
    timestamp: datetime  # GPS time
    observations: list[GnsdObservation]


class GnsdReader(GNSSDataReader):
    file_type = "gnsd"

    @property
    def source_format(self) -> str:
        return "gnsd"

    @property
    def file_hash(self) -> str:
        return file_hash(self.fpath)

    def iter_epochs(self) -> Iterator[GnsdEpoch]:
        timestamp, observations = None, []
        with self.fpath.open() as f:
            next(f)  # the line "GNSD 1.0"
            for line in f:
                parts = line.split()
                if parts[0] in ("EPOCH", "END") and timestamp is not None:
                    yield GnsdEpoch(timestamp, observations)
                if parts[0] == "END":
                    return
                if parts[0] == "EPOCH":
                    # "Z": UTC. canVODpy stores GPS time.
                    utc = datetime.fromisoformat(parts[1].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
                    timestamp, observations = utc_to_gps(utc), []
                else:
                    sv, band, code, snr = parts
                    observations.append(GnsdObservation(sv, band, code, float(snr)))

    def to_ds(self, keep_data_vars: list[str] | None = None, **kwargs) -> xr.Dataset:
        builder = DatasetBuilder(self, time_system="GPS")
        for epoch in self.iter_epochs():
            ei = builder.add_epoch(epoch.timestamp)
            for obs in epoch.observations:
                sig = builder.add_signal(sv=obs.sv, band=obs.band, code=obs.code)
                builder.set_value(ei, sig, "SNR", obs.snr)
        return builder.build(
            keep_data_vars=keep_data_vars, extra_attrs={"Format Version": "1.0"}
        )

    @cached_property
    def _epochs(self) -> list[GnsdEpoch]:
        epochs = list(self.iter_epochs())
        if not epochs:
            raise ValueError(f"No epochs in {self.fpath}")
        return epochs

    @property
    def start_time(self) -> datetime:
        return self._epochs[0].timestamp

    @property
    def end_time(self) -> datetime:
        return self._epochs[-1].timestamp

    @property
    def systems(self) -> list[str]:
        return sorted({o.sv[0] for e in self._epochs for o in e.observations})

    @property
    def num_satellites(self) -> int:
        return len({o.sv for e in self._epochs for o in e.observations})

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text: Mistake Result Instead Building the dataset by hand Wrong dimension names or float64 frequencies fail validate_dataset(), or nothing checks the dataset at all Use DatasetBuilder Epochs in UTC or local time Off by the leap seconds (18 s since 2017) or the time zone Convert with utc_to_gps() before add_epoch() class MyReader(GNSSDataReader, BaseModel) Nothing gained; GNSSDataReader is a BaseModel One parent fpath: Path in the reader The check that the file exists is lost Inherit fpath ds.dims["epoch"] for a length FutureWarning from xarray ds.sizes["epoch"]

items.title: Imports
items.text:
from canvod.readers.base import GNSSDataReader, SignalID, validate_dataset
from canvod.readers.builder import DatasetBuilder
from canvod.readers.gnss_specs.leap_seconds import utc_to_gps
from canvod.readers.gnss_specs.signals import SignalIDMapper
from canvod.utils.tools import file_hash
from canvodpy import ReaderFactory

See also RINEX v3.04, SBF, and the API reference.

items.title: Ephemeris sources
items.text: Computing satellite geometry (theta, phi) requires knowing where each satellite is at each observation epoch. canvodpy supports two ephemeris sources; a third (RINEX navigation files) is planned.

items.title: Source overview
items.text:
• Agency Final Products (SP3/CLK)

    Precise orbits (and, by default, clocks) from analysis centers (CODE, ESA, IGS). Downloaded via FTP. Final products are published about two weeks after observation.

    Input: SP3 (+ CLK, optional, see aux_data.fetch_clock) files (downloaded) Output: ECEF XYZ \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta\), \(\varphi\), \(r\)

  • SBF Broadcast (SatVisibility)

    Satellite elevation and azimuth computed by the receiver firmware from broadcast ephemerides embedded in the SBF binary stream. Immediate availability, no internet required.

    Input: SBF binary file (SatVisibility block) Output: theta, phi directly

  • RINEX NAV Broadcast (planned)

    Not implemented yet. Keplerian orbital elements from RINEX navigation files (.YYp). Propagated to target epochs using the Keplerian model (GPS/Galileo/BeiDou) or RK4 integration (GLONASS state vectors). Immediate, no internet.

    Input: .YYp / .YYn / .YYg nav files Output: ECEF XYZ \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta\), \(\varphi\), \(r\)

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: The SBF angles are stored by the receiver with a resolution of \(0.01^\circ\) (SatVisibility block), so they cannot be more precise than that. The SP3 path computes \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) from interpolated satellite positions and the receiver position. canvodpy has not quantified the difference between the two sources on its test data; until then, do not mix them in one analysis.

items.title: Agency final products (SP3/CLK)
items.text: The default path of canvodpy run (ephemeris_source: final).

items.title: Pipeline
items.text:
1. AuxDataPipeline: download SP3 (+ CLK, if aux_data.fetch_clock) from FTP (CODE/ESA/IGS)
2. Epoch grid of the day: 00:00 plus multiples of the sampling interval of the
   observations (1 s with a shared aux cache), in GPS time like the SP3 file
3. Hermite interpolation: SP3 positions → epoch grid
4. Clock piecewise linear interpolation (skipped if fetch_clock=False)
5. Write Zarr cache: 00_aux_zarr/aux_{date}.zarr
6. Per file: open Zarr → nearest grid epoch per observation epoch
   → compute_spherical_coordinates()
7. Output: ds["theta"], ds["phi"], ds["r"]

CLK is not used by the VOD formula, \(\text{VOD} = -\ln(T) \cdot \cos\theta\), which needs only transmittance and polar angle, so aux_data.fetch_clock is false by default, which skips step 1's clock download and step 4 entirely.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
# canvod-settings.yaml
processing:
  params:
    ephemeris_source: "final"
  aux_data:
    agency: "COD"
    product_type: "final"
    ftp_timeout_s: 30
    fetch_clock: false  # true: also download and interpolate CLK

items.title: Component locations
items.text: Component Package Module SP3/CLK download canvod-auxiliary pipeline.py FTP with fallback canvod-auxiliary core/downloader.py Hermite interpolation canvod-auxiliary interpolation/interpolator.py Clock interpolation (optional, aux_data.fetch_clock) canvod-auxiliary interpolation/interpolator.py ECEF \(\rightarrow\) \(\theta\), \(\varphi\), \(r\) canvod-auxiliary position/spherical_coords.py

items.title: SBF broadcast
items.text: Available when the receiver is a Septentrio unit outputting SBF binary format, with ephemeris_source: broadcast. The receiver firmware computes satellite elevation and azimuth from the satellite's almanac or broadcast ephemeris and embeds them in the SatVisibility block, together with which of the two it used.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. SBF reader scans file: extracts SatVisibility blocks
2. Azimuth and elevation are pre-computed by receiver firmware
3. Stored in the sbf_obs auxiliary dataset as broadcast_theta/broadcast_phi
   (radians), on the epochs and SIDs of the observations: each value comes
   from the SatVisibility block with the same time stamp as the observations
4. Copied to theta/phi of the observations dataset where the receiver
   computed them from the broadcast ephemeris (broadcast_angle_source = 2);
   almanac-based angles become NaN, and a file with no ephemeris-based
   angle raises an error
5. No download, no Zarr cache, no coordinate transform needed

Theta and phi convention

SBF SatVisibility provides elevation and geographic azimuth (\(0^\circ\) = North, clockwise). The reader converts elevation to the polar angle (\(\theta = 90^\circ - \text{elevation}\)) and both angles to radians, the convention used throughout canvodpy.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
processing:
  params:
    ephemeris_source: "broadcast"
  # reader_format must be "sbf" for this to work

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Only available for SBF receivers (Septentrio)
  • Theta/phi are tied to the receiver's computed position: if the receiver position is inaccurate (poor fix), geometry is slightly affected
  • No satellite distance (\(r\)), only angles

items.title: RINEX NAV broadcast
items.text:
Status: not implemented

A RinexNavProvider is planned but not built. This section records the intended design.

For RINEX receivers, broadcast ephemerides are available in navigation files (.YYp for mixed GNSS, .YYn for GPS, .YYg for GLONASS) that sit alongside observation files in the same directory.

items.title: Keplerian propagation
items.text:
GPS, Galileo, and BeiDou use a common 16-parameter Keplerian orbital model (IS-GPS-200, Galileo ICD, BeiDou ICD):

Input: orbital elements (a, e, i₀, Ω₀, ω, M₀) + correction terms
       from navigation message

Steps:
  1. Mean motion:  n = √(μ/a³) + Δn
  2. Mean anomaly: M = M₀ + n·(t - tₒₑ)
  3. Kepler's equation: E - e·sin(E) = M  (iterate ~10×)
  4. True anomaly: ν = atan2(√(1-e²)·sin(E), cos(E)-e)
  5. Argument of latitude with corrections
  6. Radius with corrections
  7. Inclination with corrections
  8. ECEF rotation from orbital plane

Output: satellite ECEF (X, Y, Z) in meters

items.title: GLONASS exception
items.text: GLONASS broadcasts state vectors (\(x\), \(y\), \(z\), \(v_x\), \(v_y\), \(v_z\)) in PZ-90 frame instead of Keplerian elements. Propagation uses fourth-order Runge-Kutta numerical integration.

items.title: NAV file types
items.text: Extension Content Constellations .YYp Mixed GNSS navigation All (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, and others) .YYn GPS-only navigation GPS .YYg GLONASS-only navigation GLONASS

items.title: Validity intervals
items.text: Broadcast ephemerides are valid for ~2-4 hours around their reference epoch (toe). The propagator must select the closest valid ephemeris set for each target epoch, not simply the first record found.

items.title: Receiver file types summary
items.text:
Extension Format Observations Broadcast ephemeris Use in canvodpy .YYo / .rnx RINEX 3 OBS No Primary observation data .YY_ / .sbf SBF binary Observations + broadcast geometry .YYp RINEX 3 NAV (mixed) No Not read (planned) .YYn RINEX 2 NAV (GPS) No Not read (planned) .YYg RINEX NAV (GLONASS) No Not read (planned) .nmea NMEA 0183 SNR only No Observations (NmeaObs); geometry from SP3 .ubx u-blox binary Not supported

NMEA is not an ephemeris source

NMEA GSV sentences carry satellite elevation and azimuth in whole degrees. NmeaObs reads the signal strengths only; the geometry of NMEA data comes from SP3 files and the receiver position of the GGA fixes (readers overview).

items.title: Choosing an ephemeris source
items.text:
When to use agency final products

Use ephemeris_source: "final" when:

  • The receivers write RINEX or NMEA (the only source for them)
  • Final products are available for the days (about two weeks after observation)
  • You have internet access during processing
When to use broadcast ephemerides

Use ephemeris_source: "broadcast" when:

  • The receivers write SBF (the geometry is embedded in the file)
  • Processing recent data, before final products are published
  • Working offline

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
The canvod-readers package provides validated parsers for GNSS observation data. It transforms raw receiver files into analysis-ready xarray Datasets, serving as the data ingestion layer for GNSS Transmissometry (GNSS-T) analysis.

Storage stack

xarray provides labeled N-D arrays with named axes and coordinates, like NumPy with named dimensions and attached metadata. Readers output xarray Datasets that flow into Zarr, a chunked, compressed array format designed for parallel cloud reads. Icechunk sits on top of Zarr and adds git-like version control: every write is a commit, a snapshot retrievable by its ID. Together they form part of the Pangeo open scientific Python ecosystem for large geoscience datasets that canvodpy builds on.

  • RINEX v3.04 (Rnxv3Obs)

    RINEX (Receiver Independent Exchange Format) is the IGS-standardized plain-text format for GNSS observations, supported by every major receiver manufacturer. Observation files (.rnx) contain timestamped pseudorange, carrier phase, Doppler, and signal-to-noise measurements per satellite and signal. Satellite geometry is not embedded; it requires external SP3 precise ephemerides (CLK clock corrections are fetched too by default, though unused for VOD; see aux_data.fetch_clock).

    RINEX format

  • RINEX v2.11 (Rnxv2Obs)

    Legacy RINEX 2 observation files (.YYo, .rnx), read into the same RINEX 3 based SV|BAND|CODE structure. RINEX 2 does not record tracking codes; where the specification leaves a code unresolved, the SID carries a lowercase marker (p, l, u) instead of a guessed RINEX 3 code.

    RINEX v2.11 format

  • SBF binary (SbfReader)

    SBF (Septentrio Binary Format) is a compact proprietary binary format with embedded receiver metadata. PVT position solution, DOP quality indicators, and SatVisibility satellite geometry are all embedded in the file, eliminating the need to download external ephemeris for geometry computation.

    SBF reader

  • NMEA 0183 v4.00 (NmeaObs)

    Signal strengths from GSV sentences (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou), epochs from RMC/GGA (UTC), checksums validated. Band and tracking code come from the GSV signal ID where the sentence has one, else the system's main band with code X. NMEA carries SNR only: no pseudorange and no phase. The receiver position is the median of the file's GGA fixes (fix indicator 1, 2, 4 or 5; ellipsoidal height = altitude + geoid separation); a run takes it from the first file of a receiver-day that has one. A day none of whose files has such a fix can't be processed.

items.title: Supported formats at a glance
items.text:
Feature Rnxv3Obs Rnxv2Obs SbfReader NmeaObs Format Plain text Plain text Binary Plain text Extension .rnx .YYo, .rnx .sbf .nmea Tracking codes Exact (RINEX 3 attribute) Exact where RINEX 2.11 defines them, else lowercase marker Exact From the GSV signal ID, else X Observables SNR, pseudorange, phase, Doppler, LLI, SSI as RINEX 3 SNR, pseudorange, phase, Doppler, SSI, flags SNR only Epoch time scale GPS time (header; other time systems refused) GPS time (header; other time systems refused) GPS time UTC, converted to GPS time Satellite geometry (\(\theta\), \(\varphi\)) SP3 download SP3 download SP3 download, or embedded (SatVisibility) SP3 download Extra metadata Header only Header only PVT · DOP · quality None to_ds_and_auxiliary() {} aux {} aux {"sbf_obs": meta_ds} {} aux

Every reader has to_ds() and iter_epochs(). Every epoch is GPS time, the time scale of the orbits and clocks (SP3, CLK), recorded in the time_system attribute of the epoch coordinate (GPS). NMEA times are UTC: the reader adds the leap seconds of the date (\(\text{GPS} - \text{UTC}\), 18 s since 2017; canvod.readers.gnss_specs.leap_seconds). Stores written before canVODpy stored every epoch in GPS time have SBF and NMEA epochs in UTC; the store refuses to append to them (EpochTimeSystemError).

Consistent output structure

All readers always produce data with the same two dimensions, time (epoch) and signal (SID), and the same required attributes, so analysis code works with RINEX and SBF data interchangeably. All readers produce (epoch × sid) xarray Datasets that pass validate_dataset(). Every row is one timestep (an epoch), every column is one signal (a SID), and every cell is one observable, for example SNR, with its unit in the units attribute. The same dimensions, coordinates, and required attributes are guaranteed, so downstream analysis code is reader-agnostic for observables. Geometry provisioning differs: RINEX datasets are augmented with satellite positions from SP3 files (by default CLK too, which is optional; see aux_data.fetch_clock); SBF datasets carry embedded SatVisibility data from the receiver.

items.title: Data flow
items.text:
graph TD
    A1["RINEX v3 File (.rnx)"] --> B1["Rnxv3Obs (+ SP3/CLK)"]
    A2["SBF File (.sbf)"] --> B2["SbfReader"]
    A3["RINEX v2 File (.YYo)"] --> B3["Rnxv2Obs (+ SP3/CLK)"]
    A4["NMEA File (.nmea)"] --> B4["NmeaObs (+ SP3/CLK)"]
    B1 --> C["validate_dataset()"]
    B3 --> C
    B2 --> C
    B4 --> C
    C --> D["`**xarray.Dataset**
    epoch x sid`"]
    B2 --> E["`**Metadata Dataset**
    DOP, PVT, theta, phi`"]
    D --> F["Downstream Analysis"]
    E --> F

items.title: Contract-based design
items.text:
All readers implement the GNSSDataReader base class, a Pydantic BaseModel and ABC. It holds the validated path fpath and declares what every reader must provide:

Abstract member What it returns to_ds(**kwargs) The (epoch × sid) dataset iter_epochs() The file's epochs one by one file_hash First 16 hex digits of the file's SHA-256 (deduplication) source_format Format identifier, for example "rinex3" or "sbf", recorded in the GNSS store start_time, end_time First and last epoch systems, num_satellites Systems and number of satellites in the file

to_ds_and_auxiliary(**kwargs) returns the dataset and a dict of auxiliary datasets; by default the dict is empty, and SbfReader fills it from the same pass over the file. A missing member fails as soon as the class is instantiated.

Subclasses only need to inherit from GNSSDataReader: no separate BaseModel import, no fpath field, no file validation boilerplate.

The reader contract

items.title: Usage examples
items.text:
RINEX for the VOD pipelineSBF quick look (no downloads)Multi-constellation analysisReaderFactory format registryTime series of several files 
from canvod.readers import Rnxv3Obs

reader = Rnxv3Obs(fpath="ROSA01TUW_R_20250010000_15M_05S_MO.rnx")
ds = reader.to_ds(keep_data_vars=["SNR"])

# Filter L-band signals
l_band = ds.where(ds.band.isin(["L1", "L2", "L5"]), drop=True)

import numpy as np
from canvod.readers.sbf import SbfReader

reader = SbfReader(fpath="rref001a00.sbf")
obs_ds, aux = reader.to_ds_and_auxiliary(keep_data_vars=["SNR"])
meta_ds = aux["sbf_obs"]

# Polar angle filter: elevation ≥ 20°
snr_filtered = obs_ds["SNR"].where(meta_ds["broadcast_theta"] <= np.deg2rad(70))

ds = reader.to_ds()

for system in ["G", "R", "E", "C"]:
    sys_ds = ds.where(ds.system == system, drop=True)
    mean_snr = sys_ds.SNR.mean(dim=["epoch", "sid"])
    print(f"{system}: {mean_snr:.2f} dB")

from canvodpy import ReaderFactory

# By name (works for all registered readers)
reader = ReaderFactory.create("rinex3", fpath="ROSA01TUW_R_20250010000_15M_05S_MO.rnx")

# Auto-detect RINEX v2/v3 from file header
reader = ReaderFactory.create_from_file("ROSA01TUW_R_20250010000_15M_05S_MO.rnx")

# Both produce identical (epoch × sid) datasets
ds = reader.to_ds(keep_data_vars=["SNR"])

import xarray as xr
from pathlib import Path

datasets = [
    Rnxv3Obs(fpath=f).to_ds(keep_data_vars=["SNR"])
    for f in sorted(Path("/data/").glob("*.rnx"))
]

time_series = xr.concat(datasets, dim="epoch")

items.title: Key components
items.text:
• SignalID (validated signal identifiers)

    Pydantic model for signal identifiers (SV|band|code). GNSS observations span six dimensions: epoch, satellite (SV), band, ranging code type, polar angle (\(\theta\)), and azimuth (\(\varphi\)). Different satellite generations broadcast different signal combinations, and a single SV may simultaneously transmit on multiple ranging code types. SignalID collapses the three dimensions that characterize a signal (SV, band in RINEX v3.04 nomenclature, and ranging code) into a single composite key, reducing the 6D observation space to 2D: (epoch, SID). Unlike most GNSS tools that aggregate or discard sub-SV signal distinctions at ingestion, canvodpy retains all signal characteristics throughout processing, treating signals as non-comparable across codes until explicitly aggregated downstream. This full signal fidelity enables per-band and per-constellation aggregation as an analysis choice, not an ingestion constraint, and is essential for rigorous validation. Validates the SV against known GNSS systems at creation time. Frozen, hashable, and used throughout the builder and readers.

    from canvod.readers import SignalID

sig = SignalID(sv="G01", band="L1", code="C")
sig.sid  # → "G01|L1|C"
sig.system  # → "G"

  • DatasetBuilder (guided dataset construction)

    Handles coordinate assembly, frequency resolution, dtype enforcement, and validation. Readers use add_epoch() \(\rightarrow\) add_signal() \(\rightarrow\) set_value() \(\rightarrow\) build() instead of manual NumPy or xarray assembly.

    from canvod.readers.builder import DatasetBuilder

builder = DatasetBuilder(reader, time_system="GPS")
ei = builder.add_epoch(timestamp)
sig = builder.add_signal(sv="G01", band="L1", code="C")
builder.set_value(ei, sig, "SNR", 42.0)
ds = builder.build()  # validated Dataset

  • GNSS Specifications

    gnss_specs provides constellation definitions for GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou, QZSS, SBAS, and IRNSS including band mappings and center frequencies.

    from canvod.readers.gnss_specs.constellations import GPS

gps = GPS()  # static SVs from IGS SINEX catalog
gps.BANDS  # {'1': 'L1', '2': 'L2', '5': 'L5'}

  • Signal ID Mapper

    SignalIDMapper provides frequency, bandwidth, and overlap-group lookups for canonical SV|Band|Code signal IDs.

    mapper = SignalIDMapper()
freq = mapper.get_band_frequency("L1")  # → 1575.42
bw = mapper.get_band_bandwidth("L1")  # → 30.69

  • validate_dataset()

    Every dataset produced by any reader must pass structural validation before it is returned. Checks dimensions, coordinate data types, required variables, and global attributes, including "File Hash", the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the source file contents that canvod-store uses as its first deduplication layer, ensuring the same physical file is never ingested twice regardless of when it is processed.

    from canvod.readers.base import validate_dataset

validate_dataset(ds)  # raises ValueError listing ALL violations

items.title: RINEX v3 parsers
items.text:
Rnxv3Obs pre-computes the full Signal ID (SID) space from the RINEX header and fills pre-allocated NumPy arrays. A pre-built lookup table maps (SV, obs_code) to the array index, and the SIDs are derived once from the header.

Two parsers fill these arrays:
