Writing a file again therefore never adds epochs, a file that now has fewer epochs leaves nothing of its earlier write, and a file written for the first time leaves the rest of its named period alone (after a receiver restart, the next file can start inside it). A file without a canonical name (possible with temporal_aggregation) replaces only the slots from its first to its last epoch.
  • The cadence of a day is the finest sampling interval in the names of the files of the day, or the bin length of processing.preprocessing.temporal_aggregation when it is set. Every cadence is stored, and days in one group can have different cadences. A day has ceil(86400 s / cadence) slots; its block holds whole chunks of 180 epochs (processing.icechunk.chunk_strategies.gnss_store.epoch), padded with empty epochs where the slots don't fill the last chunk (84 per day at 15 min, none at 1 s to 1 min). Padding epochs lie between the day's last slot and the next day, and loading leaves them out. A group keeps the chunk size it was created with: a changed setting applies to new groups only (see Chunks).
  • A group records its layout in its attributes (epoch_layout: day_blocks) and the block of each day in day_block_index (start and stop on the epoch axis, slots, cadence). A store whose groups were written by appending files to the epoch axis, by canVODpy versions before day blocks, is refused by runs until it is moved to day blocks (see Moving a store to day blocks).

GnssResearchSite.read_receiver_data() returns only the slots with data. MyIcechunkStore.read_group() returns every slot; with drop_empty=True it leaves out the empty ones (slots where every floating-point variable is missing).

items.title: The VOD store
items.text:
A VOD store group is made of day blocks when the canopy or the reference group of its analysis is. A day of VOD gets the cadence of its GNSS data: the coarser of the two groups' cadences for that day, so every VOD epoch has its own slot. Slots without VOD hold NaN.

  • A run writes the VOD of each day with its own commit. The VOD of all analyses of a day shares that commit.
  • A write covers exactly one day; a result of more than one day is refused (LayoutError). The log-book row of a write records how many epochs of the day hold VOD (epochs).
  • A result computed from the same GNSS files as a stored one isn't written; the run logs it. A result from other GNSS files, for example after more files of the day were stored, is written into the day's slots and replaces the VOD that was there. Its log-book row records the action overwrite.
  • VOD is computed only from GNSS groups made of day blocks, and written only into VOD store groups made of day blocks. Either store written by appending is refused (LayoutError, naming the command that moves it).

GnssResearchSite.read_vod_analysis() leaves out the empty slots, as read_receiver_data() does; with drop_empty=False it returns every slot.

items.title: Moving a store to day blocks
items.text:
A store written by canVODpy versions before day blocks holds groups written by appending files to the epoch axis. Runs write day blocks only, so they refuse such a store. Move it once:

canvodpy store migrate-layout SITE --store gnss
canvodpy store migrate-layout SITE --store vod

The command shows, for each group, its days, their cadences, its epochs and the duplicate entries it drops, and asks before it changes anything (--yes skips the question).

  • Each group written by appending is written again, day by day. Each day gets a block at its cadence: the finest step between its epochs, rounded to 1 ms. A day with a single epoch takes the finest cadence of the group. Days may have different cadences.
  • An epoch stored more than once, for example by unsafe_append, keeps the entry written last.
  • A group keeps its attributes, its log book and its other metadata (sbf_obs). It gets the chunks of the settings (processing.icechunk.chunk_strategies).
  • The log book gets the epochs column, so the snapshot summary counts each epoch once, for the latest write of its file.
  • Everything goes into one commit. Snapshots from before keep the old layout and stay readable.

A store written before repository metadata needs canvodpy store migrate-metadata first; migrate-layout refuses it and names that command.

items.title: How a run writes
items.text:
canvodpy run writes to both stores; in your own code, read from them.

On a file system, Icechunk can't detect two commits at the same time: both can report success while Icechunk loses one of them (Icechunk: storage). So every commit to a store first takes the store's commit lock, the file .canvodpy-commit.lock in the store directory. A commit from another thread or process, for example a second run or a scheduler task, waits until the lock is free. Write a store from one computer only.

Two Icechunk warnings don't apply to these stores, so canVODpy hides them: that the file system is not safe for concurrent commits (the commit lock covers this), and that a lost reply to a write may show up as a conflict (Icechunk's file system storage makes one try per write and keeps no write metadata). Every other Icechunk warning is shown. To set your own filter, set the environment variable ICECHUNK_LOG, for example ICECHUNK_LOG=icechunk=debug.

For each receiver and day, a run does the following:

  1. Reads the files and computes the satellite angles.
  2. Applies the preprocessing in processing.preprocessing, if set.
  3. Checks each file against the group's log book (see Duplicate checks).
  4. Writes the new data with one commit: the worker processes write the files into their slots, and one commit writes the day of all receivers. The same commit writes the snapshot summary and records the commit metadata (see canvod-store-metadata).

A write must match the group. A run stops with an error if:

  • the data has other variables than the group (GroupVariablesMismatchError);
  • the data has other sid labels than the group (GroupCoordinatesMismatchError). The labels are stored once per group, so an append with other labels, for example after you change processing.params.aggregate_glonass_fdma, would relabel the stored data;
  • the epochs aren't in GPS time, or the group doesn't record its time scale (EpochTimeSystemError). Every stored epoch is GPS time (epoch.attrs["time_system"] == "GPS"). Groups written by canVODpy before it stored every epoch in GPS time have no record (their SBF and NMEA epochs were UTC, 18 s earlier); write to a new store;
  • a day stored at a coarser cadence gets a file sampled more often (CadenceError);
  • a file would be appended to a group made of day blocks, or the store holds groups written by appending (LayoutError).

A file with two epochs in one slot, for example because its name gives a coarser sampling than its data, isn't stored: the run logs a SlotCollisionError and writes no log-book row for the file, so the next run tries it again.

If another commit lands while a write is in progress, canVODpy rebases the write onto it when the two changed different groups. If both changed the same data, the later commit fails with icechunk.RebaseFailedError and writes nothing. The run then plans and writes the whole unit again on top of the other commit, up to five tries in all, with a growing wait in between. When the last try fails too, the run records the receivers and days as failed in its run history, with the error, and goes on with the next days. It does the same when it can't add the blocks of a unit.

items.title: Duplicate checks
items.text:
Before a run writes a file, it checks the file against the group's log book, in three ways:

Check What it finds Where Hash The same file, already stored (SHA-256 of the file) The orchestrator, and again just before the commit Time span A file whose time span overlaps stored data, also when it has another name or other start and end times The orchestrator, and again just before the commit Batch Two files of one batch that cover the same time The orchestrator

A file with the same hash counts as already stored: the default write strategy, skip, doesn't write it; overwrite replaces its time range. A file with another hash over stored data stops a run with skip, and replaces the stored data with overwrite; the run checks it again just before each commit. A file that overlaps another file of its batch is skipped. For details, see Write strategies.

items.title: Read a store
items.text:
Open the stores of a configured site with Site:

from canvodpy import Site

site = Site("ExampleSite")
site.gnss_store.list_groups()  # ["canopy_01", "reference_01_canopy_01"]
site.gnss_store.get_group_info("canopy_01")

ds = site.gnss_store.read_group("canopy_01")
ds_day = site.gnss_store.read_group("canopy_01", date="2025001")
ds_range = site.gnss_store.read_group(
    "canopy_01", time_slice=slice("2025-01-01", "2025-01-15")
)

read_group() returns an xarray.Dataset that reads its data only when a value is needed, its epochs in time order. date="2025001" selects that day only: from 00:00 up to, not including, 00:00 of the next day. A time_slice includes both of its ends, and an end written as a date ("2025-01-15") means the whole of that day. For how reads load chunks, see Chunks; for earlier states of a store, see Versioning with Icechunk.

To open a store by its path, use open_gnss_store() or open_vod_store():

from canvod.store import open_gnss_store

store = open_gnss_store("/data/stores/ExampleSite/gnss")

Opening a store never creates one: a path without a store raises a FileNotFoundError that names the path. A run creates a site's stores when it first writes data, together with their metadata (see canvod-store-metadata). Site opens its stores only when you first use them, so a new site has no stores until a run writes to it. create_gnss_store() and create_vod_store() are left over from development: they open a store as well, and are removed with the next major version.

Reading a store needs no settings file, so a store you downloaded or got from a colleague opens as it is. Without a settings file the store opens with the configuration Icechunk keeps with it. Reads work, and so do branches and tags. Commits need the settings, because a commit records them, and so do expiring snapshots and garbage collection, a dry run included. On a store opened without settings they raise a FileNotFoundError that names canvodpy config init. Create the settings with it, then open the store again. A settings file that is there but can't be loaded fails the opening, as before.

items.title: Compare two stores
items.text:
compare_stores() compares two stores and returns a report of every difference, per group and variable. It works on any two stores, for example the reference stores of the test data and the stores a change produces (spec #318), or a production store before and after an upgrade. It only reads, through MyIcechunkStore (list_data_groups and read_group), and never changes how a store is written or read.

Open each store by its path, then compare:

from canvod.store import compare_stores, open_gnss_store

reference = open_gnss_store("/data/stores/ExampleSite/gnss")
new = open_gnss_store("/data/stores/ExampleSite-new/gnss")
report = compare_stores(reference, new)

report.matches  # True when the stores are the same
print(report.to_text())  # a report for a person
report.model_dump_json()  # a report for CI

The comparison uses xarray.testing: assert_allclose within the tolerance below for the float variables of the table, and assert_identical for everything else (integer and flag variables, coordinates, other floats). The report lists a group present in one store and not the other, a lost epoch or a renamed SID, a changed value (also a value present in one store and missing in the other), with the count of differing values, the largest difference and xarray's message.

Attributes are compared too, those of the store, the groups and every variable, also nested ones (the report names the inner key, for example canvod:repository_metadata.identity.title). Left out are only the attributes that change with every run or release: the creation and modification times, the store ids, the canvodpy version and the Software attribute, and the content hash of the GNSS store a VOD store was computed from (its values are compared themselves). The list is VOLATILE_ATTRIBUTES in the same module. A changed input file therefore shows as a changed File Hash. A new or changed setting shows under canvod:repository_metadata.content_settings, by name and in its hash: it changes what the store records about how it was built, so it counts as a difference.

The log books (metadata/table) are not compared. They record how a run wrote each file (write times, snapshot ids, run ids, paths); what the files hold is compared through the groups, and which files were read through File Hash.

Float variables are compared within one absolute tolerance per variable, derived from the finest resolution any format records. A float variable not in the table is compared exactly and is reported as no_tolerance, so a new variable is noticed.

Variable Tolerance Derivation SNR (also 1-minute means), Pseudorange, Phase, Doppler 5e-4 half the RINEX observation resolution, format F14.3 = 0.001 (RINEX 3.04, observation record, p. 67; RINEX 2.11, observation record). SBF (0.25 dB-Hz) and NMEA GSV (1 dB-Hz) are coarser. delta_snr 1e-3 a difference of two SNR values, 2 × 5e-4 VOD 2e-4 VOD = -(ln 10 / 10) · delta_snr · cos(theta); (ln 10 / 10) × 1e-3 = 2.3e-4, rounded down theta, phi 1e-6 rad above the float32 spacing at pi/2 (1.2e-7 rad), the precision the angles are stored with; a larger difference is a changed satellite geometry

The tolerances, with their derivation and sources, are one constant in the code: FLOAT_TOLERANCES in packages/canvod-store/src/canvod/store/comparison.py (spec #318).

The JSON form carries matches, so a CI check can read the result.

items.title: History
items.text:
Each store keeps its commits and the operations on it:

store = site.gnss_store

store.print_history(limit=20)  # commits on main, newest first
store.plot_commit_graph()  # commit graph: SVG in a notebook, text in a terminal
store.print_ops_log(limit=30)  # commits, branch operations, expiry, garbage collection

store.create_release_tag("v1.0")  # tag the latest commit on main
store.list_tags()
store.compare_snapshots(snapshot_id_1, snapshot_id_2)

items.title: Command line
items.text:
canvodpy store shows the stores of a configured site; store log --path also shows a store outside the settings:

canvodpy store list                                 # GNSS and VOD store paths of every site
canvodpy store info ExampleSite                     # branches, groups, and statistics
canvodpy store info ExampleSite --group canopy_01   # the dataset and log book of one group
canvodpy store log ExampleSite                      # commit graph
canvodpy store log ExampleSite --ops                # operations on the store
canvodpy store log --path /data/copy/gnss           # commit graph of a store outside the settings
canvodpy store log ExampleSite --svg history.svg    # commit graph as an SVG file
canvodpy store log ExampleSite --plain              # commit graph without colors, for files and CI logs
canvodpy store maintain ExampleSite                 # what expiry and garbage collection would delete
canvodpy store migrate-layout ExampleSite           # move a store written by appending to day blocks

--store vod opens the VOD store instead of the GNSS store, and --branch selects a branch other than main. For every option, see the command-line reference.

On a store on S3, maintenance is a dry run only: another machine may be writing to the store, so canvodpy store maintain reports what it would do and --execute is refused, and canvodpy store maintain-due reports a due store without changing it. See ADR 0019.

items.title: Grids and analysis results
items.text:
store_grid() writes a hemispherical grid to the grids/{grid_name} group of a store, and load_grid() reads it back. A grid read back works for cell assignment only if it's an equal-area, equal-angle, or equirectangular grid; for the other grid types, build the grid again with create_hemigrid().

from canvod.grids import create_hemigrid
from canvod.store import load_grid, store_grid

grid = create_hemigrid("equal_area", angular_resolution=4.0)
store_grid(grid, store, "equal_area_4deg")
grid = load_grid(store, "equal_area_4deg")

AnalysisStorage stores the results of an analysis on a grid in a VOD store: weights, masks, statistics, and time series per cell. The time series per cell go to the per_cell branch, one dataset per system, band, and code:

from canvod.store import AnalysisStorage

storage = AnalysisStorage("/path/to/vod_store")
storage.store_percell_timeseries(percell_ds, system="G", band="L1", code="C")
storage.list_percell_datasets()  # ['C_B2b_I', 'E_E1_C', 'G_L1_C', ...]
ds = storage.load_percell_timeseries(system="G", band="L1", code="C")

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Chunks: how the stores are chunked, and how to choose the chunk sizes.
  • Versioning with Icechunk: the store format, the Icechunk settings, and reading earlier states.
  • Write strategies: what a run does with a file that's already stored.
  • canvod-store-metadata: the metadata that describes a whole store.

items.title: Write strategies
items.text:
The write strategy sets what a run does with a file that's already in the GNSS store: a file with the same hash, or one whose time span overlaps stored data (see Duplicate checks). A run always writes new files, whatever the strategy.

Set the strategy in canvod-settings.yaml:

processing:
  storage:
    gnss_store_strategy: skip

MyIcechunkStore has no strategy argument; the strategy comes from the settings. canvodpy config show prints the strategy in use under Storage.

The VOD store

The strategy applies to the GNSS store only. A run skips a VOD result when the VOD store already holds one computed from the same GNSS files. A result from other files replaces the stored VOD of its day (see The VOD store). To compute VOD again from the same GNSS files, write to a new VOD store: set processing.storage.vod_store_name to another name, such as vod-recompute.

Stores written by appending

A run writes day blocks only. A store whose groups were written by appending files, by canVODpy versions before day blocks, is refused until it is moved to day blocks with canvodpy store migrate-layout (see Moving a store to day blocks).

items.title: The strategies
items.text:
Strategy File already stored (same hash) Another file over stored epochs New file skip (default) Not written; the run logs it. The run stops and names both files. Written overwrite Its slots are replaced; the log book says overwritten. Replaces the stored data; the log book says overwritten. Written unsafe_append As overwrite As overwrite Written

"Another file over stored epochs" is a file with another hash whose time span overlaps data stored from another file, for example a file that was exported again with other content, or another run's file for the same time. Neither file is preferred silently. The run checks this before it writes and again at the tip, just before each commit, so a run that lost a conflict to another run finds that run's files too.

items.title: skip
items.text: A file that's already stored isn't written, and the store doesn't change. Running again over the same files writes nothing new. This is the default.

items.title: overwrite
items.text:
The run writes the file into the slots of its day again, in the run's commit. Use it to correct stored data, for example after a fix in a reader or another ephemeris source.

  • All of the file's slots are replaced, also those of its earlier write (found in the log book by its canonical name) it now has no epochs for. Slots inside another stored file's span are never emptied.
  • No epoch is stored twice, and no other day is written.
  • The log book keeps all its rows and records overwritten. The sbf_obs of an SBF file stays as first stored.
  • The replaced data stays in earlier snapshots until they're expired and garbage is collected (canvodpy store maintain).

items.title: unsafe_append
items.text: Kept from versions before day blocks, where it wrote a file again next to the stored data, so the group held its epochs twice. In a store made of day blocks, a file written again goes into the same slots, so unsafe_append does what overwrite does.

items.title: canvod-store-metadata
items.text:
canvod-store-metadata keeps the metadata that describes a whole store: who created it, with which software and settings, for which site and receivers, and which period it covers. Runs write it to both stores of a site. You can read it, check it for missing fields, and list the stores of a directory with it.

Store metadata and the log book

The log book of a group ({group}/metadata/table, in canvod-store) has one row per stored file. The store metadata describes the store as a whole.

items.title: Where it's stored
items.text:
A store's metadata has three parts (ADR 0014), each kept where Icechunk keeps that kind of information:

Part Where What it holds Changes Repository metadata Icechunk's repository metadata: on no branch, in no snapshot What describes the store as a whole: identity, creator, publisher and license, site and position, receivers or VOD analyses, references Fixed fields never; amendable fields only by amendment Snapshot summary Root attributes of each snapshot What the snapshot holds: time coverage, per-receiver epochs, signals, variables, time range and position, constellations Written by every commit, from the data of that commit Commit metadata Icechunk's metadata of each commit How the commit was made: software versions, environment, settings and their hash, hash of uv.lock Written by every commit

Every commit also writes a copy of the repository metadata into the root attributes, in standard form: flat CF and ACDD global attributes, the Zarr conventions for proj, license and stac, and the lossless copy under canvod:repository_metadata. So each snapshot shows its store as it was when it was committed, and tools that read only the root group, such as xarray, see it too. The uv.lock and pyproject.toml are those of the project the run starts in: the nearest directory, from the working directory up, that holds both. A run outside such a project records neither. Their text is stored once per hash, in the reserved group canvod. A run with a lockfile the store doesn't hold yet stores it in a commit of its own ("Store the lockfile in use") before its first data commit, so the data commits of two runs never both write it. Two runs that start with the same new lockfile store it once:

store_root/                    # root attributes: root copy and snapshot summary
├── canvod/
│   └── environments/
│       └── <uv.lock hash>/    # uv_lock, pyproject_toml (text as bytes)
├── canopy_01/
│   ├── SNR
│   ├── ...
│   └── metadata/
│       ├── table              # log book (canvod-store)
│       └── sbf_obs            # SBF receivers only (canvod-store)
└── reference_01_canopy_01/
    └── ...

The fixed fields say which store this is: the store id, UUID, store type, source format, naming authority, catalog link, and creation date. The store id is {site}-{store folder}, from the site name in lowercase and the store's folder name (gnss, vod, or vod-recompute for a second VOD store). Every other field of the repository metadata is amendable.

items.title: Sections
items.text:
read_metadata() combines the three parts of one snapshot into one StoreMetadata, with a metadata_version and these sections:

Section Model Content Part identity StoreIdentity ID, UUID, naming authority, catalog link, title, description, store type, source format, keywords Repository metadata creator Creator Name, email, ORCID, institution and its ROR ID, department, research group, website Repository metadata publisher Publisher Name, URL, license (SPDX identifier or other), license URI Repository metadata temporal TemporalExtent Created; updated, first and last stored epoch, duration, resolution (the finest cadence of any day) Created: repository metadata; the rest: snapshot summary spatial SpatialExtent Site name, description and country, latitude, longitude, altitude (WGS84); bounding box Site and position: repository metadata; bounding box: snapshot summary instruments Instruments Platform; per receiver: type, directory, reader format, hardware, antenna; epochs, signals, variables, time range, cadence per time range, position Receiver description: repository metadata; counts, time range, cadences, position: snapshot summary vod_analyses VodAnalysisInfo Per VOD analysis of a VOD store: its canopy and reference receiver Repository metadata references References Repository, documentation, publications, funding Repository metadata summaries Summaries Number of epochs and signals, constellations, variables, number of files Snapshot summary processing ProcessingProvenance Versions of canvodpy and of the 11 canvod-* packages it installs, and of the main libraries (Icechunk, Zarr, xarray, Dask, NumPy, Polars, Pydantic); Python and uv versions; processing level; facility: the institution that processed the data (processing.metadata.institution) Commit metadata environment Environment Operating system, architecture, CPUs, memory, free disk space, the hash and text of uv.lock, and the text of pyproject.toml Commit metadata config ConfigSnapshot The processing, preprocessing, auxiliary data, compression, Icechunk, and signal settings, and their hash, without the settings of one computer (below) Commit metadata amendments Amendment Each amendment: field, old and new value, reason, who, when Repository metadata migration MigrationRecord For a migrated store: old id, who migrated it and when, fields given Repository metadata

Stores are shared, so they record nothing that belongs to one computer or its user account. The recorded settings leave out the folders of the computer that ran: gnss_site_data_root, aux_data_dir, shared_aux_cache_dir, log_dir, and stores_root_dir when it is a local folder (an s3:// URL is kept). The same settings on two computers therefore give the same hash. The content settings record who set them by processing.metadata.initials (the author when no initials are set), and no host name is recorded. Credentials are never recorded. With processing.metadata.record_machine: false the environment of a commit leaves the computer out too: its operating system, architecture, CPUs, memory and free disk are null. Stores that are published, such as the reference stores, set it. Stores written by canVODpy before 1.0.0 keep the folders, host name and user@host they recorded: their snapshots can't be changed.

The field names follow three metadata standards: the DataCite Metadata Schema 4.5, the Attribute Convention for Data Discovery (ACDD) 1.3, and the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) 1.1.

items.title: How runs write it
items.text:
Every run writes the metadata itself, whether it starts from the command line (canvodpy run), from Python (Site.pipeline(), site.vod, FluentWorkflow.to_store(), the write methods of GnssResearchSite) or from Airflow. All of them take the same step, ensure_store_metadata(), before they write data:

  1. Before the first write to a store, collect_metadata() builds the repository metadata from the settings, and write_metadata() writes it. A store never holds data without its metadata: a commit to a store without repository metadata is refused, and nothing is committed. Code that writes to a store directly, without a run, gives it its metadata first.
  2. Every commit, of a run or of any other canVODpy command, writes the root copy and the snapshot summary in the same commit as the data, and records the commit metadata. The snapshot summary therefore can't disagree with the data it describes. A process rebuilds the summary from the whole store at its first commit to a store's branch; from then on it updates the summary from the log-book rows each commit adds, including rows another run committed in between, so a commit costs the same however many days the store holds (ADR 0021). It rebuilds the summary from the whole store again after a failed commit, when a group's log book was written anew (its columns changed, it shrank, or its last known row differs), and for a store with a group written by appending or a log book without row numbers. summarize_store() always reads the whole store. A commit that only gives days their block and writes no data keeps the summary of the snapshot before, with its time updated; it refuses any other change, compared with the snapshot it started from.
  3. A run that writes a receiver (GNSS store) or a VOD analysis (VOD store) that the repository metadata doesn't list is refused. The error names the canvodpy store amend command that adds it. FluentWorkflow.to_store() writes VOD to the VOD analysis of the settings that pairs the receivers of its .vod() step, and refuses a pair without one.

A failed metadata write fails the commit, and the run stops with an error. A commit whose root group differs from the repository metadata, for example after an edit by hand, is refused.

The history of a store is its commit log. show_metadata() lists it, and canvodpy store log SITE draws it as a graph. Each commit records its settings, so the preprocessing of a write can be read from its commit. The full record of each file is in the group's log book (see The preprocessing record).

items.title: Settings
items.text:
The metadata comes from two parts of canvod-settings.yaml.

The creator and publisher come from processing.metadata:

processing:
  metadata:
    author: "Jane Doe"
    email: "jane.doe@example.org"
    orcid: "0000-0002-1825-0097"         # optional, ORCID's test person
    institution: "Example University"
    # institution_ror: "https://ror.org/<id>"  # optional
    department: "Department of Geodesy"     # optional
    license: "CC-BY-4.0"                 # required to create a store, SPDX identifier
    license_uri: null                    # the license text; required when license is "other"
    publisher: "Example University"      # required to create a store
    naming_authority: "org.example"      # required to create a store
    initials: "JD"                       # required to amend or migrate

DataCite requires the publisher and STAC requires the license, so a store isn't created without them.

A first run, and config validate, refuse to start when a setting the new store needs is missing (the site's store description, the publisher, the license or the naming authority).

The license is an identifier from the SPDX license list (a copy of version 3.27.0 comes with the package), as STAC 1.1 asks. A license outside SPDX is other, with license_uri naming its text. Any other value is refused when a store is created or the license is amended; the error names the field and points to the SPDX list.

The license is one of the metadata rules: rules that a standard sets for a field. The models of the package check them when metadata is made, so a store isn't created, and a field isn't amended, with a value that breaks one. The error names the field, the value, and the rule.

Field Rule Standard publisher.license SPDX identifier, or other with license_uri SPDX, STAC 1.1 creator.orcid 0000-0000-0000-000X, alone or after https://orcid.org/, with a valid check digit ORCID creator.institution_ror Nine characters starting with 0, alone or after https://ror.org/ ROR identity.persistent_identifier A DOI (10.<registrant>/<suffix>), when given as one: starting with 10., doi: or https://doi.org/; other identifiers aren't checked DataCite creator.type, publisher.type Personal, Organizational, Institutional, or an ACDD type (person, group, institution, position) DataCite, ACDD 1.3 identity.store_type gnss_store, vod_store or geodesy_store canVODpy spatial.geospatial_lat, _lat_min, _lat_max -90 to 90 WGS84 spatial.geospatial_lon, _lon_min, _lon_max -180 to 180 WGS84 spatial.bbox Four values, W, S, E, N (STAC 1.1), with W <= E and S <= N (a site never spans the 180° meridian) STAC 1.1, canvodpy temporal.time_coverage_duration, time_coverage_resolution ISO 8601 duration, such as PT5S ACDD 1.3 publisher.license_uri, publisher.url, creator.website A URL starting with http:// or https://, kept as written

The source format, the timestamps and the email address have no rule. The source format of a GNSS store is the source_format of the reader that read its files (rinex3, rinex3_stripped, rinex2, sbf or nmea), the same value as the store's source_format root attribute.

The description of the site's stores, the site description, and the location come from the site:

sites:
  ExampleSite:
    store_description: "GNSS-T observations below a beech canopy"  # required to create a store
    description: "Example GNSS-T research site"
    country: "AT"            # ISO 3166-1 code
    latitude: 47.70
    longitude: 16.30
    altitude_m: 575.0
    receivers:
      canopy_01:
        # ...

For every setting, see Configuration.

items.title: Read the metadata
items.text:
from canvod.store_metadata import metadata_exists, read_metadata, show_metadata

if metadata_exists(store_path):
    meta = read_metadata(store_path)
    print(meta.identity.title)
    print(meta.temporal.collected_start)

show_metadata(store_path)  # print all sections

read_metadata() reads the tip of main; branch= reads another branch, and snapshot_id= reads one snapshot as it was when it was committed. format_metadata(meta) returns the text of show_metadata() as a string.

To recreate the Python environment that wrote a store, extract_env() writes the stored pyproject.toml and uv.lock to a directory.

items.title: Stores on S3
items.text:
Stores on S3 covers choosing a provider, credentials, access policies and the bucket settings to avoid. The functions that read or write the metadata take a store location: a local directory, or an s3://bucket/prefix URL. A URL without a bucket or a prefix is refused, and so are other schemes such as gs://.

from canvod.store_metadata import read_metadata, show_metadata

meta = read_metadata("s3://example-bucket/stores/ExampleSite/gnss")
show_metadata("s3://example-bucket/stores/ExampleSite/gnss")

Credentials, region and endpoint come only from the environment or the shared AWS files, never from the settings or the store metadata:

  • AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, or AWS_PROFILE;
  • ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config;
  • AWS_REGION, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL for storage that isn't AWS;
  • CANVOD_S3_PATH_STYLE=1 for a self-hosted S3 service, such as Ceph, that expects the bucket in the request path (https://endpoint/bucket/...) rather than in the host name (https://bucket.endpoint/...). Unset or 0 keeps the host name, as AWS expects.

Without a credential, opening fails with an error that names the location and these sources.

Every function opens a store with open_repository(). Opening never creates a store, so a mistyped location fails instead of leaving an empty store behind. store_exists() says whether a location holds a store, without opening it. With expected_uuid=, a store with another UUID is refused, so a store replaced at the same location is never taken for the old one.

open_repository(location, create=True) creates a store. Without a config=, the new store gets the defaults of the processing.icechunk settings, the same as a store a run creates, not Icechunk's own defaults. Opening a store without a config= uses the configuration Icechunk keeps with the store.

On a local directory, commits hold a lock file in the store's directory, because Icechunk on a local file system can lose one of two concurrent commits without an error. On S3 there is no lock: Icechunk's conditional writes keep two commits from overwriting each other. The S3 service must support them (Conditional writes).

Two runs may also create one store at the same time. Only one of them creates it: the commit that creates a store does not rebase, so the second one fails. That run then waits up to a minute for the first run's repository metadata and goes on with that store, as if it had found it; its settings are checked against the store's content settings like those of any later run.

Creating, opening, reading the metadata, and refusing a conflicting commit are tested in CI against an S3 emulator.

Runs write stores on S3 when processing.storage.stores_root_dir is an s3://bucket/prefix URL (configuration guide). The run history and the file index stay in the log folder of the machine that runs. When the storage can't be reached, a run stops with an error that names the location and the credential sources listed earlier, never the credentials. The STAC catalog is written only for a local folder of stores so far.

items.title: Check against the standards
items.text:
from canvod.store_metadata import validate_all

failures = validate_all(meta, recommended=False)
# {"rules": [], "zarr_conventions": [], "acdd": [], "datacite": [], "stac": [], "fair": []}

issues = validate_all(meta)  # also recommendations and FAIR advice

validate_all() returns a list of messages per standard.

A store written before a rule existed may hold a value that breaks it. The store still opens: reading its metadata gives a MetadataRuleWarning that names the field, rules lists it, and an amendment of that field fixes it. An amendment of another field keeps the old value and warns again. The durations, the bounding box, and the latitude and longitude ranges are computed from the data; the next commit to the store computes them again. With recommended=False it lists only failures: what a standard requires, or for ACDD 1.3 what it highly recommends. A store created by canVODpy has none. Without it, the lists also hold the ACDD recommendations, marked [recommended], and the FAIR advice.

Key What is checked rules Fields that break a rule of their standard, such as a license outside SPDX zarr_conventions The proj, license and stac attributes of the root group, with zarr-cm acdd The ACDD 1.3 global attributes of the root group datacite Identifier, title, creator, creation date, store type, publisher stac Identifier, title, bounding box, time range, license fair Advice only: persistent identifier, access URL, cross-references, provenance

The tests also check a day of data exported to netCDF with IOOS compliance-checker, for CF 1.11 and ACDD 1.3. Three of its findings are known and accepted. CF has no standard names for GNSS observables, UDUNITS has no unit for dB or dB-Hz, and the grid cell ids (cell_id_*) have no units because they are indices.

items.title: Change the description: amendments
items.text:
Amendable fields change only by amendment, with a reason:

canvodpy store amend ExampleSite --store gnss \
  --set identity.title="Example site GNSS-T observations" \
  --reason "Clearer title"

The command shows the changes and asks before it writes them. Each changed field is recorded with its old and new value, the reason, who (the initials in processing.metadata.initials), and when. A new commit carries the new description. Snapshots from before keep the description they were written with; show_metadata() lists the amendments made since. A fixed field is refused: a different id or creation date means a different store.

--add-receiver NAME adds a receiver of the site's settings to a GNSS store, and --add-vod-analysis NAME adds a VOD analysis to a VOD store, so runs may write them. --update-recipe NAME records a receiver's naming recipe of the settings and the sha256 of its file in the GNSS store, after the recipe changed on purpose: every run compares each recipe with the one the GNSS store records and stops on a difference. The receiver must be in the store already, or be added with --add-receiver NAME in the same amendment. --from FILE reads the changes from a YAML file. In Python, amend_metadata() does the same.

Runs set the snapshot summary and the commit metadata themselves; they are never amended.

items.title: Move an older store to the current form
items.text:
A store written before the repository metadata keeps its metadata in one root attribute. Runs refuse such a store, and the error names the command that moves all stores of its site, their folders, metadata and layout (Upgrading to v1.0.0):

canvodpy store migrate ExampleSite \
  --gnss-set identity.description="GNSS-T observations below a beech canopy"

canvodpy store migrate-metadata ExampleSite --store gnss runs the metadata step of one store alone, with --set for what it lacks. The migration writes the repository metadata, gives the store its new id and a UUID, and keeps the old id in the migration record, with who migrated it and when. A migrated store must pass the standards checks like a new one. Fields it lacks are taken from the settings, as a new store takes them: the site's store_description, the publisher and license, the site's latitude and longitude. The command marks each one (from the settings). A field neither the store nor the settings hold is given with --set; otherwise the migration is refused and lists it. A value given with --set wins over the settings, and --set FIELD= with no value is refused. A license outside SPDX, or another value that breaks a metadata rule, is refused too, naming the field to give, for example --set publisher.license=Apache-2.0. A computed value that breaks a rule, such as a duration, only warns: the migration computes it again. In a VOD store, the attributes of VOD are replaced with the current ones, and each VOD analysis the store holds a group of (tau_omega/<analysis>) is listed, with its receivers from the settings (canVODpy 0.x listed none). Snapshots from before the migration stay readable.

canVODpy 0.x stored epochs without recording their time scale. Every stored epoch is GPS time now, and a write refuses a group whose epochs don't record it (epoch.attrs["time_system"]). The migration records it where it can tell:

  • A GNSS group read from RINEX files (it holds the attribute RINEX Version) holds the epochs as the files give them, GPS time.
  • A VOD group holds the epochs of the site's GNSS store: it's GPS time when every group of that store is.
  • A GNSS group read from SBF or NMEA files holds UTC epochs, 18 s behind GPS time. The migration stops before it writes anything. The epochs aren't shifted, because the epoch grid and the satellite positions were computed for the old epochs: rebuild the store from the raw files.

Only the attribute changes; the epochs stay as stored. In Python, label_epoch_time_system() from canvod.store_metadata.migration does the same.

A GNSS store also gets its content settings (ADR 0019), the settings that shape its data, also when it was migrated before: runs refuse a GNSS store without them. The command takes them from the settings recorded in the store's first commit, and each receiver's type and reader format from the repository metadata. A setting that commit doesn't record is not guessed: the command stops and lists it.

A setting the data show is read from the data instead, because canVODpy 0.x recorded settings its runs didn't follow:

  • processing.preprocessing is none (null) when no group shows a preprocessing step. canVODpy 0.x recorded its preprocessing settings with every run, but canvodpy run never applied them.
  • store_radial_distance is whether the GNSS groups hold r; store_delta_snr and store_radial_diff are whether the site's VOD groups hold delta_snr and radial_diff (canVODpy 0.x always wrote delta_snr). Groups that disagree make the command list the setting, to give with --set.

The paired_canopies of a reference receiver is never recorded, so give it with the value the data was written with, by its key in canvod-settings.yaml:

canvodpy store migrate-metadata ExampleSite --store gnss \
  --set sites.ExampleSite.receivers.reference_01.paired_canopies=[canopy_01]

In Python, migrate_content_settings(store_path, who=..., values=...) from canvod.store_metadata.migration does the same.

A VOD store also gets its content settings (ADR 0019): the settings that shape the VOD output (its chunks and compression, store_delta_snr and store_radial_diff), plus gnss_content_hash, the content-settings hash of the GNSS store it was computed from. The migration takes the D1 keys from the store's first commit and gnss_content_hash from the site's GNSS store where the settings put it now, or else where the settings of the first commit name it, once the GNSS store has content settings. So migrate the GNSS store first; otherwise the command lists gnss_content_hash as missing, to give with --set gnss_content_hash=.... The calculator and its parameters of each group are recorded in the group's attributes (ADR 0019 D2), not in the content settings.

Content settings are never amended, with one exception. A GNSS store written with CLK files holds a clock variable, and v1.0.0 runs read no CLK files by default. canvodpy store migrate removes the variable and records fetch_clock: false; the content settings keep the change under changes, with the old value, the old hash, who made it and why. The site's VOD store then records the GNSS store's new hash, which it accepts only if the hash it held is one the GNSS store had before such a change. In Python: drop_clock() and follow_gnss_content_hash() from canvod.store_metadata.migration.

items.title: List the stores of a directory
items.text:
from pathlib import Path

from canvod.store_metadata import scan_stores

df = scan_stores(Path("/data/stores/"))
# Polars DataFrame, one row per store: id, title, store type, source format, site, ...

A store written before stores kept repository metadata gets needs_migration in its row of scan_stores(), and migrate_command gives the command that migrates it.

items.title: Write the STAC catalog
items.text:
The catalog describes every store under the data root (storage.stores_root_dir) in STAC 1.1, so that STAC Browser, pystac and other STAC tools can find the data (ADR 0015). It is written only when you ask for it:

canvodpy stac write              # the data root of the settings
canvodpy stac write --root /data/stores/
just stac-write
canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --write-catalog   # after the run's last commit

canvodpy run --write-catalog writes the catalog of the settings' data root once every site of the run is processed. If the catalog is refused (see below), the run's data stays committed and the run exits with code 1; fix the stores it names, then run canvodpy stac write. A run without the option, a dry run and a failed run write no catalog.

from pathlib import Path

from canvod.store_metadata import write_catalog

write_catalog(Path("/data/stores/"))  # returns /data/stores/catalog.json

The catalog sits beside the stores, never inside one:

/data/stores/
├── catalog.json
├── gnss-observations/
│   ├── collection.json
│   └── org.middle-earth.fangorn-gnss/org.middle-earth.fangorn-gnss.json
├── vod/
│   ├── collection.json
│   └── org.middle-earth.fangorn-vod/org.middle-earth.fangorn-vod.json
├── gnss-geodesy/                only with geodesy stores
└── Fangorn/
    ├── gnss/                    the GNSS store
    └── vod/                     the VOD store

There is one collection per product (gnss-observations, vod, gnss-geodesy) and one item per store; a site with a second store of a kind (vod-recompute) has two items in that collection. The item id is the naming authority and the store id, for example org.middle-earth.fangorn-gnss. The items of one site (its GNSS, VOD and geodesy stores, same naming authority and site name) link each other (related). A collection's extent covers all its items: their points and their time ranges. If its items have different licenses, the collection's license is other, with a link to the text of each. Every link is relative, so the whole data root can be copied or moved and the catalog still works. The store's catalog link (identity.stac_link) points at its item. A new store has the link before its item exists: until the first catalog write, validate_all(meta, store_path=...) and just metadata-validate show a warning for it, not a failure.

Each write replaces the catalog fully. It describes the stores under the root at that moment: the item of a store that is gone is removed, and so is the collection of a product with no store left. Only files the previous write made are removed; any other file stays, and releases/ (see Publish a release) is never touched. Each file is replaced in one step, so nobody reads half a file. If two writes run at once, the last one wins.

No store is left out silently. Every store under the root is read first. If any of them can't be described, nothing is written, and one error lists each such store with its reason:

❌ No catalog was written: 2 store(s) under /data/stores cannot be described.
  Moria/gnss: needs migration to the current metadata form (ADR 0014): canvodpy store migrate Moria
  Mordor/gnss: `publisher.license` 'Apache 2' is not an SPDX license identifier (see https://spdx.org/licenses/); a license outside SPDX is 'other' with license_uri; fix it with canvodpy store amend Mordor --store gnss

The reasons: the store can't be opened, has no metadata, needs migration, has no site position, has no usable license (none, not SPDX, or other without license_uri), or holds no data yet (no time coverage: a run created the store and stopped before writing). canvodpy stac write then exits with code 1.

An item has the site as a point (longitude, latitude, ellipsoidal height), the time range of the data, the store's license, its UUID (canvod:uuid), the site name (canvod:site) and the receivers with their type and position (canvod:receivers). A license outside SPDX is other, with a license link to its text (license_uri).

Each stored dataset is one asset. Asset keys join the parts of the group path with a dot, because some tools read a / in a key as a path:

Asset key What it holds Role canopy_01 a receiver's observations (group canopy_01) data canopy_01.sbf_obs its SBF metadata, if any (canopy_01/metadata/sbf_obs) metadata canopy_01.log_book its log book (canopy_01/metadata/table) metadata tau_omega_zeroth_order.canopy_01_vs_reference_01 a VOD analysis data tau_omega_zeroth_order.canopy_01_vs_reference_01.log_book its log book metadata

The group canvod (environments, kept by canvodpy) is no asset. A receiver's asset carries the receiver's position as stored: the median of its files' header positions, ECEF X, Y, Z in meters (canvod:position_ecef_m). The assets of observations, of VOD analyses, and of SBF metadata list their dimensions and variables (the STAC datacube extension: cube:dimensions, cube:variables). A coordinate that is no dimension, such as the satellite of each SID, is an auxiliary variable.

An asset names everything needed to open it: the store (href), the group (xarray:open_kwargs) and the snapshot it describes (canvod:snapshot_id):

import icechunk
import pystac
import xarray as xr

item = pystac.Item.from_file(
    "/data/stores/gnss-observations/org.middle-earth.fangorn-gnss/org.middle-earth.fangorn-gnss.json"
)
asset = item.assets["canopy_01"]
repo = icechunk.Repository.open(
    icechunk.local_filesystem_storage(asset.get_absolute_href())
)
session = repo.readonly_session(snapshot_id=asset.extra_fields["canvod:snapshot_id"])
ds = xr.open_dataset(session.store, **asset.extra_fields["xarray:open_kwargs"])

The media type of an asset is application/vnd.zarr; version=3, as the STAC best practices for Zarr recommend. xpystac can't open these assets: it opens Icechunk only from S3, and only the root group.

items.title: Publish a release
items.text:
A release is a version of the data that never changes. A paper or a data publication can cite it. It tags main in every store under the data root with the same Icechunk tag and writes the catalog of that tag under releases/<tag>/:

canvodpy stac release v2026.1    # the data root of the settings
canvodpy stac release v2026.1 --root /data/stores/
just stac-release v2026.1

from pathlib import Path

from canvod.store_metadata import create_release

create_release(Path("/data/stores/"), "v2026.1")
# returns /data/stores/releases/v2026.1/catalog.json

The release catalog has the same tree as the latest catalog, one folder deeper:

/data/stores/
├── catalog.json                 the latest catalog
└── releases/
    └── v2026.1/
        ├── catalog.json
        ├── gnss-observations/
        └── vod/

Each asset of a release names the tag (canvod:tag) and the snapshot the tag points at (canvod:snapshot_id), and has no latest-version role: that role tells the latest catalog's assets apart. Opening an asset by its tag gives the released data, whatever was written to main since:

session = repo.readonly_session(tag=asset.extra_fields["canvod:tag"])

A release refuses, before it tags anything:

  • a tag with a /: those are canvod-store's own tags (keep/<receiver>/<yyyydoy>), and releases/<tag>/ stays one folder deep;
  • a store that can't be described, with the same error as canvodpy stac write;
  • a tag that exists in some of the stores already, naming them;
  • a tag whose release catalog exists: a release catalog is never changed.

If every store has the tag but releases/<tag>/ is missing (the catalog write failed after tagging), running the release again writes only the catalog. Later catalog writes and later releases leave releases/ as it is. Release tags are written by this command only; don't create or delete them by hand.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
The canvod-utils package holds the small tools that the other canVODpy packages share:

  • dates as year and day of year, and GPS weeks;
  • file hashes, which the store uses to recognize files it already holds;
  • decorators that mark code left over from development;
  • the plugin loader, which finds readers and VOD calculators in installed packages;
  • files read from a GitHub repository at a fixed commit or tag, such as naming recipes;
  • the run identifier and the timing of the processing stages, which go into the logs.

It depends on pydantic and structlog only. The settings live in canvod-config, and the canvodpy package holds the command line.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
from canvod.utils.tools import YYYYDOY, file_hash

YYYYDOY.from_str("2025032").date  # datetime.date(2025, 2, 1)
file_hash(path)  # first 16 hex digits of the file's SHA-256

canvod.utils.tools provides these functions and classes:

Name Purpose YYYYDOY, YYDOY Parse and format a date given as year and day of year, for example 2025032 or 25032 get_gps_week_from_filename Read the GPS week from the filename of an orbit or clock product gpsweekday GPS week and day of the week of a date; a date given as a string must be dd-mm-yyyy file_hash First 16 hex digits of a file's SHA-256; the store uses it to recognize files it already holds bytes_hash The same hash for file content that is already in memory isfloat Check whether a value can be read as a float get_version_from_pyproject Read a package version from its pyproject.toml deprecated Decorator that marks code left over from development: it warns on use and names the replacement deprecated_argument Decorator that marks one argument of a function as left over from development: it warns when the argument is passed sanitize_directory Remove the files that the operating system puts into data folders, for example .DS_Store

items.title: Plugins
items.text: canvod.utils.plugins finds readers and VOD calculators that installed packages declare as entry points. plugin_names lists the plugins of a group without importing them, load_plugins imports them, and plugin_package names the package that declares a plugin. A plugin that can't be used raises PluginError, which names that package. To write a plugin, see Your own readers and VOD calculators.

items.title: Files from a GitHub link
items.text:
canvod.utils.remote_file reads a file from a GitHub repository by its raw file link, at a commit, a tag or a branch:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<repo>/<commit>/<path>
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<repo>/refs/tags/<tag>/<path>
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<account>/<repo>/refs/heads/<branch>/<path>

You are responsible for what the link points to. fetch_remote downloads the file in every run, once per run, into a folder of the run that only you can read; there is no cache, so a run needs network access. new_run starts a new run in a process that runs more than once; canvodpy.Site and the Airflow tasks call it. The run folders are removed when the process ends (the command, the notebook kernel, the Airflow worker). parse_remote_url checks a link; sibling names another file of the same repository at the same commit, tag or branch. A file in a private repository needs a GitHub token in GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN; the token goes only to raw.githubusercontent.com and never into a message or a log. A link is shown in the terminal but never recorded: recorded_name gives the file name that stores keep, and without_urls replaces the links in a text the run history keeps (a raw file link by its file name, any other link by its host). canvod-filemap reads naming recipes given as a URL with this module.

items.title: Diagnostics
items.text: canvod.utils.logging holds the run identifier (get_run_id, set_run_id, reset_run_id, new_run_id) and the stage timing (stage_timer, timed_stage, record_stage_timing, emit_run_summary, reset_run_stats), so that every canVODpy package can use them without depending on canvodpy. The log output is configured by canvodpy.logging.configure_logging. See Diagnostics.

items.title: Purpose
items.text: The canvod-viz package provides 2D and 3D hemispheric visualization for GNSS-T grids, SNR data, and VOD results. It wraps Matplotlib (publication-quality polar plots) and Plotly (interactive 3D hemispheres) behind a unified API.

items.title: Components
items.text:
• HemisphereVisualizer

    Unified entry point combining both 2D and 3D backends. Swap between publication and interactive modes with one method call.

  • HemisphereVisualizer2D

    Matplotlib polar projection plots. Patch-based rendering of grid cells. Publication-quality output at configurable DPI.

  • HemisphereVisualizer3D

    Plotly interactive 3D hemispheres. Pan, zoom, rotate in the browser. One-call HTML export for sharing.

  • Tissot Indicatrix

    add_tissot_indicatrix overlays angular distortion circles on 2D plots to evaluate grid cell shape fidelity.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Unified API (recommended)Convenience functionsPublication outputInteractive exportSide-by-side comparison 
from canvod.grids import create_hemigrid
from canvod.viz import HemisphereVisualizer

grid = create_hemigrid("equal_area", angular_resolution=10.0)
viz = HemisphereVisualizer(grid)

# Publication-quality 2D
fig_2d, ax_2d = viz.plot_2d(data=vod_data, title="VOD Distribution")

# Interactive 3D
fig_3d = viz.plot_3d(data=vod_data, title="Interactive VOD")
fig_3d.show()

from canvod.viz import visualize_grid, visualize_grid_3d, add_tissot_indicatrix

fig, ax = visualize_grid(grid, data=vod_data, cmap="viridis")
add_tissot_indicatrix(ax, grid, n_sample=5)

fig_3d = visualize_grid_3d(grid, data=vod_data)

viz = HemisphereVisualizer(grid)
viz.set_style(create_publication_style())

fig, ax = viz.create_publication_figure(
    data=vod_data,
    title="VOD Distribution",
    save_path="figure_3.png",
    dpi=600,
)

viz.set_style(create_interactive_style(dark_mode=True))

fig = viz.create_interactive_explorer(
    data=vod_data,
    dark_mode=True,
    save_html="explorer.html",
)

(fig_2d, ax_2d), fig_3d = viz.create_comparison_plot(data=vod_data)

Cells without data

Cells without data (NaN) are not part of the color scale: 2D plots leave them white, the 3D views draw them in nan_color (default "lightgray"), so they never look like the minimum value. plot_3d_mesh draws HTM grids one triangle at a time and every other grid like plot_3d.

add_spherical_overlays(fig, elevation_rings=...) takes elevation angles in degrees (0 = horizon, 90 = zenith); the default draws rings at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75 degrees.

items.title: Styling
items.text:
Style factory Use case create_publication_style() Print-ready figures, configurable DPI, white background create_interactive_style() Browser-ready Plotly, dark mode option create_rse_style() Remote Sensing of Environment journal guidelines

Each returns a PlotStyle, passed to viz.set_style(); PlotStyle.to_polar_style() gives the PolarPlotStyle the 2D functions take.

items.title: RSE journal style
items.text:
Publication-quality styling matching Remote Sensing of Environment guidelines, with Arial or Helvetica fonts, 300 DPI, inward ticks, colorblind-friendly palette (Wong, 2011).

Context managerDecoratorGlobal apply 
from canvod.viz import rse_context

with rse_context():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(x, y)

from canvod.viz import rse_style


@rse_style
def make_figure():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(x, y)
    return fig, [ax]

from canvod.viz import apply_rse_style

apply_rse_style()  # modifies plt.rcParams globally

items.title: Colorscale
items.text:
Colormaps converted between Matplotlib and Plotly:

from canvod.viz import Colorscale

cs = Colorscale.from_matplotlib("viridis", n_colors=64)
plotly_cs = cs.to_plotly()  # [(0.0, 'rgb(...)'), ...]
mpl_cmap = cs.to_matplotlib()  # LinearSegmentedColormap

cs2 = Colorscale.from_colors(["#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"])

items.title: Interactive grid exploration
items.text:
The demo/15_grid_exploration.py marimo notebook shows interactive exploration of per-cell VOD on the hemispheric grid, with synthetic data (real per-cell time series come from canvod.store.AnalysisStorage.load_percell_timeseries()):

  • 3D view: Plotly Scatter3d with click-to-select cells (anywidget)
  • 2D view: canvas polar projection with hover tooltips (anywidget)
  • Reactive stats: selected cells display in a table with mean, std, count, and coverage
  • Time series: per-cell VOD time series plotted for selected cells
just open-notebook 15_grid_exploration.py

items.title: Interactive selectors in notebooks
items.text:
canvod.viz.widgets provides two interactive hemisphere selectors for marimo (and Jupyter) notebooks, built on anywidget. Click the cells of a hemisphere grid to select them; hover a cell for its info. The selectors need the optional extra:

pip install "canvod-viz[widgets]"

uv add "canvod-viz[widgets]"

Example (the 3D selector from demo/15_grid_exploration.py):

import marimo as mo
from canvod.viz.widgets import HemisphereSelector3D

hemisphere_3d = mo.ui.anywidget(
    HemisphereSelector3D(
        cell_centers_x=cell_x.tolist(),
        cell_centers_y=cell_y.tolist(),
        cell_centers_z=cell_z.tolist(),
        cell_values=values.tolist(),
        cell_labels=labels,
        colorscale="Viridis",
        marker_size=6,
    )
)
mo.output.replace(hemisphere_3d)

HemisphereSelector2D takes cell_theta, cell_phi, cell_values and cell_labels instead. Both expose selected_cell_ids (the indices of the selected cells) and hovered_cell_id.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
Backends

  • Matplotlib (2D) and Plotly (3D), installed with canvod-viz
  • canvod-grids: grid geometry, installed with canvod-viz
  • anywidget: only for the interactive hemisphere selectors in the marimo notebooks; installed only with the optional extra widgets (pip install "canvod-viz[widgets]"), not by default

items.title: Purpose
items.text: The canvod-vod package implements vegetation optical depth (VOD) estimation from GNSS signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) data. It provides the core scientific algorithms for the canVODpy analysis pipeline.

items.title: Physical background
items.text:
Tau-Omega Radiative Transfer Model

canvod-vod implements the zeroth-order tau-omega model for GNSS-Transmissometry, following Humphrey & Frankenberg (2022).

A reference receiver in open sky and a canopy receiver beneath vegetation observe the same satellite at polar angle \(\theta\). The SNR difference encodes the two-way canopy attenuation:

\[\Delta\text{SNR} = \text{SNR}_\text{canopy} - \text{SNR}_\text{reference}\] \[T = 10^{\Delta\text{SNR} / 10} \qquad \text{(linear transmissivity)}\] \[\text{VOD} = -\ln(T) \cdot \cos\theta\]

Assumptions: - Single-scattering approximation (no multiple canopy reflections) - Plane-parallel canopy layer - Attenuation proportional to path length through canopy

items.title: Usage
items.text:
In a run, VOD is computed by VodComputer (Site(site).vod, canvodpy run, canvodpy vod): it picks the configured canopy/reference pairs and days, calls the calculator and writes the VOD store. Use the calculator directly only for your own analyses.

Direct instantiationFrom two datasetsFrom the GNSS store 
from canvod.vod import TauOmegaZerothOrder

calculator = TauOmegaZerothOrder(canopy_ds=canopy_ds, sky_ds=sky_ds)
vod_result = calculator.calculate_vod()

from canvod.vod import TauOmegaZerothOrder

# Aligns both datasets on their shared epochs and signals
vod_result = TauOmegaZerothOrder.from_datasets(
    canopy_ds=canopy_ds,
    sky_ds=sky_ds,
)

from datetime import datetime

from canvodpy import Site

# Computes the days of the range in the worker pool, writes them to
# the VOD store and returns the VOD from start to end (write=False
# computes in memory and writes nothing)
vod_result = Site("ExampleSite").vod.compute_bulk(
    "canopy_01_vs_reference_01",
    start=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    end=datetime(2025, 1, 31, 23, 59, 59),
)

Input requirements

Both datasets must contain an SNR data variable on (epoch, sid), and the canopy dataset the polar angle theta (radians) from canvod-auxiliary. The result passes canvod.readers.validate_vod_dataset, which the VOD store checks on every write.

Calculator parameters and the GNSS store

VodComputer(site, calculator=..., calculator_params=...) passes calculator_params to the calculator. On the first write to a VOD group {calculator}/{analysis}, VodComputer records the calculator and its parameters in the group's attributes; every later write compares them, and a group never holds results computed with other parameters (ADR 0019 D2). The VOD store also records the content-settings hash of the GNSS store it was computed from (gnss_content_hash, ADR 0019 D1/D3): a run that reads a GNSS store with other content settings stops before anything is written.

items.title: Output
items.text:
calculate_vod() returns an xr.Dataset containing:

Variable Description VOD Vegetation optical depth phi Azimuth angles (from canopy dataset) theta Polar angles (from canopy dataset)

items.title: One reference receiver, several canopy receivers
items.text:
When a single reference receiver serves multiple canopy positions, satellite geometry must be recomputed relative to each canopy location. The paired_canopies field in canvod-settings.yaml (sites.<name>.receivers.<ref>.paired_canopies) drives this: the reference data is stored once per paired canopy, in the group {reference}_{canopy}.

flowchart TD
    subgraph FIELD["Field Setup"]
        C1["`**Canopy 1**
        NE position`"]
        C2["`**Canopy 2**
        SW position`"]
        R1["`**Reference**
        open sky`"]
    end

    subgraph STORE["GNSS Store Groups"]
        SG1["canopy_01"]
        SG2["canopy_02"]
        SG3["`**reference_01_canopy_01**
        geometry at canopy_01 pos.`"]
        SG4["`**reference_01_canopy_02**
        geometry at canopy_02 pos.`"]
    end

    subgraph VOD["VOD Analysis Pairs"]
        VP1["canopy_01 vs reference_01_canopy_01"]
        VP2["canopy_02 vs reference_01_canopy_02"]
    end

    C1 --> SG1
    C2 --> SG2
    R1 --> SG3
    R1 --> SG4
    SG1 --> VP1
    SG3 --> VP1
    SG2 --> VP2
    SG4 --> VP2
    VP1 --> V1["VOD @ canopy_01"]
    VP2 --> V2["VOD @ canopy_02"]

Configuration

# config/canvod-settings.yaml (sites.<name>.receivers)
receivers:
  reference_01:
    type: reference
    paired_canopies:   # or: all
      - canopy_01    # recompute geometry at canopy_01 position
      - canopy_02    # recompute geometry at canopy_02 position

items.title: Your own VOD model
items.text: A VOD calculator of your own inherits VODCalculator and implements calculate_vod(). Installed as a plugin package, it is a choice of canvodpy run --vod-calculator; see Your Own Readers and VOD Calculators.

items.title: References
items.text: Humphrey, V. and Frankenberg, C. (2022). GNSS-transmissometry: A new approach for vegetation optical depth estimation. Remote Sensing of Environment.

items.title: Retrieve VOD from your GNSS data
items.text:
Upgrading from 0.x?

Migrate your stores and check your settings first: Upgrading to v1.0.0.

There are two ways to run canVODpy, and they're equivalent:

  • From the command line, with canvodpy run. This suits processing a whole period without supervision, for example on a server.
  • From Python, with Site.pipeline(), in a script or a notebook. This suits trying things out and going straight on to analysis.

Both run the same processing, read the same settings file, and write the same stores. They also need the same setup, which this page goes through step by step:

  1. Before you start
  2. Install canVODpy
  3. Create the settings file
  4. Point canVODpy to your data
  5. Check the settings and the data
  6. Process one day
  7. Process a period
  8. Open the VOD

Where the two ways differ, the steps show a Python and a Command line tab. Choosing a tab switches all tabs on the page.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
You need:

  • GNSS data from two receivers at one site: one below the canopy and one with an unobstructed view of the sky, recording the same signals at the same time. canVODpy derives VOD from the difference in their signal-to-noise ratios; VOD retrieval explains the method.
  • A terminal: Terminal on macOS, a shell on Linux, or PowerShell on Windows. All commands on this page are typed there.
  • uv, the tool that installs canVODpy and Python for you. Follow the uv installation guide. canVODpy needs Python 3.14; if you don't have it, uv downloads it.
  • An internet connection during processing, to download the satellite orbits and clocks.
No data of your own yet? Use the demo data

canvodpy.demo_data() downloads one day of the Rosalia site from Hugging Face: a receiver below the canopy and a reference receiver, on 2025-01-01. It downloads only the kind of data you ask for, checks each archive against its sha256, and keeps the files in your user cache folder, so a second call needs no network.

from canvodpy import demo_data

root = demo_data("rinex")  # RINEX v3.04, the whole day
root = demo_data("sbf")  # SBF, 00:00 to 02:00
root = demo_data("aux")  # SP3 orbits, CLK clocks, auxiliary store

These three return the same folder. In it, the RINEX files of the two receivers are in rinex_v3_04/01_Rosalia/01_reference and rinex_v3_04/01_Rosalia/02_canopy, the SBF files in sbf/01_Rosalia/01_reference and sbf/01_Rosalia/02_canopy. Use the site folder as gnss_site_data_root and the receiver folders as directory in step 3. The pipeline still downloads the orbits and clocks from the agencies; the "aux" files are a copy for when that fails.

demo_data("stores") downloads the GNSS store and the VOD store that canVODpy writes from the RINEX day, to look at a store without a run first. They are in stores/rosalia_rinex_v3_04/gnss and stores/rosalia_rinex_v3_04/vod of the folder it returns. Copy them before you write to them: the next call returns the same folder.

items.title: 1. Install canVODpy
items.text:
PythonCommand line

Add canVODpy to the uv project you work in. A uv project is a folder with a pyproject.toml file that lists the packages your code needs; uv keeps them in an environment of their own in that folder. If you don't have a project yet, create one (see Working on projects):

uv init my-analysis && cd my-analysis

Then add canVODpy:

uv add canvodpy

Your scripts and notebooks in the project can now import canvodpy.

This also installs the canvodpy command into the environment of the project. Run it through uv, from inside the project:

uv run canvodpy --help

This page writes the commands as canvodpy ...; in a project, type uv run canvodpy ....

Install canVODpy as a uv tool:

uv tool install canvodpy
uv tool update-shell   # once: puts the tool folder on your PATH

uv installs canVODpy into an environment of its own and puts the canvodpy command into a folder on your PATH, the list of folders in which the terminal looks for commands (see Using tools). Open a new terminal, and you can run the command from any folder, without uv run:

canvodpy --help

To update or remove the tool, run uv tool upgrade canvodpy or uv tool uninstall canvodpy.

Run the command from a clone of the repository

To have canvodpy on your PATH and follow your local edits, link the command from the environment of the clone:

cd /path/to/canvodpy && uv sync
ln -s "$(pwd)/.venv/bin/canvodpy" ~/.local/bin/canvodpy

After git pull, run uv sync again; the link stays valid. If you move the clone, recreate the environment and the link:

rm -rf .venv && uv sync
ln -sf "$(pwd)/.venv/bin/canvodpy" ~/.local/bin/canvodpy

To remove the command, delete the link: rm ~/.local/bin/canvodpy.

items.title: 2. Create the settings file
items.text:
canVODpy needs to know where your data is, who you are, and which receivers to compare. It reads all of this from one file, canvod-settings.yaml. The file is in YAML, a plain text format in which each line holds a name: value pair and the indentation, with spaces, shows which setting belongs to which section. The file has three sections:

Section What it sets processing: Your name and institution for the metadata, where to write the stores and the log files, ephemeris products, and processing parameters sites: Your sites, the folder of each receiver, and the receiver pairs to compute VOD for sids: The signals to keep

Only a few settings are required; the minimal example shows them. All others have defaults.

The settings wizard creates the file for you. It asks for your name, your email address, your institution, the folder for the stores, the folder for the log files, your site, and the folders of the two receivers. Then it writes the file and checks it:

canvodpy config init --interactive

To see what a question sets, answer ?: the wizard prints the setting's description and asks again.

Without --interactive, the command copies the template and you fill it in yourself, with canvodpy config edit or any text editor. Each setting in the template has a link to its entry in the Settings reference, and canvodpy config explain SETTING prints that entry in the terminal.

items.title: Where the file is
items.text:
canVODpy looks for the settings file in this order:

  1. The folder in the environment variable CANVOD_CONFIG_DIR, or the folder you give with --config-dir.
  2. The config/ folder of a canVODpy clone, if you work in one.
  3. ~/.config/canvodpy/ (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/canvodpy/).

To see which file canVODpy found and whether it's valid, run:

canvodpy doctor

Python finds the file the same way: Site("ExampleSite") reads the site from the file that canvodpy doctor names.

The Configuration guide describes every setting and how to keep machine-specific settings in a separate file.

Try it in a notebook

Open Configuration in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: 3. Point canVODpy to your data
items.text:
Each site has a data folder, gnss_site_data_root. Each receiver has a folder of its own inside it, directory:

sites:
  ExampleSite:
    gnss_site_data_root: /data/ExampleSite
    receivers:
      reference_01:
        type: reference          # the receiver with an unobstructed view of the sky
        directory: 01_reference
        paired_canopies: all
      canopy_01:
        type: canopy             # the receiver below the canopy
        directory: 02_canopy
    vod_analyses:
      canopy_01_vs_reference_01:
        canopy_receiver: canopy_01
        reference_receiver: reference_01

Inside a receiver folder, the layout is up to you: all files in one folder, one folder per day, or deeper. Keep the files of each receiver in their own folder.

items.title: File names
items.text:
canVODpy takes the receiver and the day of each file from its name, so the files must follow the canVOD file naming convention, for example:

FANR01INK_R_20250010000_01D_05S_AA.rnx

This name says: site FAN, reference receiver 01, data from The Inklings, starting on day 001 of 2025 at 00:00, one day of data, sampled every 5 seconds, in RINEX. The file naming convention explains each field.

Try it in a notebook

Open Naming convention in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

If your files have other names, for example the names your receiver gives them, you don't have to rename them. A naming recipe maps them to the convention; it needs the optional canvod-filemap extension (see Optional extensions).

canVODpy reads RINEX v2.11, RINEX v3.04, Septentrio SBF, and NMEA files. It doesn't read compressed files, including Hatanaka-compressed RINEX; decompress them first. The canopy receiver and the reference receiver must record the same file format.

items.title: Ephemeris products
items.text: To compute where each satellite was, canVODpy downloads precise satellite orbits (SP3 files) and clocks (CLK files) from the European Space Agency (ESA). This needs no account and no setup. To add the NASA Crustal Dynamics Data Information System (CDDIS) as a fallback, see Ephemeris data sources.

items.title: 4. Check the settings and the data
items.text:
Before the first run, check one site:

canvodpy config validate --site ExampleSite

The check finds the files of each receiver exactly as a run does. It lists the days and files a run would process, the files it would skip, and the problems that would stop the run, for example two files that cover the same time.

items.title: 5. Process one day
items.text:
canVODpy names a day by its year and day of year, as YYYYDDD. For example, 2025001 is January 1, 2025 and 2025032 is February 1, 2025.

PythonCommand line 
from canvodpy import Site

site = Site("ExampleSite")
with site.pipeline() as pipeline:
    for unit in pipeline.run("2025001", "2025001"):
        print(unit.days, unit.vod.written)

run reads the files of each receiver, adds the satellite positions from the ephemeris products, and writes the observations to the site's Icechunk store. Then it computes VOD for every receiver pair in vod_analyses and writes it to the site's VOD store. To work with the observations in Python, pipeline.process_date("2025001") returns one dataset per receiver, read back from the store.

canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --start 2025001 --end 2025001

The run reads the files of each receiver, adds the satellite positions from the ephemeris products, writes the observations to the site's Icechunk store, and computes VOD for every receiver pair in vod_analyses and writes it to the site's VOD store.

Before it reads a file, a run finds the files of every receiver in the site. On a network drive this can take minutes. The CLI says, for each receiver, which folder it is scanning, and afterwards how many files and days it found, so you can see that the run is working. The next run is faster: it lists only the folders of the days it processes and takes the others from a file index.

To see what a run would process without running it, add --dry-run.

Files that are already in the store are skipped.

Try it in a notebook

Open Site pipeline, Running the pipeline from the command line in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: 6. Process a period
items.text:
PythonCommand line

run processes the days in units of several days and yields what it stored and computed for each unit:

with site.pipeline() as pipeline:
    for unit in pipeline.run("2025001", "2025031"):
        print(sorted(unit.days), unit.vod.missing)

process_range("2025001", "2025031") yields the datasets of one day at a time instead, read back from the store.

canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --start 2025001 --end 2025031

Leave out --end and the run processes up to today. Once the store holds data, --update-to-latest instead of the dates processes the days from the last stored day up to the latest files:

canvodpy run --site ExampleSite --update-to-latest

A run processes one site; for several, run it once per site (Several sites).

By default, canVODpy uses all but two of the machine's CPU cores. To set limits, see Parallel processing.

To follow a long run while it's in progress, add --dashboard. It opens the performance dashboard, which shows how long each step took per day and receiver. The diagnostics guide explains it under See where a run spends its time.

Try it in a notebook

Open Batch processing in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.

items.title: 7. Open the VOD
items.text:
However you processed the data, the VOD is in the site's VOD store, and you open it in Python. The store is an Icechunk repository, which keeps a history of every write, like git:

from canvodpy import Site

site = Site("ExampleSite")
site.vod_store.print_tree()
vod = site.vod_store.read_group("tau_omega/canopy_01_vs_reference_01")

Each receiver pair has one group, <VOD calculator>/<entry in vod_analyses>. print_tree lists them. read_group returns an xarray Dataset, with VOD per time and signal.

To look at the stores from the command line, without opening Python:

canvodpy store list                          # every site's stores and their status
canvodpy store info ExampleSite --store vod  # the groups of the VOD store
canvodpy store log ExampleSite --store vod   # the history of its writes

Try it in a notebook

Open VOD retrieval, Icechunk store in molab, the online notebook service of marimo.
